The layout behind the benefit

A file contains row groups, each holding a batch of records. Inside a row group, values are separated into column chunks. A reader asking for country and amount can locate those chunks without loading every other field.

The file footer stores metadata describing the schema and where the columns are located. Available column statistics can help the reader decide which row groups are relevant.

Smaller storage, less repeated work

Similar values within a column are good candidates for encoding, such as representing repeated country names with compact codes, and compression, which reduces stored size further.

Parquet fits cleaned datasets, historical reporting, and data shared across analytical tools. It is especially useful when queries repeatedly scan many records but select a subset of fields.

> On the job: Parquet is the default storage file for lakehouses (Fabric, Databricks, Snowflake external tables, BigQuery external data). Most of the files your pipelines write will be Parquet, often inside a Delta or Iceberg table.

Remember: Parquet's value comes from typed storage, efficient compression, and the ability to read less data for a query.

Sources: Parquet file structure, Parquet motivation, Parquet logical types.

passages.heading: 12. How a Parquet query reads less
passages.text:
Parquet in practice · projection and filter pushdown

Suppose the three orders are stored in orders.parquet. In DuckDB, this query asks for sales by country:

Select the columns you need

SELECT country, SUM(amount) AS total_sales
FROM read_parquet('orders.parquet')
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY country;

The result is GB = 40 and US = 40. Only country and amount are needed. Projection pushdown means the engine passes that column selection to the reader, so it can avoid loading order_id.

Use filters to skip sections

Now imagine a much larger file and a filter WHERE amount >= 100. If a row group's recorded maximum amount is 40, it cannot contain a match and may be skipped.

This is one benefit of filter pushdown: the engine gives the condition to the reader early. Skipping requires useful statistics; groups that might contain a match still need their values checked.

> On the job: Selecting only the columns you need and filtering on partition or sorted columns is how you keep scans, and cloud bills, small. EXPLAIN output and query profiles in Fabric, Databricks or Snowflake show how many files and bytes were actually read.

Remember: selecting fewer columns and filtering on well-organized data can reduce reading. The format enables this; the query engine implements it.

Sources: DuckDB Parquet projection and filter pushdown.

passages.heading: 13. ORC: columnar storage with built-in indexes
passages.text:
File formats · .orc · Optimized Row Columnar

ORC is a typed, binary, columnar format developed for analytical workloads in Apache Hive. Like Parquet, it combines efficient compression with selective reading and can represent nested data.

Stripes and statistics

An ORC file is divided into stripes, batches of rows with their columns stored separately. Statistics at several levels describe the values, helping readers skip parts that cannot match a query.

For example, a report filtered to recent order dates may avoid older stripes when their date ranges rule out a match. These indexes help reduce scans; they are not the same as a database index that directly locates an individual order.

Choosing between ORC and Parquet

ORC is a strong fit when a Hive-based platform already uses it effectively. Parquet is a common choice across general analytical tooling. Both target similar problems, so the engine and workload matter more than a universal speed ranking.

For a real comparison, use representative queries: selected columns, typical filters, and your actual data. A full-table read alone may hide the benefits you care about.

Remember: ORC's strengths are efficient column storage and metadata-assisted skipping in compatible analytical systems.

Sources: ORC background, ORC indexes.

passages.heading: 14. Match the file format to the workload
passages.text:
Choose a file · match it to the job

These are common starting points, not exclusive uses. The same orders may move through more than one format.

| Format | Main strength | Reach for it when… |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CSV | A simple table that many tools can open | You are sharing an export with a person or partner. |
| JSON | Named values, nested groups, and lists | You receive data from an API or application. |
| Avro | Compact records with a shared schema | Your event pipeline exchanges many structured records. |
| Parquet | Efficient storage and column-based reading | You keep cleaned data for repeated analysis. |
| ORC | Efficient column-based reading in compatible platforms | Your Hive-based reporting environment already uses ORC. |

Remember: first ask, “Am I sharing a file, receiving application data, moving events, or building reports?” That narrows the choice.

Sources: CSV specification, Avro introduction, Parquet overview.

passages.heading: 15. A practical conversion: CSV to typed Parquet
passages.text:
Hands-on · specify types, then verify the result

Save the three sample orders as orders.csv. Run the following in DuckDB from the folder containing the file. The output is a Parquet file that you can query repeatedly.

Write with an explicit schema

COPY (
  SELECT * FROM read_csv('orders.csv',
    header = true,
    columns = {
      'order_id': 'VARCHAR',
      'country': 'VARCHAR',
      'amount': 'DECIMAL(12,2)'
    })
) TO 'orders.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET);

VARCHAR keeps IDs as text. DECIMAL(12,2) reserves 12 digits in total, including two after the decimal point, for exact monetary values.

Check meaning as well as storage

SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders,
       SUM(amount) AS total
FROM read_parquet('orders.parquet');
-- Expected: 3 orders, total 80.00

Also compare field types and a few records. Changing the format should preserve your intended values and row count. This tiny example checks correctness; it is too small for a meaningful speed comparison.

> On the job: Converting landed CSV to typed Parquet (or a Delta table) is one of the first transformations in nearly every pipeline. Checking row counts and a control total after the conversion is the habit that catches type and parsing mistakes.

Remember: converting to Parquet gives typed analytical storage. Creating a managed Delta, Iceberg, or Hudi table is an additional step.

Sources: DuckDB CSV reader, DuckDB Parquet export.

passages.heading: 16. Scenarios: evaluate the tradeoff
passages.text:
Scenarios · reveal the reasoning behind each choice

Each situation suggests a starting point. There can be other valid choices depending on the tools already in use.

A colleague wants a small list of orders to open in Excel.

Start with CSV. The data is a simple table, and the recipient needs a widely supported export.

A shop API sends one order with a customer and a list of items.

Expect JSON. Its objects and arrays can keep those related details together.

You run the same sales summaries over a growing historical dataset.

Start with Parquet. Its column layout helps readers select the fields needed by reports, and it supports efficient compression.

An event pipeline sends millions of small, typed order messages, and producers and consumers are deployed separately.

Consider Avro with a schema registry. Records are compact, and compatible schema changes can be checked before a producer breaks a consumer.

Remember: a useful answer includes both a format and a reason tied to the task.

Sources: CSV specification, Parquet overview.

passages.heading: 17. Glossary: working vocabulary
passages.text:
Quick reference · connect the terms to their purpose

| Term | What it means in practice |
|---|---|
| Schema / schema evolution | The expected fields and types / supported changes to that structure over time. |
| Grain / record key | What one row represents / the value that identifies a record for matching updates. |
| Projection / filter pushdown | Pass column selections / conditions to the reader so it can reduce work. |
| Row group / stripe | A batch of records stored in columnar form inside Parquet / ORC. |
| Partitioning | Group data by a useful dimension, such as date, so queries can avoid unrelated groups. |
| Schema registry | Shared schema storage used by message producers and consumers. |

passages.heading: 18. Recap: connect storage choices to pipeline design
passages.text:
Recap · connect each name to a practical job

1. A file format is a representation: text or binary, rows or columns, schema embedded or supplied.
2. CSV is for sharing flat tables; declare types on import so IDs, dates and money survive.
3. JSON keeps nested application data; choose the reporting grain before flattening it.
4. Avro carries compact typed records with a schema that both sides agree on and evolve compatibly.
5. Parquet and ORC store values by column, so analytical queries read fewer bytes; select only the columns you need.

Five ways to represent data

CSV makes a simple table easy to share. JSON represents named values, groups, and lists from applications. Avro carries compact records with an agreed schema.

Parquet and ORC group values by column to support analysis. Parquet has broad analytical tool support; ORC is a strong fit in compatible Hive-based environments.

What comes next

Files hold data; they do not manage a changing table. Updates, consistent versions and history are the job of a table format (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi), covered in the Table formats deck.

Remember: explain the job first, then choose the format: share a table, receive application data, move events, or store for analysis.

passages.heading: 19. References: further reading, when you need it
passages.text:
References · optional next steps

The shop examples connect format design to practical workloads. These references provide implementation detail when you need it; sources are also linked beside the relevant explanations.

- CSV specification and JSON specification: the rules behind the two text formats.
- Avro introduction: schemas and records.
- Parquet overview and ORC background: formats designed for analysis.
- DuckDB: reading Parquet: try a query on a local file.

A readable overview on Medium, “A comprehensive guide to file formats in data engineering”, inspired the explanatory style. Technical explanations here use the project documentation linked above. Format choices are practical guidance, not universal performance rankings.

passages.heading: 20. Cheat sheet: file formats
passages.text:
Keep this slide · five file formats

File formats organize values inside files or messages. Table formats coordinate data files, schemas, and table versions. They work together: a Delta table, for example, stores its data in Parquet.

File formats — representation, structure, and fit

| Format | Layout & schema | Strong fit | Useful tradeoff |
|---|---|---|---|
| CSV .csv | Flat text records; types supplied or inferred on import. | Portable exports, partner exchange, simple reference tables. | Easy to inspect; repeated parsing and no embedded column statistics. |
| JSON .json | Text objects and arrays; basic value types, optional external schema. | APIs, application events, nested source data. | Flexible structure; validate types and choose a reporting grain. |
| Avro .avro | Binary records; schema embedded in container files or shared for messages. | Event streams, complete-record exchange, compatible schema evolution. | Compact and compressible; readers need the writer’s schema. |
| Parquet .parquet | Binary columns within row groups; embedded types and metadata. | Repeated analytics, historical datasets, broad analytical tool use. | Compression and selective reads; managed row updates require another layer. |
| ORC .orc | Binary columns within stripes; embedded types, statistics, and indexes. | Hive-based analytics and compatible SQL platforms. | Efficient compression and skipping; choose according to engine support. |

Decision shortcuts: share a flat table → CSV · exchange nested application data → JSON · send typed events → Avro · store for analysis → Parquet / ORC · maintain a changing lake table → a table format (next deck).

Terms to retain: pushdown = let the reader use selected columns or filters early · partitioning = group data to narrow reads · row group / stripe = the batch inside a columnar file.

passages.heading: Table formats: Delta, Iceberg, Hudi & CDC
passages.text:
Companion to data-table-formats.html: the same lessons with the same numbering.

This deck has no runnable code; it explains concepts with the same three sample orders. Format features and engine support change between versions, so check the linked project documentation for the version you use. This deck is one half of the former “Data formats in practice” guide (the other half is File formats).

Additions in this split: On-the-job notes on the main lessons, two table-format scenarios, and a table-format cheat sheet.

passages.heading: 1. Table formats
passages.text:
A folder of Parquet files is not yet a table you can update safely. Table formats add the bookkeeping: which files are current, how a change is committed, and how to read an earlier version.

Explore Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi, and the change data capture (CDC) pipelines that feed them. It builds on the File formats deck.

- From files to tables: Table formats. Track the current files, commit changes, keep versions
- The three formats: Delta · Iceberg · Hudi. Transaction log, snapshots and catalogs, record-level updates
- Feeding the table: Change data capture. Keep a copy in step with database changes
- Put it together: Choose by workload. How file and table formats work together in a pipeline

Part of a split series. This deck is the second half of the former “Data formats in practice” guide; the first half is File formats.

Added in this split: On-the-job notes on each format, two table-format scenarios (shared tables, recovery with time travel), and a table-format cheat sheet.

Prefer an article? Select Read to see every lesson together, or Markdown ↗ for the companion.

passages.heading: Why this matters · Why this matters on the job
passages.text:
Why this matters · the need behind the topic

Parquet files alone cannot tell a reader which files make up today’s table, apply an update safely, or show yesterday’s version. Table formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi) add that bookkeeping, and they are the storage layer of every modern lakehouse, including Fabric and Databricks.

Where you will use it

- Fabric lakehouses and Databricks: every managed table is a Delta table.
- MERGE-based loads of CDC and deduplicated batches into Silver tables.
- Recovering from a bad load with table history (time travel).

What goes wrong without it

- Readers see half-written data while a job is still writing files.
- Updates rewritten by hand as “delete the folder and reload everything”.
- Two engines disagree about which files belong to the table.

Who expects you to know it

- Data engineers and platform engineers running lakehouses.
- Interviewers: “how does the Delta log give ACID?”, “Delta vs Iceberg?”, “what is CDC?”.

> On the job: A nightly job merges corrected orders into a Delta table. One night the source sends bad data; you query the previous version to confirm, restore it, fix the input and re-run. Without a table format this would be a manual file-level recovery.

> The main idea: table formats turn folders of files into tables with commits, versions and updates; they are the backbone of the lakehouse.

Read more: Delta Lake documentation, Fabric: lakehouse and Delta tables.

passages.heading: Why this matters · When to reach for it, and when not to
passages.text:
Why this matters · choosing the right tool

| Situation | Reach for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Spark, Databricks or Fabric pipelines | Delta Lake | Native support, MERGE, time travel |
| One table shared by several engines | Apache Iceberg with a catalog | Engine-neutral metadata, hidden partitioning |
| Frequent record-level upserts from CDC | Hudi (or Delta / Iceberg with MERGE) | Built around record keys and incremental pulls |
| Keep a copy of an operational database current | Log-based CDC into a table format | Applies inserts, updates and deletes in order |
| Static files that never change | Plain Parquet files | A table format adds little |

How interviews test it

- “How does a transaction log make writes atomic?”
- “Delta vs Iceberg vs Hudi: how would you choose?”
- “What is CDC, and how do you apply it to a lake table?”

Where it sits in your learning path

- Builds on: File formats (Parquet in particular).
- Next: Delta Lake operations in Spark (MERGE, OPTIMIZE, VACUUM) and storage architecture (lake, warehouse, lakehouse).
- Later: ingestion tools and CDC in practice.

> The main idea: use a table format whenever a lake table changes over time or is shared; keep plain files for static exchange.

passages.heading: 2. One dataset, several workloads
passages.text:
Foundations · follow the orders through a pipeline

We will use the same orders throughout. Amounts are in US dollars, and each row represents one order. This is the table's grain: what a single record represents.

| order_id | country | amount |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 101 | US | 25.00 |
| 102 | GB | 40.00 |
| 103 | US | 15.00 |

Exchanging complete records

A partner needs a daily export. An application sends a new order. A payment service publishes a status change. These jobs usually move complete records, so readability, message size, and an agreed structure matter.

Analyzing and maintaining a dataset

A report totals sales across millions of orders but reads only a few columns. Meanwhile, refunds change existing records. Now selective reading, efficient storage, and consistent updates become important.

Remember: choose a format for the work being done with the data. The same dataset can use several formats at different stages.

Sources: Parquet overview, DuckDB CSV import settings.

passages.heading: 3. From one file to a table that keeps changing
passages.text:
Table formats · why we need another idea

Our shop grows. Orders are now saved across many files in cloud storage. A data lake is a place where a team stores datasets as files, often in a service such as Amazon S3.

Yesterday was straightforward

A report reads yesterday's saved orders and adds up the amounts. If those orders are fixed, a collection of Parquet files may be enough for the job.

Today, order 101 is refunded. We need to change its status. New orders are also arriving while someone runs a report.

Now we need coordination

Which files contain the current orders? When is an update complete? Can a report see one consistent version while changes are happening?

A table format adds bookkeeping and rules around the data files. Delta Lake, Iceberg, and Hudi help tools manage those files as a changing table.

A lakehouse brings table-management features to data kept in a lake, allowing file storage and database-like operations to work together.

Remember: the file format handles the contents of individual files. The table format helps manage the whole table over time.

Sources: Delta Lake introduction, Iceberg introduction.

passages.heading: 4. A table format keeps track of the current data
passages.text:
Table formats · a concrete example of a table version

Imagine a simplified table with two files. One contains order 101; another contains orders 102 and 103. To record the refund, our tool writes a replacement for the first file and records a new table version.

Version 1: original order 101 + orders 102 and 103
Version 2: refunded order 101 + orders 102 and 103
The table's bookkeeping tells the reader which files to use.

The bookkeeping is called metadata: information describing the data, such as its schema and which files belong to a version. A snapshot is a particular version of the table.

A commit publishes the new version after its data is ready. The unchanged file can be reused across both versions; each snapshot does not need a complete copy of the table.

> On the job: In a Fabric lakehouse or Databricks workspace every managed table is a Delta table: Parquet files plus a log. Knowing what the log tracks explains why you should not add or delete files in the table folder by hand.

Remember: Parquet and a table format can work together. Parquet holds the order values; the table format records how the files make up the table. The diagram is one simplified update strategy.

Sources: Delta table versions, Iceberg reliability.

passages.heading: 5. Transactions, versions, and schema changes
passages.text:
Table formats · what a managed table adds

Table formats give compatible engines rules for coordinating files, updates, and metadata. Their value becomes clear when several jobs read or change the same dataset.

Publish a complete change

A transaction publishes a set of changes together. A refund job might write several files before committing the new version. Readers can keep using a consistent snapshot while that work completes.

This is part of ACID behavior: atomicity (all-or-nothing changes), consistency (declared rules remain valid), isolation (concurrent work is coordinated), and durability (committed changes persist). These guarantees do not prove that a business calculation is correct.

Evolve and reproduce the table

Schema enforcement checks incoming structure; schema evolution permits supported changes, such as adding a column. Their exact behavior depends on the engine and configuration.

Time travel queries an earlier version so a report can be reproduced. Both its metadata and required data files must still be retained. An upsert updates a matching record or inserts a new one.

> On the job: Atomic commits are why a failed nightly load does not leave half-written data for the morning dashboard, and versions are how you answer “what did this table look like yesterday?” during an incident.

Remember: table formats add coordinated changes and table-level structure around the files. Use tools that understand the table's metadata.

Sources: Delta Lake features, Delta schema and history, Iceberg reliability.

passages.heading: 6. Delta Lake: Parquet plus a transaction log
passages.text:
Table formats · updates, history, and batch or streaming workflows

A Delta table stores its data in Parquet files and records table changes in a transaction log, conventionally under _delta_log. A Delta-aware reader uses the log to identify a consistent table version.

Apply changes with MERGE

Suppose a daily delivery contains a refund for order 101 and a new order 104. A MERGE operation can match on order_id, update 101, and insert 104 in one table operation.

This is useful for maintaining a current reporting table from incoming changes. Delta also supports schema checks and retained table history, so you can inspect changes and reproduce earlier results.

Where Delta fits

Delta is a natural fit for Spark and Databricks pipelines, including scheduled batches and streaming ingestion. Spark processes the data; Delta defines how the table is stored and updated.

Read the dataset as a Delta table rather than selecting every Parquet file in its folder. Old files may still be present for earlier versions, so the transaction log determines which files belong to the selected version.

> On the job: MERGE into Delta is the standard way to apply updates and deduplicated CDC batches in Spark and Fabric pipelines; OPTIMIZE and VACUUM are the routine maintenance jobs that keep those tables fast and small.

Remember: Delta combines Parquet's analytical storage with a transaction log that coordinates changes to the whole table.

Sources: Delta Lake introduction, Delta MERGE operations, Delta reads and history.

passages.heading: 7. Apache Iceberg: shared tables that can evolve
passages.text:
Table formats · multiple engines, snapshots, and partitioning

Iceberg tracks snapshots through metadata and manifests, lists describing data files. It commonly uses Parquet, and also supports ORC and Avro data files. A catalog helps engines locate the table's current metadata.

Share a table across engines

One team might prepare orders with Spark while another queries the same Iceberg table with Trino. Both must use compatible connectors and the appropriate catalog; support for particular write operations still varies.

Iceberg identifies columns internally with stable IDs. That allows supported changes such as renaming a column without confusing its identity with another field.

Partition by a useful business dimension

Partitioning groups data by values such as order date so queries can avoid unrelated groups. Iceberg's hidden partitioning lets a date filter use that organization without requiring a separate partition column in the query.

Its layout can also evolve. A table might start grouped by month and later write new data grouped by day; readers can work with both layouts without immediately rewriting the older files.

> On the job: Iceberg is the common choice when several engines (Spark, Trino, Snowflake, BigQuery) must share one table through a catalog. Platform teams pick it to avoid locking data into one vendor.

Remember: Iceberg is a strong fit for shared analytical tables whose schema and storage layout need to evolve over time.

Sources: Iceberg introduction, Iceberg evolution, Iceberg partitioning.

passages.heading: 8. CDC: keep a copy in step with database changes
passages.text:
Before Hudi · change data capture

The shop's application database stores the live orders. We also want a copy for reporting. CDC means change data capture: detecting inserts, updates, and deletes in the source database and passing those changes to another system.

| What happens in the shop | Change to pass along | What the reporting copy should do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Order 104 is placed | Insert order 104 | Add the new order. |
| Order 101 is refunded | Update order 101 | Change its status to refunded. |
| A test order is removed | Delete that order | Remove the corresponding record. |

After an initial copy, a CDC tool can read database change logs and send the changes instead of recopying every row. Events typically identify the record, the operation, and an ordering position or timestamp.

The destination uses those details to apply changes to the right record in the intended order. Capture and application are separate jobs: Debezium can capture the changes, while a pipeline applies them to a Delta, Iceberg, or Hudi table.

> On the job: Keeping a warehouse copy of an operational database in step is a classic data-engineering task. Log-based CDC tools such as Debezium, Fivetran or Fabric mirroring read the database log and emit inserts, updates and deletes for the pipeline to merge.

Remember: CDC is a process, not a file format. It explains why a reporting table may need frequent updates as well as new rows.

Sources: Debezium: capturing database changes.

passages.heading: 9. Apache Hudi: optimize for changing records
passages.text:
Table formats · upserts and incremental processing

Hudi combines an open table format with ingestion and maintenance tools. A record key, such as order_id, identifies the order to update. Its focus on upserts and incremental work makes it useful for CDC-fed reporting tables.

Two ways to handle updates

Copy on Write merges changes into new versions of columnar base files during a write. Queries read the resulting base files, which keeps reads straightforward but can require more rewriting.

Merge on Read can first store updates in log files. Queries combine base data with those updates for the latest view; a later compaction merges them into base files. This moves some work from ingestion to reads and maintenance.

Work on the changed data

Hudi's timeline records table actions. Incremental queries can retrieve records changed since an earlier point, allowing a downstream job to process a smaller update set instead of rescanning the entire table.

This fits orders whose status changes frequently. Choose the write strategy according to how quickly changes must arrive and how much work reads can afford. Main data files commonly use Parquet.

> On the job: Hudi appears in high-churn ingestion (many updates per record) and in AWS-heavy stacks. Even if your platform uses Delta or Iceberg, interviewers may ask you to compare the three.

Remember: Hudi is especially relevant when record-level changes, ingestion latency, and incremental downstream processing drive the design.

Sources: Hudi overview, Hudi table and query types.

passages.heading: 10. Delta, Iceberg, or Hudi: choose by workload
passages.text:
Choose a table · start with the project you actually have

All three help manage changing tables over files. Their capabilities overlap, so these are useful starting points rather than a feature ranking.

| Option | A good reason to explore it | Our shop example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Delta Lake | Your team or course already works with Delta in Spark or Databricks. | Maintain an orders table and review its history after refunds. |
| Apache Iceberg | Several compatible data tools need to share analytical tables. | Prepare orders in one tool and query the same table in another. |
| Apache Hudi | Frequent record updates and incremental processing are central to the pipeline. | Keep a reporting copy current as database changes arrive. |

Compare the actual readers and writers you need, the frequency of updates, and whether downstream jobs need change-based processing. Then confirm that the platform supports the required table features. For a local, fixed dataset, a Parquet file may already meet the need.

Remember: you usually choose one table format for a given table. You do not need to use all three in one project.

Sources: Delta Lake documentation, Apache Iceberg introduction, Apache Hudi overview.

passages.heading: 11. How the formats can work together
passages.text:
Put it together · one possible journey for our orders

A data pipeline is a series of steps that moves and prepares data. Different steps can use different formats because they do different jobs.

1. Receive orders as JSON. The shop's API returns orders with customer details and purchased items.
2. Prepare the data. Your program selects useful fields, checks amounts, and produces a consistent table of orders.
3. Save for reporting. A simple project can save Parquet files. A project needing managed updates could use a Delta table, whose data files are Parquet.
4. Answer business questions. A data tool calculates daily sales or refund totals.
5. Share a result as CSV. A colleague opens the summary in a spreadsheet.

In an event-based version of this pipeline, order messages might arrive as Avro. In another platform, the reporting table might use Iceberg or Hudi instead.

Remember: you do not have to force the whole pipeline into one format. Choose a suitable representation at each step.

Sources: Fabric: lakehouse and Delta tables, Parquet overview.

passages.heading: 12. Scenarios: evaluate the tradeoff
passages.text:
Scenarios · reveal the reasoning behind each choice

Each situation suggests a starting point. There can be other valid choices depending on the tools already in use.

A database sends frequent order corrections into a reporting lake.

Explore Hudi in a CDC pipeline. Its focus on record updates and incremental work fits this need. Delta and Iceberg can also handle updates; existing platform support still matters.

Spark jobs write a sales table that analysts also query from another engine, and the platform team wants to avoid tying the data to one vendor.

Consider Iceberg with a shared catalog. It is designed for tables shared across engines. Check that every engine’s connector supports the features you need, such as row-level deletes.

Yesterday’s load overwrote a Delta table with bad data, and a report needs the previous figures now.

Use the table history. Query or restore the earlier version (time travel), then fix and re-run the load. This works only while the old files are still retained.

Remember: a useful answer includes both a format and a reason tied to the task.

Sources: Delta Lake: time travel, Apache Iceberg introduction, Apache Hudi overview.

passages.heading: 13. Glossary: working vocabulary
passages.text:
Quick reference · connect the terms to their purpose

| Term | What it means in practice |
|---|---|
| Schema / schema evolution | The expected fields and types / supported changes to that structure over time. |
| Grain / record key | What one row represents / the value that identifies a record for matching updates. |
| Partitioning | Group data by a useful dimension, such as date, so queries can avoid unrelated groups. |
| Metadata / catalog | Information describing the data / a service that helps locate and manage named tables. |
| Transaction / snapshot | A change committed as a unit / a particular version of a table. |
| CDC / upsert | Capture database inserts, updates, and deletes / update a match or insert a new record. |
| Incremental / compaction | Process what changed / reorganize files or merge logged changes to improve reads. |

passages.heading: 14. Recap: connect storage choices to pipeline design
passages.text:
Recap · connect each name to a practical job

1. A table format tracks which data files make up the current table, so readers never see half-written changes.
2. Every change is a commit; earlier versions stay readable while their files are retained (time travel).
3. Delta Lake = Parquet + a transaction log; Iceberg = snapshots and manifests located through a catalog; Hudi = a timeline built around record keys.
4. CDC captures inserts, updates and deletes from a database so a lake table can be kept in step with MERGE or upserts.
5. Choose by the platform and the workload, then verify the features your engines actually support.

Three ways to manage changing tables

Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi keep track of a table’s data files and changes. They let compatible tools offer features such as updates and consistent table versions.

For example, a Delta table stores order data in Parquet files and records which files make up each version. That is the practical difference between a file format and a table format.

Choosing between them

Start from the platform and the workload: Delta where Spark, Databricks or Fabric lead; Iceberg for tables shared across engines through a catalog; Hudi for record-level upserts and incremental CDC pipelines. Feature support changes quickly, so check the engine’s documentation.

Remember: “I want to keep a reporting table current” is a table-format need: commits, versions and updates on top of the data files.

passages.heading: 15. References: further reading, when you need it
passages.text:
References · optional next steps

The shop examples connect format design to practical workloads. These references provide implementation detail when you need it; sources are also linked beside the relevant explanations.

- Parquet overview and ORC background: formats designed for analysis.
- Delta Lake documentation: tables, updates, and history.
- Apache Iceberg introduction: shared analytical tables.
- Apache Hudi overview: tables and incremental pipelines.
- Debezium documentation: capturing database changes.
- Fabric: lakehouse and Delta tables: how a managed platform uses Delta.

A readable overview on Medium, “A comprehensive guide to file formats in data engineering”, inspired the explanatory style. Technical explanations here use the project documentation linked above. Format choices are practical guidance, not universal performance rankings.

passages.heading: 16. Cheat sheet: table formats
passages.text:
Keep this slide · three table formats

File formats organize values inside files or messages. Table formats coordinate data files, schemas, and table versions. They work together: a Delta table, for example, stores its data in Parquet.

Table formats — management above the data files

| Format | Data & bookkeeping | Strong fit | Key operating idea |
|---|---|---|---|
| Delta Lake | Parquet data + transaction log. | Spark/Databricks workflows, merges, batch and streaming tables. | Use a Delta reader; the log identifies the selected table version. |
| Apache Iceberg | Parquet, ORC, or Avro data + snapshots and manifests; catalog locates metadata. | Shared tables across engines, schema and partition-layout evolution. | Hidden partitioning connects filters to layout; verify connector capabilities. |
| Apache Hudi | Commonly Parquet base files + timeline; update logs for Merge on Read. | Frequent upserts, CDC ingestion, incremental processing. | Record keys match updates; Copy on Write favors simple reads, Merge on Read defers some write work. |

Shared table capabilities: coordinated commits, evolving schemas, updates/deletes, and retained versions through compatible engines. Read and write support varies by engine and feature; history needs retained files and metadata.

Terms to retain: CDC = capture database changes · upsert = update or insert · partitioning = group data to narrow reads · compaction = reorganize files or merge updates for better reads.

passages.heading: Window functions
passages.text:
SQL for data engineering · lesson deck · PostgreSQL-flavoured standard SQL
 Let a row see
 its neighbours. 
 Window functions: OVER, partitions, ordering, frames, and every function family.
 A window function adds a calculation over related rows without collapsing them . It answers “what share of the customer’s spend is this order?”, “what was the previous order?”, and “what is the running total?” in one pass.
 Every example uses the same six orders, so you can check each result by hand.
 Meet the orders table → 19 short lessons 

 The route through the deck Part A · basics GROUP BY vs window, OVER( ), logical order, frames The one idea everything else builds on, and the default-frame gotcha

 Part B · function families ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE, LAG/LEAD, FIRST/LAST_VALUE, window aggregates What each family returns, and how ties change the answer

 Part C · everyday use Running totals, moving averages, period-over-period The window patterns used in nearly every metrics model

 Practice Name the pattern Decide grain, partition, order and function before revealing

 Part of a split series. This deck is one lesson of the former “SQL beyond GROUP BY” guide. Sibling decks: Window functions , Classic SQL patterns , Query structure: recursion and clean SQL .
 Added in this split: On-the-job notes on each lesson. Next deck: Classic SQL patterns (top-N, dedupe, gaps and islands, sessions).
 Prefer an article? Select Read to see every slide together. Use Contents to jump, or Print / PDF to save.

passages.heading: Why this matters on the job
passages.text:
Why this matters · the need behind the topic
 Why this matters on the job
 Most analytics questions compare a row with related rows: its share of the customer total, the previous order, the running total so far. Window functions answer these in one readable pass, without self-joins, and they are the single most tested SQL topic in data interviews.
 Where you will use it
 dbt models and warehouse views: running totals, rankings, percent-of-total columns.
 Period-over-period metrics in business reviews (LAG over monthly aggregates).
 Silver-layer cleaning: ROW_NUMBER to pick one version of each record.
 What goes wrong without it
 Self-joins and correlated subqueries that are slow and hard to review.
 Running totals that jump on tied dates because of the default RANGE frame.
 Rankings that change between runs because ties were never decided.
 Who expects you to know it
 Data engineers, analytics engineers and BI developers.
 Live SQL interviews: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK, LAG/LEAD and frames come up in most loops.

 On the job A finance analyst asks for each customer’s orders with a running balance and the change from the previous order. With windows it is one SELECT over the orders table: SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY order_date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) and amount - LAG(amount) OVER (...).

 The main idea window functions give each row context from related rows; they are a daily transformation tool and an interview staple.
 why

passages.heading: When to reach for it, and when not to
passages.text:
Why this matters · choosing the right tool
 When to reach for it, and when not to
 Situation Reach for Why 
 Detail rows plus a group number side by side Window aggregate (SUM/AVG OVER PARTITION BY) GROUP BY would collapse the rows 
 Position inside a group (rank, top, first) ROW_NUMBER / RANK / DENSE_RANK Pick the function by how ties should behave 
 Compare with the previous or next row LAG / LEAD No self-join on “previous” keys 
 Cumulative or moving numbers SUM / AVG OVER (ORDER BY … ROWS …) Explicit frame; fill missing days first 
 Plain totals per group GROUP BY A window adds nothing here 

 How interviews test it
 “What is the difference between ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK?” on a tied example.
 “Why is this running total wrong?”: do you know the default frame?
 “Why can’t I use the window in WHERE?”: logical query order.
 “Month-over-month change”: LAG over an aggregate, and what happens to the first month.
 Where it sits in your learning path
 Builds on: SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY.
 Next: Classic SQL patterns (top-N, dedupe, gaps and islands, sessions), which are built from these functions.
 Later: the same ideas in pandas (groupby/transform/shift) and Polars (over()).

 The main idea reach for a window whenever a row needs context from related rows but you must keep every row.
 why

passages.heading: Start with six orders
passages.text:
Start here · one example throughout the guide
 Start with six orders
 Our shop has six orders from three customers. Notice the deliberate details: two orders share a date, and three orders share the amount 40. Ties and duplicates are where window functions get interesting.
 order_id customer order_date amount 
 1 Maya 2026-01-03 25 
 2 Maya 2026-01-05 40 
 3 Leo 2026-01-05 40 
 4 Maya 2026-01-09 15 
 5 Leo 2026-01-10 60 
 6 Ana 2026-01-10 40 

 Totals to keep in mind
 Maya: 25 + 40 + 15 = 80 . Leo: 40 + 60 = 100 . Ana: 40 . All orders: 220 .
 Why so small?
 Every result in this guide can be checked with mental arithmetic. When you practise, do the same: invent five rows, predict the output, then run the query.

 The main idea keep a tiny, tricky dataset in your head (ties, shared dates, NULLs). It is the fastest way to test any SQL you write, especially in an interview.
 02

passages.heading: GROUP BY collapses rows. A window keeps them.
passages.text:
Window basics · the one idea everything else builds on
 GROUP BY collapses rows. A window keeps them.
 Both queries add up amounts per customer. The difference is what happens to the rows.
 Compare the two results 

 SQL 
 SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS customer_total
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer;

 customer customer_total 
 Ana 40 
 Leo 100 
 Maya 80 

 Six rows went in, three came out. The individual orders are gone.

 SQL 
 SELECT order_id, customer, amount,
 SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer) AS customer_total
FROM orders;

 order_id customer amount customer_total 
 1 Maya 25 80 
 2 Maya 40 80 
 3 Leo 40 100 
 4 Maya 15 80 
 5 Leo 60 100 
 6 Ana 40 40 

 Six rows went in, six came out. Each order also carries its customer’s total.

 What is a window?
 A window is the set of rows a function is allowed to look at for the current row . OVER (…) defines it.
 Why it matters
 You can now compare a row with its group in one pass: “what share of Maya’s spend is order 2?” needs both the order amount and Maya’s total on the same row.

 On the job Analysts ask for “each order with its share of the customer’s spend” all the time. In a dbt model or a warehouse view this is one window aggregate, not a GROUP BY joined back to the detail rows.

 The main idea if the question needs detail rows and a group-level number side by side, you want a window function, not GROUP BY.
 03

passages.heading: The anatomy of OVER ( )
passages.text:
Window basics · three optional parts, always in this order
 The anatomy of OVER ( )
 SQL 
 function_name(args) OVER (
 PARTITION BY customer -- 1. split rows into independent groups
 ORDER BY order_date -- 2. sort rows inside each group
 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
 AND CURRENT ROW -- 3. frame: which sorted rows count right now
)

 01 PARTITION BY
 “Per what?” Restarts the calculation for each group. Leave it out and the whole result set is one partition.
 02 ORDER BY
 “In what sequence?” Required for ranking and LAG/LEAD. For aggregates it turns a group total into a running total.
 03 Frame
 “Which rows up to or around me?” Only used by aggregate and value functions. If you omit it, a default applies — next slides.

 The main idea read every window aloud as “for each partition , in order , looking at frame ”. If you cannot finish that sentence, the query is not ready.
 04

passages.heading: When do window functions run?
passages.text:
Window basics · logical query processing order
 When do window functions run?
 SQL is written SELECT-first but evaluated in a different order. Windows are computed late — after grouping, before the final sort.
 01 FROM / JOIN build the row set 
 Tables are combined.

 02 WHERE filter rows 
 Window results do not exist yet, so you cannot filter on them here.

 03 GROUP BY → HAVING aggregate and filter groups 
 Windows see the grouped rows, so SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () is legal.

 04 Window functions compute OVER (…) 
 Evaluated on the rows that survived.

 05 SELECT → DISTINCT pick and dedupe columns 
 Aliases are created here.

 06 ORDER BY → LIMIT sort and cut 
 You may ORDER BY a window alias.

 So how do I filter on a rank?
 Wrap it: compute the window in a CTE, filter in the outer query. Some engines (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, DuckDB, Teradata) add QUALIFY as a shortcut.
 Example
 SQL 
 WITH ranked AS (
 SELECT order_id, customer,
 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer
 ORDER BY order_date DESC) AS rn
 FROM orders
)
SELECT order_id, customer
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1; -- each customer's latest order

 On the job Knowing the logical order explains real errors you will meet in Fabric, Snowflake or Databricks: “window functions are not allowed in WHERE” means the filter must move to an outer query or QUALIFY.

 The main idea “window function in WHERE” is a classic interview error. Say it out loud: “windows run after WHERE, so I’ll filter in an outer query.”
 05

passages.heading: Frames: which rows count “so far”?
passages.text:
Window basics · the default frame is the #1 window gotcha
 Frames: which rows count “so far”?
 Orders 2 and 3 share the date 2026-01-05. Watch what that does to a running total under each frame.
 Pick a frame 

 SQL 
 SELECT order_id, order_date, amount,
 SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS s
FROM orders;

 order_id order_date amount s 
 1 2026-01-03 25 25 
 2 2026-01-05 40 105 
 3 2026-01-05 40 105 
 4 2026-01-09 15 120 
 5 2026-01-10 60 220 
 6 2026-01-10 40 220 

 With ORDER BY and no frame, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW . Rows with the same date are peers and are added together.

 SQL 
 SELECT order_id, order_date, amount,
 SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date, order_id
 ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS s
FROM orders;

 order_id order_date amount s 
 1 2026-01-03 25 25 
 2 2026-01-05 40 65 
 3 2026-01-05 40 105 
 4 2026-01-09 15 120 
 5 2026-01-10 60 180 
 6 2026-01-10 40 220 

 ROWS counts physical rows, so the total climbs one order at a time. Add a tie-breaker (order_id) so the sequence is deterministic.

 SQL 
 SELECT order_id, order_date, amount,
 SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date, order_id
 ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS s
FROM orders;

 order_id order_date amount s 
 1 2026-01-03 25 25 
 2 2026-01-05 40 65 
 3 2026-01-05 40 80 
 4 2026-01-09 15 55 
 5 2026-01-10 60 75 
 6 2026-01-10 40 100 

 A sliding frame: this row plus the one before it. This is how moving averages and rolling sums are built.

 SQL 
 SELECT order_id, order_date, amount,
 SUM(amount) OVER () AS s
FROM orders;

 order_id order_date amount s 
 1 2026-01-03 25 220 
 2 2026-01-05 40 220 
 3 2026-01-05 40 220 
 4 2026-01-09 15 220 
 5 2026-01-10 60 220 
 6 2026-01-10 40 220 

 With no ORDER BY the frame is the whole partition, so every row sees the grand total.

 ROWS = count physical rows. RANGE = include every row whose ORDER BY value falls in the range (all peers). Some engines also support RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW and GROUPS .
 On the job Running balances in finance marts and cumulative sign-ups on dashboards are where the default RANGE frame bites: tied dates silently jump together. Reviewers ask for an explicit ROWS frame.

 The main idea whenever you write ORDER BY inside OVER for a SUM/AVG/LAST_VALUE, write the frame explicitly. It documents intent and removes the tie surprise.
 06

passages.heading: Five families of window functions
passages.text:
Window functions · a map before the details
 Five families of window functions
 Family Functions Question it answers ORDER BY? 
 Ranking ROW_NUMBER RANK DENSE_RANK Where does this row place in its group? Required 
 Distribution NTILE PERCENT_RANK CUME_DIST Which bucket or percentile is this row in? Required 
 Offset LAG LEAD What was on the previous / next row? Required 
 Value FIRST_VALUE LAST_VALUE NTH_VALUE What is the first / last / Nth value in the frame? Required in practice; watch the frame 
 Aggregate SUM AVG COUNT MIN MAX What is the total so far, or for the whole group? Optional: with it = running; without = whole group 

 Ranking, distribution and offset functions ignore any frame — they always look at the whole partition. Only value and aggregate functions use the frame.

 The main idea identify the family first (“I need a position / a neighbour / a running number”), then pick the exact function.
 07

passages.heading: ROW_NUMBER: a unique sequence per group
passages.text:
Window functions · ranking · ROW_NUMBER()
 ROW_NUMBER: a unique sequence per group
 Number each customer’s orders
 SQL 
 SELECT customer, order_date, order_id,
 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
 PARTITION BY customer
 ORDER BY order_date, order_id
 ) AS order_seq
FROM orders;

 customer order_date order_seq 
 Ana 2026-01-10 1 
 Leo 2026-01-05 1 
 Leo 2026-01-10 2 
 Maya 2026-01-03 1 
 Maya 2026-01-05 2 
 Maya 2026-01-09 3 

 How it behaves
 Always 1, 2, 3… with no gaps and no ties , even if two rows are identical on the ORDER BY columns.
 That means ties are broken arbitrarily unless you add a tie-breaker. Two runs of the same query can number tied rows differently — a real source of flaky pipelines.
 Use it for: “exactly one row per group” (dedupe, latest record), first purchase vs repeat purchase, pagination, and the gaps-and-islands trick.

 The main idea ROW_NUMBER guarantees exactly one row per position. Always end its ORDER BY with a unique column so the result is deterministic.
 08

passages.heading: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK
passages.text:
Window functions · ranking · the tie question
 ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK
 Rank all orders by amount, highest first. Three orders tie at 40.
 SQL 
 SELECT order_id, amount,
 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS row_number,
 RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rank,
 DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM orders;

 order_id amount ROW_NUMBER RANK DENSE_RANK 
 5 60 1 1 1 
 2 40 2 2 2 
 3 40 3 2 2 
 6 40 4 2 2 
 1 25 5 5 3 
 4 15 6 6 4 

 RANK — “Olympic” ranking
 Ties share a rank, then the next rank skips (1, 2, 2, 2, 5 ). Use when position should reflect how many rows are ahead.
 DENSE_RANK — no gaps
 Ties share a rank, next rank is consecutive (1, 2, 2, 2, 3 ). Use for “Nth highest distinct value” and “top 3 salary levels”.
 ROW_NUMBER — no ties
 Forces 2, 3, 4 on the tied rows. Order among them is arbitrary here — add order_id to make it stable.

 On the job Leaderboards, “top sellers” reports and ranking features for ML all depend on the tie rule. Write the rule (shared rank, gaps or not) into the model’s documentation, not just the SQL.

 The main idea in an interview, ask “how should ties be handled?” before writing a ranking query. The answer picks the function.
 09

passages.heading: NTILE, PERCENT_RANK, CUME_DIST
passages.text:
Window functions · distribution · buckets and percentiles
 NTILE, PERCENT_RANK, CUME_DIST
 SQL 
 SELECT order_id, amount,
 NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS quartile,
 PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS pct_rank,
 CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS cume_dist
FROM orders;

 order_id amount NTILE(4) PERCENT_RANK CUME_DIST 
 5 60 1 0.00 0.17 
 2 40 1 0.20 0.67 
 3 40 2 0.20 0.67 
 6 40 2 0.20 0.67 
 1 25 3 0.80 0.83 
 4 15 4 1.00 1.00 

 NTILE(n)
 Deals rows into n buckets as evenly as possible; earlier buckets get the extra rows (6 rows / 4 = 2, 2, 1, 1). Ties can be split across buckets — orders 2 and 3 both have 40 but land in different quartiles.
 PERCENT_RANK
 (rank − 1) / (rows − 1). Ranges 0 to 1. “What fraction of rows are ranked above me?” Ties share a value.
 CUME_DIST
 rows at or before me (including peers) / rows. Ranges just above 0 to 1. “Top 10%” ⇒ CUME_DIST() <= 0.10 when ordering descending.

 The main idea NTILE for “split into equal-size groups”; PERCENT_RANK / CUME_DIST for “top X percent” where ties must stay together.
 10

passages.heading: LAG and LEAD: look at the neighbour row
passages.text:
Window functions · offset · LAG(col, n, default) / LEAD(col, n, default)
 LAG and LEAD: look at the neighbour row
 Maya’s order-to-order change
 SQL 
 SELECT order_date, amount,
 LAG(amount) OVER w AS prev_amount,
 LEAD(amount) OVER w AS next_amount,
 amount - LAG(amount) OVER w AS change,
 order_date - LAG(order_date) OVER w
 AS days_since_prev
FROM orders
WHERE customer = 'Maya'
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY customer
 ORDER BY order_date);

 order_date amount prev next change days 
 01-03 25 NULL 40 NULL NULL 
 01-05 40 25 15 +15 2 
 01-09 15 40 NULL −25 4 

 How it behaves
 LAG(x) returns x from the previous row in the window order; LEAD(x) from the next. The optional second argument is the offset ( LAG(x, 7) ), the third is a default instead of NULL ( LAG(x, 1, 0) ).
 The first row has no predecessor, so LAG returns NULL — and any arithmetic with it is NULL. Decide whether that should be NULL, 0, or filtered out.
 The WINDOW w AS (…) clause names a window once and reuses it (PostgreSQL, MySQL 8, SQLite, BigQuery, DuckDB, SQL Server 2022).
 Use it for: month-over-month change, time between events, detecting status changes, sessionization.

 On the job Change-since-last-period metrics, “days since previous order”, and detecting status changes in CDC feeds are LAG/LEAD in everyday pipelines.

 The main idea whenever a question compares a row with “the previous one” or “the next one”, reach for LAG/LEAD instead of a self-join.
 11

passages.heading: FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE
passages.text:
Window functions · value · and the LAST_VALUE trap
 FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE
 Run LAST_VALUE with two frames 

 SQL 
 SELECT order_date, amount,
 FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY order_date) AS first_amt,
 LAST_VALUE(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY order_date) AS last_amt
FROM orders WHERE customer = 'Maya';

 order_date amount first_amt last_amt 
 01-03 25 25 25 
 01-05 40 25 40 
 01-09 15 25 15 

 LAST_VALUE just echoes the current row: the default frame stops at CURRENT ROW, so the “last” row in the frame is me.

 SQL 
 SELECT order_date, amount,
 FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER w AS first_amt,
 LAST_VALUE(amount) OVER w AS last_amt,
 NTH_VALUE(amount, 2) OVER w AS second_amt
FROM orders WHERE customer = 'Maya'
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY order_date
 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING);

 order_date amount first_amt last_amt second_amt 
 01-03 25 25 15 40 
 01-05 40 25 15 40 
 01-09 15 25 15 40 

 With the frame widened to the whole partition, every row sees Maya’s first, last, and second order amounts.

 Tip: LAST_VALUE(x) OVER (ORDER BY d) can also be written as FIRST_VALUE(x) OVER (ORDER BY d DESC) , which needs no frame. NTH_VALUE is not available in SQL Server.
 On the job Opening and closing balances, first touch / last touch attribution and “first status of the day” use value functions; the LAST_VALUE frame trap is a frequent bug in production reports.

 The main idea value functions respect the frame. For “first/last in the group”, use a full frame or flip the sort and use FIRST_VALUE.
 12

passages.heading: SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX as windows
passages.text:
Window functions · aggregate · same functions, new superpower
 SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX as windows
 SQL 
 SELECT customer, order_date, amount,
 SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY order_date
 ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running_total,
 ROUND(100.0 * amount
 / SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer), 1) AS pct_of_customer,
 amount - AVG(amount) OVER () AS vs_avg
FROM orders
WHERE customer = 'Maya'; -- note: AVG OVER () here is Maya's average, because WHERE ran first

 order_date amount running_total pct_of_customer vs_avg 
 01-03 25 25 31.3 −1.67 
 01-05 40 65 50.0 +13.33 
 01-09 15 80 18.8 −11.67 

 With ORDER BY → running
 Cumulative revenue, running count of orders, “max so far” ( MAX(x) OVER (ORDER BY d) ) for record highs.
 Without ORDER BY → whole group
 Share of total, difference from group average, “flag rows above their group’s mean”. Multiply by 100.0 to avoid integer division.
 Windows over aggregates
 Because windows run after GROUP BY: SUM(amount) * 100.0 / SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () gives each customer’s share of all revenue in one grouped query.

 On the job Moving averages for monitoring dashboards and “percent of total” columns in semantic models are window aggregates; they keep the detail rows that BI tools need for drill-down.

 The main idea every aggregate you know becomes a window function by adding OVER. ORDER BY in the window decides “so far” vs “whole group”.
 13

passages.heading: Pattern: running totals and moving averages
passages.text:
Interview patterns · “cumulative revenue” and “7-day rolling average”
 Pattern: running totals and moving averages
 Aggregate to the grain first
 SQL 
 WITH daily AS (
 SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS revenue
 FROM orders
 GROUP BY order_date
)
SELECT order_date, revenue,
 SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_date
 ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS cumulative_revenue,
 AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_date
 ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
 AS rolling_7_row_avg
FROM daily;

 Two traps interviewers probe
 Missing days. ROWS 6 PRECEDING means 6 rows , not 6 days . Our data has no orders on Jan 4, 6, 7, 8, so a “7-row” window spans far more than a week. Fix: join to a calendar (recursive CTE, later) or use RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW where supported.
 Partial windows. The first six days average fewer than 7 values. If that matters, also compute COUNT(*) OVER (same frame) and show NULL when it is below 7.

 On the job Cumulative revenue, month-to-date targets and 7-day rolling averages in KPI dashboards are window aggregates. Fill missing days first (a date spine) or the ROWS frame counts the wrong days.

 The main idea aggregate to one row per period, make sure every period exists, then apply an explicit ROWS frame.
 14

passages.heading: Pattern: period-over-period change
passages.text:
Interview patterns · month-over-month, year-over-year
 Pattern: period-over-period change
 Month-over-month growth
 SQL 
 WITH monthly AS (
 SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
 SUM(amount) AS revenue
 FROM orders
 GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)
)
SELECT month, revenue,
 LAG(revenue) OVER w AS prev_revenue,
 ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER w)
 / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER w, 0), 1) AS pct_change
FROM monthly
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY month);

 Details that earn points
 Year-over-year on monthly rows: LAG(revenue, 12) OVER (ORDER BY month) — only correct if all 12 months exist. Safer: self-join on month - INTERVAL '1 year' , or fill months first.
 Divide safely: NULLIF(prev, 0) avoids divide-by-zero; 100.0 avoids integer division.
 Per segment: add PARTITION BY region so each region compares with its own previous month.

 On the job Month-over-month and year-over-year columns in business reviews are LAG over a monthly aggregate. Check that every period exists first, otherwise LAG compares with the wrong month.

 The main idea period-over-period = aggregate per period, then LAG. Mention gaps and divide-by-zero before the interviewer does.
 15

passages.heading: Practice: name the pattern
passages.text:
Try it · decide before revealing
 Practice: name the pattern
 For each prompt, decide grain, partition, order, and function. Then open the answer.
 Find each customer’s first order date and the number of days until their second order. ROW_NUMBER or LEAD. Partition by customer, order by order_date. LEAD(order_date) OVER (…) - order_date on the row where ROW_NUMBER() = 1 . Customers with one order get NULL.
 Show each product’s revenue rank within its category; tied products should share a rank and there should be no gaps. DENSE_RANK partitioned by category, ordered by revenue DESC — after aggregating revenue per product.
 Flag days where revenue dropped compared with the previous day. LAG. Aggregate to one row per day (fill missing days), then revenue < LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day) in an outer query or CASE.
 Find users who placed orders in 3 consecutive months. Gaps and islands. Distinct (user, month); month index minus ROW_NUMBER gives the island; HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 . Alternatively, LAG(month, 2) equals month − 2 months.
 What is wrong with: SELECT *, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount) AS r FROM orders WHERE r = 1? Window functions run after WHERE, and the alias r does not exist yet. Compute in a CTE and filter outside, or use QUALIFY.

 The main idea a strong answer names the pattern, the partition, the order, and one edge case (ties, NULLs, or gaps).
 16

passages.heading: A small glossary to come back to
passages.text:
Quick reference · the words used in this deck
 A small glossary to come back to
 Term Meaning 
 Window The set of rows a window function can see for the current row, defined by OVER (…). 
 Partition An independent group of rows inside a window (PARTITION BY). Calculations restart per partition. 
 Frame The subset of the sorted partition used right now: ROWS, RANGE, or GROUPS BETWEEN … AND …. 
 Default frame With ORDER BY and no frame clause: RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes tied peers. 
 Peers Rows with equal ORDER BY values. RANGE frames and RANK treat them together. 
 Ranking / offset / value / aggregate / distribution functions The five window families: positions; neighbour rows; first/last/nth values; sums and averages; buckets and percentiles. 
 Running total A cumulative sum over the rows so far, in a stated order. 
 QUALIFY A clause in some engines that filters on window results, like HAVING does for aggregates. 
 Grain What one row represents: one order, one customer per day, one event. 

 17

passages.heading: Recap: what to remember when you close this deck
passages.text:
Recap · connect each tool to a question
 Recap: what to remember when you close this deck
 A window keeps every row and adds a calculation over related rows; GROUP BY collapses them.
 Read every window as partition → order → frame . Leave out PARTITION BY and the whole result is one partition.
 Windows run after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING ; filter on them in an outer query or with QUALIFY.
 With ORDER BY and no frame, the default RANGE frame includes tied rows. Write ROWS BETWEEN … when you mean rows.
 ROW_NUMBER never ties, RANK leaves gaps, DENSE_RANK does not. Decide ties before choosing.
 LAG/LEAD replace self-joins for “previous / next”; the first row gets NULL unless you give a default.
 LAST_VALUE needs a full frame (or flip the sort and use FIRST_VALUE).

 The main idea name the partition, the order and the frame out loud; then the function choice is usually obvious.
 18
