passages.heading: Classic SQL patterns
passages.text:
SQL for data engineering · lesson deck · PostgreSQL-flavoured standard SQL
 Hear the pattern,
 then write the query. 
 Classic SQL patterns: top-N per group, dedupe latest, gaps and islands, sessions.
 Most SQL interview questions and many pipeline steps are one of about ten patterns. This deck teaches you to recognise the signal words, apply a four-question method, and write each pattern from memory.
 It builds on the Window functions deck; every example uses the same six orders.
 Meet the orders table → 14 short lessons 

 The route through the deck Part A · recognise Signal words and a four-question method Grain → partition → order → family → filter

 Part B · patterns Top-N per group, dedupe latest, Nth highest, above the group average Ranking patterns and their tie rules

 Part C · sequences Gaps and islands, sessionization The row-number-difference trick and running sums of flags

 Practice Name the pattern, then a repeatable interview routine Decide before revealing; talk through it like an interview

 Part of a split series. This deck is one lesson of the former “SQL beyond GROUP BY” guide. Sibling decks: Window functions , Classic SQL patterns , Query structure: recursion and clean SQL .
 Added in this split: On-the-job notes and sources on each pattern. Running totals and period-over-period are taught in Window functions .
 Prefer an article? Select Read to see every slide together. Use Contents to jump, or Print / PDF to save.

passages.heading: Why this matters on the job
passages.text:
Why this matters · the need behind the topic
 Why this matters on the job
 Interviewers and real tickets rarely say “use ROW_NUMBER”. They say “latest record per customer”, “top 3 products per category”, “users active 3 days in a row”, or “split clicks into visits”. Recognising which pattern a question needs is most of the work; the SQL for each pattern is short once you know it.
 Where you will use it
 Silver-layer dedupe of CDC and API feeds: the latest version per key.
 Leaderboards and “top sellers per category” in reporting models.
 Product analytics: streaks, retention runs, and sessions from raw events.
 What goes wrong without it
 A dedupe without a tie-breaker returns different rows on every run.
 Top-N with the wrong ranking function drops or duplicates tied rows.
 Streak and session logic written as nested self-joins that nobody can review.
 Who expects you to know it
 Data and analytics engineers who own cleaning and metrics models.
 Timed SQL interviews (DataLemur / LeetCode style): these patterns are most of the medium questions.

 On the job A product manager asks for “how many users had a 7-day login streak last month”. You recognise gaps and islands: one row per user per active day, date minus ROW_NUMBER gives an island key, then count island lengths. Ten minutes, one reviewable query.

 The main idea pattern recognition turns vague business questions into short, standard SQL, and it is exactly what timed SQL interviews measure.
 why

passages.heading: When to reach for it, and when not to
passages.text:
Why this matters · choosing the right tool
 When to reach for it, and when not to
 Situation Reach for Why 
 “Latest / current version per key” ROW_NUMBER … = 1 with a tie-breaker Exactly one row per key, deterministic 
 “Top N per group”, ties should all appear DENSE_RANK or RANK, filter outside ROW_NUMBER would drop tied rows 
 “Consecutive days / months” Gaps and islands (value − ROW_NUMBER) Groups each continuous run 
 “New visit after 30 minutes idle” LAG + running SUM of start flags Sessions without self-joins 
 A single overall maximum MAX or ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 No window needed 

 How interviews test it
 Timed problems: “second highest salary”, “top 3 per department”, “consecutive logins”.
 Follow-ups: “now handle ties”, “now the data has duplicates”, “now 1 billion rows”.
 Interviewers listen for the grain and tie rule before you type.
 Where it sits in your learning path
 Builds on: Window functions (ranking, LAG/LEAD, running sums).
 Next: Query structure (recursion and clean SQL) and SQL correctness (joins and grain).
 Practice: the SQL interview patterns lab file and the DataLemur catalog.

 The main idea learn the signal words; once the pattern is named, write it with a CTE, a deterministic order and a filter outside.
 why

passages.heading: Start with six orders
passages.text:
Start here · one example throughout the guide
 Start with six orders
 Our shop has six orders from three customers. Notice the deliberate details: two orders share a date, and three orders share the amount 40. Ties and duplicates are where window functions get interesting.
 order_id customer order_date amount 
 1 Maya 2026-01-03 25 
 2 Maya 2026-01-05 40 
 3 Leo 2026-01-05 40 
 4 Maya 2026-01-09 15 
 5 Leo 2026-01-10 60 
 6 Ana 2026-01-10 40 

 Totals to keep in mind
 Maya: 25 + 40 + 15 = 80 . Leo: 40 + 60 = 100 . Ana: 40 . All orders: 220 .
 Why so small?
 Every result in this guide can be checked with mental arithmetic. When you practise, do the same: invent five rows, predict the output, then run the query.

 The main idea keep a tiny, tricky dataset in your head (ties, shared dates, NULLs). It is the fastest way to test any SQL you write, especially in an interview.
 02

passages.heading: Hear the signal words, pick the function
passages.text:
Interview patterns · recognition cheat-sheet
 Hear the signal words, pick the function
 If the question says… Reach for Shape of the answer 
 top N per highest in each best-selling per ROW_NUMBER / RANK / DENSE_RANK Rank in a CTE, filter rnk <= N outside 
 latest most recent remove duplicates keep one ROW_NUMBER rn = 1 with a deterministic ORDER BY 
 Nth highest second largest ties count once DENSE_RANK dr = N ; handle “no Nth value” 
 previous next change since days between LAG / LEAD Subtract the neighbour; think about the first row’s NULL 
 running cumulative to date so far SUM / COUNT OVER (ORDER BY …) Explicit ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING 
 rolling moving average last 7 days AVG OVER (ROWS/RANGE BETWEEN …) Fill missing days first if using ROWS 
 share of % of total vs group average SUM / AVG OVER (PARTITION BY …) No ORDER BY in the window 
 consecutive streak continuous ranges ROW_NUMBER difference Gaps and islands 
 sessions inactivity gap new visit after 30 min LAG + running SUM Flag starts, then cumulative sum the flags 
 quartile top 10% bucket NTILE / PERCENT_RANK / CUME_DIST Ask whether ties may be split 
 first / last value opening / closing FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE Full frame or flipped sort 

 The main idea most window-function interview questions are one of about ten patterns. Recognizing the pattern is 80% of the answer.
 03

passages.heading: A four-question method for any window problem
passages.text:
Interview patterns · say this out loud before typing
 A four-question method for any window problem
 What is one output row? (the grain) — one per order? per customer? per day? This tells you whether you need GROUP BY, a window, or both.
 Per what? → PARTITION BY . “For each customer” ⇒ PARTITION BY customer . “Overall” ⇒ no partition.
 In what order? → ORDER BY inside OVER. “Latest” ⇒ date DESC. “Highest” ⇒ amount DESC. Add a unique tie-breaker.
 Which family? position → ranking; neighbour → LAG/LEAD; “so far” / group total → aggregate; bucket → distribution.
 Filter after. Put the window in a CTE and filter in the outer query (or QUALIFY where supported). Then test against ties, NULLs, and single-row groups.

 Example: “For each customer, return their single biggest order.” Grain: one row per customer. Per: customer. Order: amount DESC, order_id. Family: ranking → ROW_NUMBER (one row, even with ties). Filter: rn = 1 .

 The main idea narrating grain → partition → order → family → filter shows the interviewer structured thinking even before the SQL is perfect.
 04

passages.heading: Pattern: top N per group
passages.text:
Interview patterns · “top 2 orders per customer”
 Pattern: top N per group
 The query
 SQL 
 WITH ranked AS (
 SELECT customer, order_id, amount,
 DENSE_RANK() OVER (
 PARTITION BY customer
 ORDER BY amount DESC
 ) AS amount_rank
 FROM orders
)
SELECT customer, order_id, amount
FROM ranked
WHERE amount_rank <= 2
ORDER BY customer, amount_rank;

 Choosing the ranking function
 Requirement Use 
 Exactly N rows per group, ties broken somehow ROW_NUMBER + tie-breaker 
 Top N values ; include everyone tied DENSE_RANK 
 Top N positions ; ties may push past N RANK 

 Leo’s result: order 5 (60, rank 1) and order 3 (40, rank 2). Maya: 40 and 25. Ana: only one order, so one row — confirm that is acceptable.
 Snowflake / BigQuery / DuckDB shortcut: QUALIFY DENSE_RANK() OVER (…) <= 2 .

 The main idea top-N per group = rank inside a partition, filter outside. The interview follow-up is always “what about ties?”
 05

passages.heading: Pattern: deduplicate and keep the latest row
passages.text:
Interview patterns · the most common data-engineering use
 Pattern: deduplicate and keep the latest row
 A CDC feed delivered the same customer three times. We want the current version of each customer.
 Raw rows
 customer_id email updated_at load_id 
 7 a@old.com 2026-01-01 09:00 1 
 7 a@new.com 2026-01-04 12:00 2 
 7 a@new.com 2026-01-04 12:00 3 
 8 b@x.com 2026-01-02 08:00 1 

 Keep one row per key
 SQL 
 WITH ranked AS (
 SELECT customer_id, email, updated_at,
 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
 PARTITION BY customer_id
 ORDER BY updated_at DESC,
 load_id DESC -- tie-breaker
 ) AS rn
 FROM customer_changes
)
SELECT customer_id, email, updated_at
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;

 Why not SELECT DISTINCT ? It only removes rows identical in every column. Why not GROUP BY customer_id with MAX(updated_at) ? You then need a join back to fetch the other columns — and ties still return duplicates.
 On the job This is the most common Silver-layer transformation: CDC and API feeds deliver several versions of a record, and the pipeline keeps the latest per key. A missing tie-breaker makes nightly runs non-deterministic.

 The main idea “latest per key” and “remove duplicates” are both ROW_NUMBER … = 1. The tie-breaker is what makes the pipeline repeatable.
 06

passages.heading: Pattern: consecutive streaks (gaps and islands)
passages.text:
Interview patterns · “users who logged in 3+ days in a row”
 Pattern: consecutive streaks (gaps and islands)
 Consecutive dates increase by 1 each day; ROW_NUMBER also increases by 1 each row. Subtract one from the other and every date in the same streak gets the same anchor value .
 See the trick
 login_date rn login_date − rn streak 
 01-01 1 12-31 A 
 01-02 2 12-31 A 
 01-03 3 12-31 A 
 01-05 4 01-01 B 
 01-06 5 01-01 B 
 01-09 6 01-03 C 

 The query
 SQL 
 WITH days AS (
 SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date
 FROM logins -- one row per day!
), grouped AS (
 SELECT user_id, login_date,
 login_date - CAST(ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
 PARTITION BY user_id
 ORDER BY login_date) AS INT) AS grp
 FROM days
)
SELECT user_id,
 MIN(login_date) AS streak_start,
 MAX(login_date) AS streak_end,
 COUNT(*) AS streak_days
FROM grouped
GROUP BY user_id, grp
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

 SQL Server: DATEADD(day, -ROW_NUMBER() OVER (…), login_date) . Alternative: flag a new island when login_date - LAG(login_date) > 1 , then running-SUM the flags — the same technique as sessions on the next slide.
 On the job Streaks (consecutive active days), uptime and outage windows, and “continuous subscription periods” in billing data are gaps-and-islands problems.

 The main idea “consecutive”, “streak”, or “continuous range” ⇒ gaps and islands. Deduplicate to one row per unit first, or the trick breaks.
 07

passages.heading: Pattern: sessionize events
passages.text:
Interview patterns · “a new session starts after 30 minutes of inactivity”
 Pattern: sessionize events
 Flag starts, then count them
 SQL 
 WITH flagged AS (
 SELECT user_id, event_time,
 CASE
 WHEN event_time - LAG(event_time) OVER (
 PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time)
 <= INTERVAL '30 minutes'
 THEN 0
 ELSE 1 -- first event or gap > 30 min
 END AS is_new_session
 FROM events
)
SELECT user_id, event_time,
 SUM(is_new_session) OVER (
 PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time
 ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_no
FROM flagged;

 Trace it
 event_time gap is_new session_no 
 09:00 — 1 1 
 09:10 10m 0 1 
 09:25 15m 0 1 
 10:30 65m 1 2 
 10:45 15m 0 2 

 The first event’s LAG is NULL, the comparison is NULL (not true), so ELSE marks it as a new session — exactly what we want.
 From here: session length = MAX − MIN per (user, session_no); events per session = COUNT(*) .

 On the job Product analytics teams turn raw click events into sessions this way before computing session length, bounce rate or conversion per session.

 The main idea “running SUM of a 0/1 flag” turns change points into group IDs. It solves sessions, islands, and “status changed” problems.
 08

passages.heading: Pattern: Nth highest and “above the group average”
passages.text:
Interview patterns · two classics in one slide
 Pattern: Nth highest and “above the group average”
 Second-highest order amount
 SQL 
 SELECT MAX(amount) AS second_highest -- MAX → NULL if none
FROM (
 SELECT amount,
 DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS dr
 FROM orders
) ranked
WHERE dr = 2;

 Answer: 40 (not 40, 40, 40). DENSE_RANK makes “second” mean second distinct value; wrapping in MAX returns a single row, or NULL when there is no second value — a common hidden test case.
 Orders above their customer’s average
 SQL 
 WITH scored AS (
 SELECT order_id, customer, amount,
 AVG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer)
 AS customer_avg
 FROM orders
)
SELECT order_id, customer, amount, customer_avg
FROM scored
WHERE amount > customer_avg;

 Maya’s average is 26.67, so only order 2 (40) qualifies; Leo’s is 50, so order 5 (60). Ana’s single order equals her average and is excluded. Without windows you would need a correlated subquery per row.

 The main idea compare-to-group questions are a window with PARTITION BY and no ORDER BY, followed by an outer filter.
 09

passages.heading: Practice: name the pattern
passages.text:
Try it · decide before revealing
 Practice: name the pattern
 For each prompt, decide grain, partition, order, and function. Then open the answer.
 Find each customer’s first order date and the number of days until their second order. ROW_NUMBER or LEAD. Partition by customer, order by order_date. LEAD(order_date) OVER (…) - order_date on the row where ROW_NUMBER() = 1 . Customers with one order get NULL.
 Show each product’s revenue rank within its category; tied products should share a rank and there should be no gaps. DENSE_RANK partitioned by category, ordered by revenue DESC — after aggregating revenue per product.
 Flag days where revenue dropped compared with the previous day. LAG. Aggregate to one row per day (fill missing days), then revenue < LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day) in an outer query or CASE.
 Find users who placed orders in 3 consecutive months. Gaps and islands. Distinct (user, month); month index minus ROW_NUMBER gives the island; HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 . Alternatively, LAG(month, 2) equals month − 2 months.
 What is wrong with: SELECT *, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount) AS r FROM orders WHERE r = 1? Window functions run after WHERE, and the alias r does not exist yet. Compute in a CTE and filter outside, or use QUALIFY.

 The main idea a strong answer names the pattern, the partition, the order, and one edge case (ties, NULLs, or gaps).
 10

passages.heading: How to work a SQL interview question
passages.text:
Clean SQL · interviews · a repeatable routine
 How to work a SQL interview question
 Restate and clarify. “Per customer or overall? How should ties count? Can amounts be NULL? Do cancelled orders count?”
 State the grain. Of each input table, and of the output: “one row per customer per month”.
 Sketch the CTE steps in words before typing: filter → aggregate to grain → window → filter on window → final columns.
 Write it cleanly. Named CTEs, explicit joins, explicit frames, deterministic ORDER BY.
 Test on a tiny example. Walk through 4–6 rows including a tie, a NULL, a single-row group, and an empty result.
 Mention trade-offs. Alternative approaches (self-join vs LAG, QUALIFY), indexes or partitions, and what changes at large scale.

 The main idea interviewers grade the reasoning as much as the query. Clean structure makes your reasoning visible.
 11

passages.heading: A small glossary to come back to
passages.text:
Quick reference · the words used in this deck
 A small glossary to come back to
 Term Meaning 
 Pattern A recurring question shape with a known solution, such as top-N per group or gaps and islands. 
 Signal words Phrases in a question that point to a pattern: “latest”, “top 3 per”, “consecutive”, “inactivity gap”. 
 Grain What one output row represents: one per customer, one per day, one per session. 
 Tie-breaker A unique column added to ORDER BY so a ranking or dedupe gives the same result on every run. 
 Deduplicate Keep exactly one row per key, usually the latest version (ROW_NUMBER … = 1). 
 QUALIFY A clause in some engines that filters on window results, like HAVING does for aggregates. 
 Gaps and islands Finding continuous runs (islands) and breaks (gaps) in ordered data. 
 Session A run of events by one user with no gap longer than an inactivity threshold. 

 12

passages.heading: Recap: what to remember when you close this deck
passages.text:
Recap · connect each pattern to a question
 Recap: what to remember when you close this deck
 Listen for signal words : “top N per” → ranking; “latest / keep one” → ROW_NUMBER; “consecutive” → gaps and islands; “inactivity” → sessions.
 Say the four questions out loud: grain, per what, in what order, which family; then filter outside.
 Top-N : rank in a CTE, filter outside; choose ROW_NUMBER, RANK or DENSE_RANK by the tie rule.
 Dedupe : ROW_NUMBER with a deterministic ORDER BY (add a unique tie-breaker), keep rn = 1 .
 Gaps and islands : sequence value minus ROW_NUMBER is constant inside a run; group by it.
 Sessions : flag a new session with LAG, then a running SUM of the flags numbers the sessions.
 In interviews, restate, state the grain, sketch the steps, write cleanly, test on a tiny example .

 The main idea name the pattern first; the SQL for each pattern is short once you recognise it.
 13

passages.heading: Query structure: recursion and clean SQL
passages.text:
SQL for data engineering · lesson deck · PostgreSQL-flavoured standard SQL
 Loops in SQL,
 and SQL others can read. 
 Query structure: recursive CTEs, CTE pipelines, correctness traps and clean style.
 Recursive CTEs let a query repeat until it is done: calendars, org charts, category trees. Clean SQL (named CTE steps, explicit joins, sargable filters, deterministic ordering) makes those queries easy to review and trust.
 Every example uses the same six orders and a small org chart.
 Meet the orders table → 18 short lessons 

 The route through the deck Part A · recursion Anchor + step + stop, calendars, org charts How a recursive CTE runs, one iteration at a time

 Part B · recursion safely Down, up and roll-ups; depth limits and cycles When a question needs recursion, and how to make it stop

 Part C · clean SQL Formatting, CTEs as named steps, correctness traps, performance habits Write for the next reader and for the optimizer

 Practice Recursion drills and a code-review exercise Spot the problem before revealing

 Part of a split series. This deck is one lesson of the former “SQL beyond GROUP BY” guide. Sibling decks: Window functions , Classic SQL patterns , Query structure: recursion and clean SQL .
 Added in this split: On-the-job notes, and a pointer to set operations (UNION / INTERSECT / EXCEPT), which are taught with executed examples in the SQL aggregation deck.

passages.heading: Why this matters on the job
passages.text:
Why this matters · the need behind the topic
 Why this matters on the job
 Two things make SQL hard to trust: logic that needs to repeat an unknown number of times, and queries nobody else can read. Recursive CTEs solve the first (hierarchies, calendars, paths); clean structure with named CTE steps solves the second, and it is what code review, dbt projects and interviewers all expect.
 Where you will use it
 Date spines and calendar tables behind every daily metric.
 Org charts, cost centres, bill-of-materials and category trees.
 Every dbt model and shared warehouse view: CTE pipelines that others maintain.
 What goes wrong without it
 Hierarchies flattened with a fixed number of self-joins that break at the next level.
 A recursion over dirty data that never stops (a cycle) and burns warehouse credits.
 One 300-line query with nested subqueries that nobody dares to change.
 Who expects you to know it
 Analytics engineers and data engineers who write shared transformation code.
 Interviewers, who judge readability and test recursion with “walk this org chart”.

 On the job An HR analyst asks for headcount under each manager, at any depth. You write a recursive CTE that walks the reporting lines with a depth counter and a visited path, aggregate in a final CTE, and the reviewer can follow every step.

 The main idea recursion handles unknown depth; clean CTE structure makes any query reviewable, testable and safe to change.
 why

passages.heading: When to reach for it, and when not to
passages.text:
Why this matters · choosing the right tool
 When to reach for it, and when not to
 Situation Reach for Why 
 Hierarchy of unknown depth Recursive CTE with depth cap and cycle check Fixed self-joins break at the next level 
 Need every date in a range Generated calendar (recursive CTE or generate_series) Missing days must appear as zeros 
 Long query with several stages Named CTE steps, one idea each Reads top to bottom, each step testable 
 Combine two result sets UNION ALL (UNION only to remove duplicates) UNION silently removes legitimate duplicates 
 A fixed two-level hierarchy Plain joins Recursion adds nothing 

 How interviews test it
 “Find every employee under manager X” or “build a date spine”.
 “What stops this recursion?” and “what if the data has a cycle?”
 Code-review prompts: spot the NOT IN, the WHERE on a LEFT JOIN, the missing tie-breaker.
 Where it sits in your learning path
 Builds on: Window functions and Classic SQL patterns.
 Next: SQL correctness (joins, grain, NULLs) and SQL aggregation (set operations, GROUPING SETS).
 Later: dbt, where every model is a CTE pipeline checked by a linter.

 The main idea reach for recursion only when depth is unknown or you must generate rows; reach for clean CTE structure every time.
 why

passages.heading: Start with six orders
passages.text:
Start here · one example throughout the guide
 Start with six orders
 Our shop has six orders from three customers. Notice the deliberate details: two orders share a date, and three orders share the amount 40. Ties and duplicates are where window functions get interesting.
 order_id customer order_date amount 
 1 Maya 2026-01-03 25 
 2 Maya 2026-01-05 40 
 3 Leo 2026-01-05 40 
 4 Maya 2026-01-09 15 
 5 Leo 2026-01-10 60 
 6 Ana 2026-01-10 40 

 Totals to keep in mind
 Maya: 25 + 40 + 15 = 80 . Leo: 40 + 60 = 100 . Ana: 40 . All orders: 220 .
 Why so small?
 Every result in this guide can be checked with mental arithmetic. When you practise, do the same: invent five rows, predict the output, then run the query.

 The main idea keep a tiny, tricky dataset in your head (ties, shared dates, NULLs). It is the fastest way to test any SQL you write, especially in an interview.
 02

passages.heading: Recursive CTEs: a loop written as a query
passages.text:
Recursion · WITH RECURSIVE · anchor + recursive member
 Recursive CTEs: a loop written as a query
 A normal CTE names a query. A recursive CTE refers to itself, so it can keep producing rows until there is nothing new. It is how SQL walks hierarchies of unknown depth and generates sequences.
 Count to five
 SQL 
 WITH RECURSIVE numbers AS (
 SELECT 1 AS n -- anchor member: runs once
 UNION ALL
 SELECT n + 1 -- recursive member
 FROM numbers -- reads only the previous step
 WHERE n < 5 -- stop condition
)
SELECT n FROM numbers; -- 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

 What the engine does
 01 Anchor working set = {1} 
 Runs once. Its rows seed the result.

 02 Recursive member reads {1} → {2} 
 Sees only the rows produced by the previous step, not the full result.

 03 Repeat {2}→{3}→{4}→{5} 
 Each step’s output becomes the next step’s input.

 04 Stop {5} → ∅ 
 When a step returns no rows, the loop ends.

 05 Result UNION ALL of every step 
 The outer SELECT sees all rows.

 The main idea anchor seeds, recursive member extends, an empty step stops. If nothing in the recursive member can become false, the query never ends.
 03

passages.heading: Generate a calendar to fill missing days
passages.text:
Recursion · sequences · the most practical everyday use
 Generate a calendar to fill missing days
 Our orders skip Jan 4, 6, 7, and 8. A report that GROUPs BY date silently drops those days — and rolling averages over ROWS become wrong. Generate every date, then LEFT JOIN the facts.
 Build the date spine
 SQL 
 WITH RECURSIVE calendar AS (
 SELECT DATE '2026-01-03' AS cal_date
 UNION ALL
 SELECT cal_date + 1
 FROM calendar
 WHERE cal_date < DATE '2026-01-10'
)
SELECT c.cal_date,
 COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS revenue
FROM calendar AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
 ON o.order_date = c.cal_date
GROUP BY c.cal_date
ORDER BY c.cal_date;

 Result
 cal_date revenue 
 01-03 25 
 01-04 0 
 01-05 80 
 01-06 0 
 01-07 0 
 01-08 0 
 01-09 15 
 01-10 100 

 Dialect notes: SQL Server drops RECURSIVE and uses DATEADD(day, 1, cal_date) . PostgreSQL also offers generate_series ; BigQuery has GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY . In a warehouse, a permanent calendar table is cleaner still.

 On the job A date spine is used in nearly every metrics model: daily revenue must show zero-revenue days, otherwise charts skip days and rolling averages divide by the wrong count. Most warehouses keep a calendar table generated once this way.

 The main idea “include days with zero sales” or “fill the gaps” ⇒ generate the spine, LEFT JOIN facts, COALESCE to zero.
 04

passages.heading: Walk an org chart, one level per step
passages.text:
Recursion · hierarchies · step through the iterations
 Walk an org chart, one level per step
 Everyone under the CEO, with depth and path
 SQL 
 WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
 SELECT emp_id, name, manager_id,
 1 AS depth,
 CAST(name AS VARCHAR(500)) AS path
 FROM employees
 WHERE manager_id IS NULL -- anchor: the CEO
 UNION ALL
 SELECT e.emp_id, e.name, e.manager_id,
 o.depth + 1,
 CAST(o.path || ' > ' || e.name AS VARCHAR(500))
 FROM employees AS e
 JOIN org AS o
 ON e.manager_id = o.emp_id -- children of last step
)
SELECT emp_id, name, depth, path
FROM org
ORDER BY path;

 The CAST matters: the anchor fixes each column’s type, and a growing string can overflow a short name type (PostgreSQL and SQL Server raise a type-mismatch error).
 Step through it
 Iteration 

 emp_id name manager_id depth 
 1 Ava NULL 1 
 2 Ben 1 
 3 Cara 1 
 4 Dan 2 
 5 Eli 2 
 6 Fay 3 
 7 Gus 4 

 Anchor finds the row with no manager: Ava.

 emp_id name manager_id depth 
 1 Ava NULL 1 
 2 Ben 1 2 
 3 Cara 1 2 
 4 Dan 2 
 5 Eli 2 
 6 Fay 3 
 7 Gus 4 

 Rows whose manager_id is in {1}: Ben and Cara.

 emp_id name manager_id depth 
 1 Ava NULL 1 
 2 Ben 1 2 
 3 Cara 1 2 
 4 Dan 2 3 
 5 Eli 2 3 
 6 Fay 3 3 
 7 Gus 4 

 Managers {2, 3} → Dan, Eli, Fay.

 emp_id name manager_id depth 
 1 Ava NULL 1 
 2 Ben 1 2 
 3 Cara 1 2 
 4 Dan 2 3 
 5 Eli 2 3 
 6 Fay 3 3 
 7 Gus 4 4 

 Manager {4} → Gus. Path: Ava > Ben > Dan > Gus.

 emp_id name manager_id depth 
 1 Ava NULL 1 
 2 Ben 1 2 
 3 Cara 1 2 
 4 Dan 2 3 
 5 Eli 2 3 
 6 Fay 3 3 
 7 Gus 4 4 

 Nobody reports to Gus: the step returns no rows, so recursion stops.

 On the job Org-chart roll-ups (“total headcount under each manager”), cost-centre hierarchies in finance, and product category trees all need recursion when the depth is not fixed.

 The main idea each iteration joins the base table to only the previous level . Depth = iteration number; path = breadcrumbs you carry along.
 05

passages.heading: Down, up, and roll-ups
passages.text:
Recursion · hierarchies · three variants interviewers ask for
 Down, up, and roll-ups
 01 Down: all reports of Ben
 SQL 
 WITH RECURSIVE team AS (
 SELECT emp_id, name
 FROM employees WHERE emp_id = 2
 UNION ALL
 SELECT e.emp_id, e.name
 FROM employees AS e
 JOIN team AS t
 ON e.manager_id = t.emp_id
)
SELECT name FROM team
WHERE emp_id <> 2; -- Dan, Eli, Gus

 02 Up: Gus’s management chain
 SQL 
 WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
 SELECT emp_id, name, manager_id
 FROM employees WHERE emp_id = 7
 UNION ALL
 SELECT m.emp_id, m.name, m.manager_id
 FROM employees AS m
 JOIN chain AS c
 ON m.emp_id = c.manager_id -- flip
)
SELECT name FROM chain;
-- Gus, Dan, Ben, Ava

 03 Roll-up: bill of materials
 SQL 
 WITH RECURSIVE bom AS (
 SELECT child_part, qty
 FROM components
 WHERE parent_part = 'bike'
 UNION ALL
 SELECT c.child_part, b.qty * c.qty
 FROM components AS c
 JOIN bom AS b
 ON c.parent_part = b.child_part
)
SELECT child_part, SUM(qty) AS total_qty
FROM bom GROUP BY child_part;

 Direction is just which side of the join you follow. For roll-ups, carry a multiplied value down the tree, then aggregate in the outer query — most engines forbid aggregates and GROUP BY inside the recursive member.

 The main idea down = join child.manager_id to the previous level; up = join parent.emp_id to the previous level’s manager_id. Aggregate after the recursion, not inside it.
 06

passages.heading: Make recursion stop: depth limits and cycles
passages.text:
Recursion · safety · and the dialect differences
 Make recursion stop: depth limits and cycles
 Guard against loops
 SQL 
 WITH RECURSIVE reach AS (
 SELECT to_id,
 ARRAY[from_id, to_id] AS path,
 1 AS hops
 FROM edges WHERE from_id = 'A'
 UNION ALL
 SELECT e.to_id,
 r.path || e.to_id,
 r.hops + 1
 FROM reach AS r
 JOIN edges AS e ON e.from_id = r.to_id
 WHERE e.to_id <> ALL (r.path) -- not visited yet
 AND r.hops < 10 -- hard depth cap
)
SELECT DISTINCT to_id FROM reach;

 Real hierarchies get bad data (A manages B, B manages A). Carry the visited path and refuse to revisit; add a depth cap as a seatbelt. PostgreSQL 14+ also has a built-in CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path clause.
 Dialect differences
 Engine Keyword Built-in limit 
 PostgreSQL WITH RECURSIVE None — add your own; CYCLE / SEARCH clauses 
 MySQL 8 WITH RECURSIVE cte_max_recursion_depth = 1000 
 SQL Server WITH (no RECURSIVE) OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) , default 100 
 Oracle WITH + column list CYCLE clause; legacy CONNECT BY 
 Snowflake / BigQuery / DuckDB WITH RECURSIVE Engine-specific iteration limits 

 UNION instead of UNION ALL discards rows already produced, which can stop exact-duplicate cycles — but it costs a dedupe each step and will not catch cycles if a path or depth column makes every row unique.

 On the job Real hierarchy data contains mistakes: an employee recorded as their own manager’s manager creates a cycle. A depth cap and a visited path stop a scheduled job from running until it times out.

 The main idea every recursive query needs a reason to stop: data that ends, a visited-check, and a depth cap. Know your engine’s default limit.
 07

passages.heading: When does a question need recursion?
passages.text:
Recursion · interview patterns · recognize the signal
 When does a question need recursion?
 If the question says… Pattern Anchor → recursive step 
 all levels any depth org chart all subordinates Hierarchy down Root(s) → children of previous level 
 chain of command all ancestors root of each node Hierarchy up Start node → its parent 
 every date include zero days numbers 1..N Sequence generation Start value → value + step, until end 
 total parts exploded cost roll-up Bill of materials Top assembly → components, multiply qty 
 can A reach B degrees of separation shortest path Graph traversal Start node → neighbours, track path, MIN(hops) 
 split a string expand ranges into rows Row expansion Whole value → peel one element per step 

 Is a fixed number of self-joins enough?
 If the depth is known and small (“employee and their manager”), a self-join is simpler and faster. Recursion is for unknown or variable depth.
 What to say
 “Anchor is … ; each step joins … to the previous level; it stops when … ; I’ll guard against cycles with a visited path and cap depth at … .”

 The main idea “unknown depth” or “generate rows that are not in any table” are the two signals for a recursive CTE.
 08

passages.heading: Practice: recursion
passages.text:
Try it · write the anchor and step in your head first
 Practice: recursion
 For every employee, return the name of their top-level boss. Anchor: roots ( manager_id IS NULL ), carrying emp_id AS root_id . Step: children of the previous level inherit root_id . Join root_id back to employees for the name.
 Return each employee’s depth and the number of people (direct and indirect) under them. Walk down from each employee: anchor = every employee as its own top_id ; step = children. Then COUNT(*) - 1 GROUP BY top_id . Depth comes from a separate walk from the root.
 List every month between a customer’s first and last order, with 0 for months without orders. Per customer, anchor = first month; step = month + 1 while < last month (join the customer’s bounds). LEFT JOIN monthly revenue, COALESCE to 0.
 Your recursive query runs forever on production data. What happened, and how do you fix it? A cycle in the data (or a stop condition that never becomes false). Add a visited path check, a depth cap, and on SQL Server keep MAXRECURSION at a sensible value rather than 0.

 The main idea if you can say “anchor, step, stop, safety” for a problem, the SQL almost writes itself.
 09

passages.heading: Write SQL for the next reader
passages.text:
Clean SQL · formatting and naming
 Write SQL for the next reader
 Same query, two styles 

 SQL 
 select c.customer_name,sum(o.amount) tot,count(*) from customers c,orders o where c.id=o.customer_id and o.order_date>='2026-01-01' group by 1 having count(*)>1 order by 2 desc

 It runs. But which join type? What is “tot”? What does “group by 1” mean after someone adds a column?

 SQL 
 SELECT
 c.customer_id,
 c.customer_name,
 SUM(o.amount) AS total_revenue,
 COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM customers AS c
INNER JOIN orders AS o
 ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY
 c.customer_id,
 c.customer_name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

 One clause per line, explicit JOIN, named aggregates, grouping by the key — and two customers with the same name are no longer merged.

 Layout
 One column per line; each clause starts a line; indent what belongs to it. Pick upper- or lower-case keywords and stay consistent. Leading or trailing commas — choose one per codebase.
 Names
 snake_case ; descriptive aliases ( o for orders is fine, a, b, c is not); name every derived column with AS ; avoid reserved words like date or user .
 Explicit over implicit
 ANSI JOIN … ON , not commas in FROM. Column names, not SELECT * or GROUP BY 1 . Qualify columns with their table alias when more than one table is in scope.

 On the job Most teams enforce a SQL style automatically (for example SQLFluff in CI with the dbt style rules). Following it makes your pull requests about logic, not formatting.

 The main idea clean SQL is not decoration: explicit joins, named columns, and grouping by keys prevent real bugs.
 10

passages.heading: Use CTEs as named steps
passages.text:
Clean SQL · structure · read top to bottom
 Use CTEs as named steps
 Same logic, two structures 

 SQL 
 SELECT customer_id, avg_amount
FROM (
 SELECT customer_id, AVG(amount) AS avg_amount
 FROM (
 SELECT o.customer_id, o.amount
 FROM orders AS o
 WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
 AND o.customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE country = 'US')
 ) t1
 GROUP BY customer_id
) t2
WHERE avg_amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled');

 Read inside-out. The “not cancelled” rule is written twice and could drift apart.

 SQL 
 WITH valid_orders AS (
 SELECT customer_id, amount
 FROM orders
 WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
),

us_customers AS (
 SELECT customer_id
 FROM customers
 WHERE country = 'US'
),

customer_avg AS (
 SELECT v.customer_id, AVG(v.amount) AS avg_amount
 FROM valid_orders AS v
 INNER JOIN us_customers AS u
 ON u.customer_id = v.customer_id
 GROUP BY v.customer_id
)

SELECT customer_id, avg_amount
FROM customer_avg
WHERE avg_amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM valid_orders);

 Read top-down like a recipe. Each step has one job and a name that says what it contains; the business rule lives in one place.

 Good CTE habits
 Name CTEs after their contents ( valid_orders ), not their mechanics ( t1 , cte2 ). One responsibility each. Filter and select only needed columns early. End with a simple final SELECT.
 What CTEs are not
 They are not automatically faster. Most engines inline them like subqueries; some (older PostgreSQL before 12, or MATERIALIZED hints) compute them once. Use them for clarity; check the plan for speed.

 On the job dbt models are written exactly like this: import CTEs, logical CTEs, a final SELECT. Reviewers can test and reason about each named step.

 The main idea a query built from small named CTEs can be debugged one step at a time: SELECT from any CTE to see its output.
 11

passages.heading: Correctness traps clean SQL avoids
passages.text:
Clean SQL · bugs that return a plausible wrong answer
 Correctness traps clean SQL avoids
 Trap What goes wrong Clean fix 
 = NULL WHERE coupon = NULL is never true; NULL compared with anything is unknown. IS NULL / IS NOT NULL ; IS DISTINCT FROM for null-safe comparison. 
 NOT IN with NULLs WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT ref_id …) returns no rows if any ref_id is NULL. NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 … WHERE r.ref_id = t.id) . 
 WHERE on a LEFT JOIN LEFT JOIN payments p … WHERE p.status = 'ok' removes unmatched rows — it is now an inner join. Move the condition into ON , or state the inner join explicitly. 
 Join fan-out Joining orders to order_items before SUM(order.amount) counts each order once per item. Aggregate to the right grain in a CTE first, then join. Know each table’s grain. 
 COUNT confusion COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs; COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique values. Choose deliberately and name the column accordingly. 
 Integer division 1 / 4 is 0 in PostgreSQL and SQL Server. 100.0 * a / NULLIF(b, 0) or CAST to decimal. 
 Non-determinism LIMIT without ORDER BY; ROW_NUMBER without a unique tie-breaker. Always order by something unique when position matters. 
 DISTINCT as a bandage Duplicates from a bad join are hidden, not fixed — and cost a sort. Find the fan-out; fix the join or aggregate first. 

 On the job These traps produce believable wrong numbers with no error. They are the first things to check when a dashboard total disagrees with finance.

 The main idea before trusting a result, ask “what is the grain of each table, and what happens to NULLs?” Those two questions catch most silent bugs.
 12

passages.heading: Performance-minded habits
passages.text:
Clean SQL · write queries the optimizer can help
 Performance-minded habits
 Keep predicates sargable
 SQL 
 -- Hides order_date inside a function:
WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2026

-- Lets an index or partition pruning work:
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
 AND order_date < DATE '2027-01-01'

 Sargable (Search ARGument-able) means the engine can use an index, partition, or file statistics to skip data. Keep the column bare; transform the constant instead. A half-open range also handles timestamps correctly.
 Small habits, big effects
 Select only needed columns — essential on columnar storage like Parquet.
 Filter early , in the CTE that reads the table, not at the end.
 UNION ALL unless you truly need duplicates removed; UNION adds a sort or hash.
 EXISTS for “has at least one”, instead of JOIN + DISTINCT.
 One window, many functions: reuse the same PARTITION BY / ORDER BY (or a named WINDOW) so the engine sorts once.
 Read the plan with EXPLAIN before guessing.

 On the job On cloud warehouses that bill by data scanned (BigQuery, Fabric capacity, Snowflake credits), non-sargable filters and SELECT * cost real money, not just time.

 The main idea performance in interviews is about intent: show you would filter early, keep predicates sargable, avoid needless sorts, and verify with EXPLAIN.
 13

passages.heading: Clean habits for windows and recursion
passages.text:
Clean SQL · applying it to this guide’s topics
 Clean habits for windows and recursion
 Window functions
 SQL 
 SELECT
 customer,
 order_date,
 amount,
 ROW_NUMBER() OVER by_date AS order_seq,
 SUM(amount) OVER by_date AS running_total,
 LAG(amount) OVER by_date AS prev_amount
FROM orders
WINDOW by_date AS (
 PARTITION BY customer
 ORDER BY order_date, order_id -- unique tie-breaker
 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
 AND CURRENT ROW -- explicit frame
);

 Name repeated windows once.
 Always state the frame for running/value functions.
 End ORDER BY with a unique column.
 Alias ranks by meaning: amount_rank , not r .
 Recursive CTEs
 SQL 
 WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
 -- anchor: top of the hierarchy
 SELECT emp_id, manager_id, 1 AS depth
 FROM employees
 WHERE manager_id IS NULL

 UNION ALL

 -- step: direct reports of the previous level
 SELECT e.emp_id, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1
 FROM employees AS e
 INNER JOIN org AS o
 ON e.manager_id = o.emp_id
 WHERE o.depth < 20 -- safety cap
)
SELECT emp_id, depth
FROM org;

 Comment the anchor and the step.
 Keep the recursive member minimal; enrich in the final SELECT.
 Put the stop condition where a reader will see it.
 Carry depth even if the question does not ask for it — it helps debugging.

 The main idea the two hardest-to-read SQL features become easy to review when the frame, tie-breaker, anchor, step, and stop are explicit.
 14

passages.heading: Practice: spot the problem
passages.text:
Try it · code review in your head
 Practice: spot the problem
 SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.order_date >= '2026-01-01' GROUP BY c.name The WHERE on o.order_date discards customers with no orders, turning the LEFT JOIN into an inner join; move it into ON. Also group by c.id (names are not unique) and alias the SUM.
 SELECT * FROM products WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items) If any product_id is NULL, the result is empty. Use NOT EXISTS . Also list the columns you need instead of * .
 SELECT o.order_id, SUM(o.amount), COUNT(i.item_id) FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY o.order_id Fan-out: o.amount is summed once per item. Use MAX(o.amount) at order grain, or aggregate items in a CTE and join to orders.
 WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-01-05' Not sargable. Use created_at >= '2026-01-05' AND created_at < '2026-01-06' .
 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1 — the dedupe returns different rows each run. Ties on updated_at . Add a unique tie-breaker such as the load or event ID.

 The main idea most review comments fall into four buckets: NULLs, grain/fan-out, non-determinism, and sargability.
 15

passages.heading: A small glossary to come back to
passages.text:
Quick reference · the words used in this deck
 A small glossary to come back to
 Term Meaning 
 CTE (common table expression) A named subquery defined with WITH and used like a table in the rest of the query. 
 Recursive CTE A CTE that references itself: an anchor query plus a recursive member that runs until it returns no rows. 
 Anchor / recursive member The seed query of a recursive CTE / the part that references the CTE and runs repeatedly. 
 Date spine A generated list of every date in a range, joined to facts so missing days show up as zeros. 
 Cycle A loop in hierarchical or graph data that makes naive recursion run forever. 
 Set operation UNION [ALL], INTERSECT, EXCEPT: combine whole rows of two queries (see the SQL aggregation deck). 
 Grain What one row represents: one order, one customer per day, one event. 
 Fan-out Row multiplication from joining to a table with many matches per key. 
 Sargable A predicate the engine can use to seek an index or skip data. 

 16

passages.heading: Recap: what to remember when you close this deck
passages.text:
Recap · connect each tool to a question
 Recap: what to remember when you close this deck
 A recursive CTE is anchor + step + stop . Use it for unknown-depth hierarchies, graphs and generated sequences.
 Guard every recursion with a depth cap and a visited path ; know your engine’s limit (MAXRECURSION, cte_max_recursion_depth).
 Generate a calendar once and left-join facts to it, so missing days appear.
 Structure queries as named CTE steps that read top to bottom: import, filter, aggregate to grain, join, final select.
 Avoid the classic traps: WHERE on the optional side of a LEFT JOIN, NOT IN with NULLs, fan-out before SUM, non-deterministic ORDER BY .
 Keep filters sargable and select only the columns you need.
 Combine whole result sets with UNION ALL unless you really need duplicates removed (details in the SQL aggregation deck).

 The main idea make the anchor, step and stop explicit, then write the whole query as small named steps a reviewer can check one by one.
 17

passages.heading: SQL correctness: joins, grain, and NULLs
passages.text:
Companion to sql-joins-grain.html: same lessons, same numbering, same queries and results. Hints and solutions are in Appendices A and B.

Tested engine and dialect: DuckDB 1.5.6 (Python package, CPython 3.12.10, Windows 11). Queries are written in PostgreSQL-flavoured standard SQL; DuckDB-only syntax is labelled, and lessons have dialect notes for PostgreSQL, SQL Server (T-SQL), Spark SQL, Snowflake, and BigQuery. Every SQL query in this document was executed in DuckDB while it was built, and the result shown under it is the real result. Other-dialect syntax appears only in the dialect tables and was not executed. Timing figures are labelled as measured on the build machine; yours will differ.

Prerequisites: the Window functions deck (its six-row orders table is reused here) and the dimensional modeling decks (grain, fan-out, bridge tables). This deck is one half of the former SQL correctness deck; the other half is SQL aggregation. New terms are defined on first use and collected in the glossary. Most lessons end with an On the job note. The exercises follow common SQL interview patterns (fan-out, outer-join filters, NOT IN with NULL, as-of joins, conditional aggregation, subtotals, pivots, percentiles), researched in October 2026.

Additions beyond the original brief are marked (added): grain tests before and after joins; DISTINCT as a bandage (SUM(DISTINCT)); NULL-safe join keys and change detection; a reconciliation toolkit (control totals, EXCEPT ALL diffs); a grain-first interview routine; a dialect cheat sheet.

passages.heading: 1. SQL correctness: joins, grain, and NULLs
passages.text:
The most expensive SQL bugs do not raise errors. A join quietly doubles revenue. A NOT IN quietly returns nothing. A filter quietly turns an outer join into an inner join. This deck shows each trap with a believable query, its wrong result, the reason, and the fix.

Every query in this deck ran in DuckDB while the deck was built. The result under each query is the real result.

- Part A · joins and grain: Cardinality, fan-out, pre-aggregation, outer-join filters, semi and anti joins, NOT IN. Know how many rows a join returns before you run it
- Part B · NULLs: Three-valued logic, NULL-safe comparison, NULLs in joins, aggregates, and sorting. Unknown is not false, and not equal to itself
- Part C · joins beyond equality: Self-joins, range joins, as-of joins. Match rows by intervals and “latest known value”
- Part D · verify and practise: Reconciliation toolkit, interview routine, bug clinic, 5 exercises, 4-step lab. Several joins inflate revenue until you fix them

Additions beyond the brief (marked (added)): grain tests before and after joins; DISTINCT as a bandage (SUM(DISTINCT)); NULL-safe join keys and change detection; a reconciliation toolkit (control totals, EXCEPT ALL diffs); a grain-first interview routine; a dialect cheat sheet.

Part of a split series. This deck is one lesson of the former “SQL correctness: joins, grain, NULLs, and aggregation” deck. Sibling deck: SQL aggregation. Both reuse the same lab tables, so lesson 3 appears in each.

Companion: the Markdown version (Markdown ↗) has the same lessons; hints and solutions are in its appendices. Use Contents to jump, Read for article mode.

passages.heading: Why this matters · Why this matters on the job
passages.text:
Why this matters · the need behind the topic

The most dangerous SQL bugs do not raise errors: they return believable numbers that are wrong. A join that fans out, a filter that turns an outer join into an inner join, a NOT IN that meets a NULL. Data engineers own the tables that every dashboard sums, so they are expected to catch these before anyone else does.

Where you will use it

- Building marts and dbt models that join facts to dimensions and child tables.
- Reconciling a warehouse model with finance, an ERP, or a payment provider.
- Reviewing pull requests: “what is the grain of this join?”.

What goes wrong without it

- Revenue doubled by a one-to-many join, reported for weeks.
- Customers with no orders silently vanish from a “per customer” report.
- “Has none” queries that return nothing because of one NULL.

Who expects you to know it

- Data and analytics engineers, BI developers, and the finance teams that consume their tables.
- Interviewers: fan-out, NOT IN with NULL, and LEFT JOIN filters are classic trick questions.

> On the job: A classic escalation: “the dashboard shows $1.2M but finance says $370K”. The fix is almost never in the dashboard; it is a join at the wrong grain. This deck’s reconciliation lab rehearses exactly that investigation.

> The main idea: correct joins, grain and NULL handling are what make numbers trustworthy; reconciliation is how you prove it.

Read more: PostgreSQL: table expressions, joins, LATERAL, GROUPING SETS, PostgreSQL: EXISTS, IN, NOT IN.

passages.heading: Why this matters · When to reach for it, and when not to
passages.text:
Why this matters · choosing the right tool

| Situation | Reach for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Measures from a parent plus a 1:N child | Pre-aggregate the child to the parent key | Prevents fan-out |
| “Customers who have / never …” | Semi-join EXISTS / anti-join NOT EXISTS | No duplicates; NULL-safe |
| Keep every row of one side, filter the other | Condition in LEFT JOIN … ON | WHERE would drop the unmatched rows |
| Value valid at the time of an event | As-of join or half-open range join | No leakage, no fan-out |
| Comparing nullable columns | IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM | = returns unknown on NULL |

How interviews test it

- “Why is this total too high?” (find the fan-out).
- “Why does NOT IN return nothing here?”
- “Customers with no orders in January” (LEFT JOIN filter placement or anti-join).
- Interviewers listen for you to state the grain before writing the join.

Where it sits in your learning path

- Builds on: Window functions, Classic SQL patterns, dimensional modeling (grain, bridges).
- Next: SQL aggregation (conditional aggregation, subtotals, pivots, percentiles).
- Later: the same checks as dbt tests and data-quality rules.

> The main idea: state the grain first, join on unique keys, use semi/anti joins for existence, handle NULLs explicitly, and reconcile every total to a control.

Why so small?

Every wrong answer in this deck can be checked by hand. That is the point: a counterexample is a small input that proves a query wrong. In interviews and code reviews, inventing one is faster than arguing.

> The main idea: keep a tiny, tricky dataset: duplicates on the many side, a missing child, a NULL, and an orphan. Most SQL bugs show up on four rows.

passages.heading: 4. Five words that prevent most wrong totals
passages.text:
Start here · grain, key, cardinality, fan-out, control total

| Term | Meaning | In the lab |
|---|---|---|
| Grain | What one row represents. Say it as “one row per …”. | orders: one row per order. order_items: one row per order line. payments: one row per payment. |
| Key | Columns whose values are unique per row at that grain. A foreign key is a column that points to another table’s key. | order_items key is (order_id, line_no); its order_id is a foreign key to orders. |
| Cardinality | How many rows on each side can match: one-to-one (1:1), one-to-many (1:N), many-to-many (N:M). | orders → order_items is 1:N. customers → orders is 1:N. order_items ↔ payments (through order_id) is N:M. |
| Fan-out | A join that repeats rows from one side, once per match on the other. Measures on the repeated side then get counted several times. | Joining orders to items repeats order 2’s amount twice. |
| Control total | A trusted total from the source (row count, sum of amounts) that every downstream result must reconcile to. | Revenue = 220. Payments = 180. |

How each lesson works

- Question: a realistic business question.
- Believable, but wrong: a query a competent person might write, and its real result.
- Why: the rule it broke.
- Fixed: a correct query and its real result.
- Dialect notes and an On the job note.

The one habit

Before writing a join, say the grain of every input and the grain you want out. Before trusting a result, compare it to a control total.

> On the job: Data engineers own the tables that dashboards and finance reports sum. A fan-out bug in a shared model can double a KPI for every consumer at once. Teams protect themselves with grain tests (dbt unique tests, for example) and reconciliation checks in the pipeline.

> The main idea: grain first, then keys, then cardinality. If you can state those three, you can predict a join’s row count and spot fan-out before it happens.

Read more: PostgreSQL: table expressions, joins, LATERAL, GROUPING SETS, DuckDB: FROM and JOIN (semi, anti, lateral, ASOF).

passages.heading: 5. Join cardinality: predict the row count
passages.text:
Joins and grain · how many rows will this join return?

A join pairs each left row with every right row that matches. So the output has, for each left row, as many rows as it has matches. An inner join keeps only matched pairs. A left outer join also keeps unmatched left rows, padding the right side with NULLs. A cross join pairs every row with every row.

Row counts, measured

SELECT 1 AS step, 'customers' AS input, COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM customers
UNION ALL SELECT 2, 'orders', COUNT(*) FROM orders
UNION ALL SELECT 3, 'customers JOIN orders', COUNT(*)
          FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer = c.customer
UNION ALL SELECT 4, 'customers LEFT JOIN orders', COUNT(*)
          FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer = c.customer
UNION ALL SELECT 5, 'orders JOIN order_items', COUNT(*)
          FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
UNION ALL SELECT 6, 'customers CROSS JOIN orders', COUNT(*) FROM customers CROSS JOIN orders
ORDER BY step;

Result (6 rows):

| step | input | row_count |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | customers | 4 |
| 2 | orders | 6 |
| 3 | customers JOIN orders | 6 |
| 4 | customers LEFT JOIN orders | 7 |
| 5 | orders JOIN order_items | 10 |
| 6 | customers CROSS JOIN orders | 24 |

Zoe has no orders: the inner join drops her, the left join keeps her (7 rows). Each order has 1 or 2 items, so the join to items grows from 6 to 10 rows.

Is the join key unique on the other side?

SELECT 'orders.order_id' AS candidate_key, COUNT(*) AS row_count, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS distinct_values FROM orders
UNION ALL SELECT 'order_items.order_id', COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) FROM order_items
UNION ALL SELECT 'order_items.(order_id, line_no)', COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT (order_id, line_no)) FROM order_items
UNION ALL SELECT 'payments.order_id', COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) FROM payments
ORDER BY candidate_key;

Result (4 rows):

| candidate_key | row_count | distinct_values |
|---|---|---|
| order_items.(order_id, line_no) | 10 | 10 |
| order_items.order_id | 10 | 6 |
| orders.order_id | 6 | 6 |
| payments.order_id | 6 | 5 |

If the key you join on is unique on the right side (a many-to-one join), left rows are never repeated. order_id is unique in orders but not in order_items or payments. Joining to those repeats orders.

passages.text:

> On the job: Before joining to a new table, run the “row count vs distinct key” check above. It takes seconds and answers the most important question: will this join repeat my rows? In dbt this is a unique test on the key; in Spark it is df.groupBy(key).count().filter("count > 1").

> The main idea: rows out = sum over left rows of max(matches, 1 if outer). If the right-side key is not unique, your left rows will repeat.

Read more: PostgreSQL: table expressions, joins, LATERAL, GROUPING SETS, DuckDB: FROM and JOIN (semi, anti, lateral, ASOF).

passages.heading: 6. Fan-out: a one-to-many join inflates sums
passages.text:
Joins and grain · “revenue and item count per customer”

Question: show revenue and number of items per customer. The amount lives on orders; the items live on order_items. A single join and a single GROUP BY looks natural.

✗ Believable, but wrong

SELECT o.customer,
       SUM(o.amount)    AS revenue,
       COUNT(i.line_no) AS items
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.customer
ORDER BY o.customer;

Result (3 rows):

| customer | revenue | items |
|---|---|---|
| Ana | 80 | 2 |
| Leo | 200 | 4 |
| Maya | 120 | 4 |

Revenue adds to 400, not 220. Every order amount was summed once per item line.

✓ Fixed

WITH items_per_order AS (      -- one row per order
    SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS items
    FROM order_items
    GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT o.customer,
       SUM(o.amount) AS revenue,
       SUM(i.items)  AS items
FROM orders o
JOIN items_per_order i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.customer
ORDER BY o.customer;

Result (3 rows):

| customer | revenue | items |
|---|---|---|
| Ana | 40 | 2 |
| Leo | 100 | 4 |
| Maya | 80 | 4 |

Aggregate the many side to the grain of orders first. Now the join is one-to-one and nothing repeats.

Why

After the join, the grain is one row per order line. o.amount is an order-level measure, so it appears once per line: order 2 (two lines) contributes 40 + 40. COUNT(i.line_no) is correct because items are at line grain. Rule: only sum a measure at its own grain.

Another valid fix

Sum a line-level measure instead: SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) is correct after this join, because it lives at line grain. Pick the measure whose grain matches the rows you are summing.

> On the job: Fan-out is the classic “numbers are too high” incident: a new join to a detail table (lines, payments, events, tags) is added to an existing report. In dimensional models it is why measures live on facts at a declared grain, and why you join facts to dimensions many-to-one.

> The main idea: after any join, re-state the grain. A measure from the “one” side of a one-to-many join is repeated and must not be summed.

Read more: PostgreSQL: table expressions, joins, LATERAL, GROUPING SETS, PostgreSQL: aggregate functions.

passages.heading: 7. Two children of one parent: the multiplication trap
passages.text:
Joins and grain · items × payments per order

Question: per customer, show item revenue and amount paid. Both child tables join to orders on order_id. Joining both at once pairs every item of an order with every payment of that order. This many-to-many pattern is often called a chasm trap.

✗ Believable, but wrong

SELECT o.customer,
       SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS item_revenue,
       SUM(p.amount)             AS paid
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i   ON i.order_id = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.customer
ORDER BY o.customer;

Result (3 rows):

| customer | item_revenue | paid |
|---|---|---|
| Ana | 40 | NULL |
| Leo | 100 | 200 |
| Maya | 120 | 120 |

Leo’s revenue looks right (100), so a quick check passes. His payments are doubled, Maya’s revenue and payments are both inflated, and Ana’s paid is NULL, not 0.

✓ Fixed

WITH items AS (
    SELECT order_id, SUM(qty * unit_price) AS item_revenue
    FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id
), paid AS (
    SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS paid
    FROM payments GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT o.customer,
       SUM(i.item_revenue)       AS item_revenue,
       COALESCE(SUM(p.paid), 0)  AS paid
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN paid  p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.customer
ORDER BY o.customer;

Result (3 rows):

| customer | item_revenue | paid |
|---|---|---|
| Ana | 40 | 0 |
| Leo | 100 | 100 |
| Maya | 80 | 80 |

Each child is collapsed to one row per order before joining. Totals: 220 revenue, 180 paid.

Why: count the rows per order

SELECT o.order_id,
       COUNT(DISTINCT i.line_no)    AS item_rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.payment_id) AS payment_rows,
       COUNT(*)                     AS joined_rows
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i     ON i.order_id = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN payments p   ON p.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.order_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;

Result (6 rows):

| order_id | item_rows | payment_rows | joined_rows |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 2 | 2 | 4 |
| 3 | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 5 | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| 6 | 2 | 0 | 2 |

Order 2 has 2 items and 2 payments, so 4 joined rows: every item is counted twice and every payment twice. Leo was “right” only because each of his orders has one payment.

The general rule

passages.heading: 7. Two children of one parent: the multiplication trap
passages.text:
so 4 joined rows: every item is counted twice and every payment twice. Leo was “right” only because each of his orders has one payment.

The general rule

Joining one parent to two independent children gives items × payments rows per parent. No measure in that result is at a meaningful grain. Never sum across two 1:N branches in one join.

> On the job: This is the most common reason a finance dashboard disagrees with the ledger: orders joined to lines and payments (or shipments, refunds, tags) in one model. The fix is always the same: one CTE per child, aggregated to the shared key, then join.

> The main idea: if two tables both have many rows per key, aggregate each one to that key first. Then join one-to-one.

Read more: PostgreSQL: table expressions, joins, LATERAL, GROUPING SETS, DuckDB: FROM and JOIN (semi, anti, lateral, ASOF).

passages.heading: 8. Pre-aggregate to the grain, then prove it
passages.text:
Joins and grain · a repeatable pattern and its tests (added)

1. State the output grain (one row per …): e.g. one row per order. Write it as a comment above the query.
2. Aggregate each child (GROUP BY the output key): One CTE per detail table, grouped by the key of the output grain.
3. Join on unique keys (many-to-one or one-to-one): Every join should match at most one row on the right.
4. Test the grain (COUNT(*) = COUNT(DISTINCT key)): If the key repeats, a join fanned out.
5. Reconcile (compare to control totals): Sum each measure and compare to the source table’s total.

WITH items AS (SELECT order_id, SUM(qty * unit_price) AS item_revenue FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id),
     paid  AS (SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS paid FROM payments GROUP BY order_id),
     order_grain AS (                 -- one row per order
    SELECT o.order_id, o.amount, i.item_revenue, COALESCE(p.paid, 0) AS paid
    FROM orders o
    LEFT JOIN items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    LEFT JOIN paid  p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
)
SELECT COUNT(*)                          AS row_count,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)          AS distinct_orders,
       SUM(item_revenue)                 AS item_revenue,
       (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders)  AS revenue_control,
       SUM(paid)                         AS paid,
       (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payments) AS paid_control
FROM order_grain;

Result (1 row):

| row_count | distinct_orders | item_revenue | revenue_control | paid | paid_control |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 6 | 220 | 220 | 180 | 180 |

What a failing test looks like

Run the same test on the wrong query from the previous slide (joined rows, not order grain): 12 rows but only 6 distinct orders, item revenue 260, payments 320. Each number disagrees with its control total, so the bug is caught before anyone reads a dashboard.

Pre-aggregate or not?

Pre-aggregation is also faster: it shrinks the detail tables before the join. Modern optimizers sometimes do it for you, but correctness must not depend on that.

> On the job: In a dbt project this pattern is a model per grain plus unique and not_null tests on the key and a reconciliation test (for example dbt_utils.equality or a custom “sum matches source” test). In Spark it is groupBy before join.

passages.text:
tests on the key and a reconciliation test (for example dbt_utils.equality or a custom “sum matches source” test). In Spark it is groupBy before join.

> The main idea: a model is correct at a grain only if you can prove it: key unique, measures equal to control totals. Make both checks part of the pipeline, not a one-off.
