passages.heading: Appendix A · Hints
passages.text:
Hint 1 · Card share per customer and overall

GROUP BY ROLLUP (customer) gives a total row; label it with GROUPING(). Use FILTER (or CASE) for the card amount, * 1.0 and NULLIF for the division.

passages.heading: Appendix A · Hints
passages.text:
Hint 2 · A pivot that reconciles

Start from order_items (the grain of qty) and join up to region: both joins are many-to-one, so no fan-out. One SUM(CASE … ELSE 0 END) per SKU.

passages.heading: Appendix A · Hints
passages.text:
Hint 3 · Medians by region, and the overall median

Ordered-set aggregates work with ROLLUP like any other aggregate. Label the total row with GROUPING(), so it can’t be confused with the real NULL region.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text: Every solution query below was executed in DuckDB during the build, and its result was checked against the expected rows or totals.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 1 · Card share per customer and overall

SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(o.customer) = 1 THEN 'All customers'
            ELSE o.customer END                           AS customer,
       SUM(p.amount)                                      AS paid,
       COALESCE(SUM(p.amount) FILTER (WHERE p.method = 'card'), 0) AS card_paid,
       ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(p.amount) FILTER (WHERE p.method = 'card'), 0) * 1.0
             / NULLIF(SUM(p.amount), 0), 3)               AS card_share
FROM payments p
JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = p.order_id
GROUP BY ROLLUP (o.customer)
ORDER BY GROUPING(o.customer), customer;

Result (3 rows):

| customer | paid | card_paid | card_share |
|---|---|---|---|
| Leo | 100 | 100 | 1 |
| Maya | 80 | 55 | 0.688 |
| All customers | 180 | 155 | 0.861 |

Why it works. The total row divides the sums (155 ÷ 180 = 0.861), a ratio of sums (lesson 9). The average of the customer shares, (1 + 0.688) ÷ 2 = 0.844, would weight Maya’s 80 the same as Leo’s 100. Maya’s payment 105 has no method: it counts in paid but not in card_paid, which is the honest treatment of an unknown method. In SQL Server, replace FILTER with SUM(CASE WHEN p.method = 'card' THEN p.amount ELSE 0 END).

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 2 · A pivot that reconciles

SELECT COALESCE(c.region, 'Unknown')                       AS region,
       SUM(CASE WHEN i.sku = 'KIT'   THEN i.qty ELSE 0 END)   AS kit,
       SUM(CASE WHEN i.sku = 'MUG'   THEN i.qty ELSE 0 END)   AS mug,
       SUM(CASE WHEN i.sku = 'SPOON' THEN i.qty ELSE 0 END)   AS spoon,
       SUM(CASE WHEN i.sku = 'TEA'   THEN i.qty ELSE 0 END)   AS tea,
       SUM(i.qty)                                             AS total_units
FROM order_items i
JOIN orders o    ON o.order_id = i.order_id
JOIN customers c ON c.customer = o.customer
GROUP BY COALESCE(c.region, 'Unknown')
ORDER BY region;

Result (3 rows):

| region | kit | mug | spoon | tea | total_units |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| East | 1 | 0 | 5 | 2 | 8 |
| Unknown | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| West | 0 | 2 | 0 | 2 | 4 |

SELECT SUM(qty) AS control_units FROM order_items;

Result (1 row):

| control_units |
|---|
| 14 |

Why it works. Joining from the line table up to orders and customers is many-to-one, so each line is counted once. ELSE 0 turns empty cells into zeros, and total_units sums the rows rather than adding the pivot columns, so a SKU missing from the list would show up as a gap between the columns and the total: 8 + 2 + 4 = 14. A DuckDB PIVOT … USING SUM(qty) would give NULLs instead of zeros (lesson 14).

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 3 · Medians by region, and the overall median

SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(c.region) = 1 THEN 'All regions'
            ELSE COALESCE(c.region, 'Unknown') END              AS region,
       COUNT(*)                                                 AS orders,
       percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY o.amount)    AS median_amount,
       percentile_disc(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY o.amount)    AS p90_disc
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer = o.customer
GROUP BY ROLLUP (c.region)
ORDER BY GROUPING(c.region), region;

Result (4 rows):

| region | orders | median_amount | p90_disc |
|---|---|---|---|
| East | 2 | 50 | 60 |
| Unknown | 1 | 40 | 40 |
| West | 3 | 25 | 40 |
| All regions | 6 | 40 | 60 |

Why it works. The All-regions row is computed from all six rows: sorted amounts 15, 25, 40, 40, 40, 60 give a median of 40. Averaging the regional medians, (50 + 40 + 25) ÷ 3 = 38.33, ignores how many orders each region has and how they are spread; percentiles are non-additive (lesson 16). p90_disc is always an actual order amount; percentile_cont(0.9) on East would interpolate to 58. In SQL Server, percentiles need OVER (PARTITION BY …) and cannot be combined with ROLLUP directly.

passages.heading: Why dimensional modeling
passages.text:
Data engineering · dimensional modeling · lesson deck
 Model data
 people can ask questions of. 
 Why dimensional modeling: OLTP vs analytics, facts and dimensions, the star schema, grain, and the four-step process.
 Dimensional modeling is how analytics teams organise data so that business questions such as “revenue by category by month” become simple, fast, and consistent.
 You only need to know what tables, rows, keys, and joins are. Every new term is explained the first time it appears.
 Start the lesson → 19 short lessons 

 The route through the deck Part A · the problem App databases are built for writing Why reports need a different shape of data

 Part B · building blocks Facts · dimensions · the star schema The two kinds of table and how every star query looks

 Part C · grain Grain, three rules, the classic mistake The one decision that comes first

 Part D · method The four-step design process Process → grain → dimensions → facts, applied to Leafy

 Part of a split series. This deck is one lesson of the former “Dimensional modeling” course. Sibling decks, in order: Why dimensional modeling , Fact tables , Dimension tables , Model a business end to end (bus matrix and the FitHub project).
 Added in this split: On-the-job notes on most lessons. Next deck: Fact tables .
 Prefer an article? Select Read to see every slide together. Use Contents to jump, or Print / PDF to save.

passages.heading: Why this matters on the job
passages.text:
Why this matters · the need behind the topic
 Why this matters on the job
 Business users want the same answer to the same question, every time, from every report. Dimensional modeling is how data teams arrange warehouse tables so that “revenue by category by month” is one simple query and totals do not double count. It starts with two ideas: facts versus dimensions, and the grain.
 Where you will use it
 Designing Gold layers and marts: fact and dimension tables.
 Power BI and Fabric semantic models, which are built for star schemas.
 dbt marts ( fct_ and dim_ models) reviewed by your team.
 What goes wrong without it
 Reports query the normalised app database and every analyst joins it differently.
 Mixed grains: an order-level fee on line rows inflates totals.
 One wide table per dashboard, each with its own definition of “customer”.
 Who expects you to know it
 Data and analytics engineers building warehouses and marts.
 BI developers building semantic models.
 Interviewers: “OLTP vs OLAP?”, “fact vs dimension?”, “what is the grain?”.

 On the job A stakeholder asks for “a dashboard of orders by product and region”. Before writing SQL you name the business process (orders), declare the grain (one row per order line), list the dimensions (date, product, customer, region) and the facts (quantity, amount). Everything after that is mechanical.

 The main idea dimensional modeling turns raw app tables into trusted, consistent, fast reporting, and it starts with a clear grain.
 why

passages.heading: When to reach for it, and when not to
passages.text:
Why this matters · choosing the right tool
 When to reach for it, and when not to
 Situation Reach for Why 
 Reporting and BI on a business process Star schema at a declared grain Simple joins, consistent totals 
 Operational application storage Normalised (3NF) model Built for writes, not analysis 
 One dashboard needs one wide table A wide table built from the star Convenient output, not the source of truth 
 Raw history from many changing sources Data Vault or a staging layer first Integration layer; usually still feeds stars 
 A one-off analysis on a small extract Query the extract directly A model is not worth it yet 

 How interviews test it
 “Explain OLTP vs OLAP and why we denormalise for analytics.”
 “What is the grain of this table?” is the most common modeling question.
 “Walk me through how you would design a model for X” (the four steps).
 Where it sits in your learning path
 Builds on: tables, keys, JOIN and GROUP BY.
 Next: Fact tables (measures and fact types), then Dimension tables (keys, SCDs, special dimensions).
 Later: dbt marts and semantic models built on these stars.

 The main idea use a star schema at a declared grain whenever people will analyse a business process; keep normalised models for applications.
 why

passages.heading: Before we start: five words you already need
passages.text:
Start here · a 60-second refresher
 Before we start: five words you already need
 Dimensional modeling is built on ordinary database ideas. If these five feel familiar, you are ready. If one is new, read its line twice — it will come up constantly.
 Word Meaning Tiny example 
 Table, row, column A table stores one kind of thing. Each row is one item; each column is one property. A products table: one row per product, with columns name and price . 
 Primary key (PK) A column whose value uniquely identifies each row in its table. product_id = P-1 identifies exactly one product. 
 Foreign key (FK) A column that stores another table’s primary key, to point at a row there. An order line stores product_id = P-1 to say which product was bought. 
 JOIN Combine rows from two tables where the keys match. Join order lines to products to see the product name next to each sale. 
 GROUP BY + SUM Collapse rows into groups and add up a number per group. SUM(amount) … GROUP BY category gives revenue per category. 

 What this course adds
 How to arrange tables so that those joins and sums answer business questions correctly — and keep answering them correctly as the business changes.
 How to read the diagrams
 Table boxes list their columns. Small tags explain each column’s role: PK FK M measure, and others introduced as we go.

 The main idea you do not need advanced SQL. You need to be comfortable reading a join and a GROUP BY; the rest is design thinking, which this course teaches.
 02

passages.heading: Meet Leafy, our example business
passages.text:
Start here · one example used throughout the course
 Meet Leafy, our example business
 Leafy is a small online plant shop. Customers order plants and accessories; warehouses in Austin and Denver ship them. The owner wants answers such as “Which product categories sell best each month?” and “Did customers who moved cities change what they buy?” 
 Here are Leafy’s first three orders. We will reuse these exact numbers in almost every lesson, so it is worth a careful look.
 order_number order_date customer line product qty unit_price line_amount 
 SO-5001 2026-03-02 Maya (Austin) 1 Monstera 1 40.00 40.00 
 SO-5001 2026-03-02 Maya (Austin) 2 Ceramic Pot 2 12.00 24.00 
 SO-5002 2026-03-02 Leo (Denver) 1 Snake Plant 1 25.00 25.00 
 SO-5003 2026-03-09 Maya (Denver) 1 Fertilizer 3 6.00 18.00 

 Numbers to remember
 Order totals: SO-5001 = 64 , SO-5002 = 25 , SO-5003 = 18 . All sales = 107 . Shipping fees (charged per order): 8, 5, and 0.
 Notice the details
 One order can contain several lines (products). Maya moved from Austin to Denver between her two orders — that will matter a lot when we talk about history.

 The main idea learning works best with a small example you can check by hand. Whenever a query result appears in this course, try to predict it from this table first.
 03

passages.heading: The problem: app databases are built for writing
passages.text:
Why dimensional modeling · two very different jobs
 The problem: app databases are built for writing
 Leafy’s website runs on an operational database (also called OLTP, online transaction processing). It is designed so the app can save an order quickly and never store the same fact twice. To do that, information is split into many small tables. This splitting is called normalization .
 customers source table 
 customer_id PK 
 name 
 address_id FK 

 addresses source table 
 address_id PK 
 city_id FK 
 street 

 cities source table 
 city_id PK 
 city_name 
 state_code 

 orders source table 
 order_id PK 
 customer_id FK 
 created_at 
 status_code 

 order_items source table 
 order_id FK 
 product_id FK 
 qty 
 price 

 products source table 
 product_id PK 
 name 
 subcategory_id FK 

 subcategories source table 
 subcategory_id PK 
 category_id FK 
 name 

 categories source table 
 category_id PK 
 name 

 Great for the app
 Changing a city name means updating one row in cities . Saving an order touches only a few rows. Nothing is duplicated, so nothing can get out of sync.
 Painful for analysis
 “Revenue by category and customer city” needs seven joins across eight tables. Status is a cryptic code. Each analyst may write the joins a little differently and get a different number.

 On the job When a new analytics project starts, the first thing you usually get is read access to the app database: dozens of normalised tables. Explaining why reports should not query them directly, and what you will build instead, is a conversation data engineers have with every stakeholder.

 The main idea operational databases are optimised for recording one transaction at a time. Analytics needs the opposite: reading millions of rows and slicing them by many descriptions. That is the gap dimensional modeling fills.
 04

passages.heading: Dimensional modeling in one sentence
passages.text:
Why dimensional modeling · the core idea
 Dimensional modeling in one sentence
 Store each business process as a table of measurements , surrounded by tables of descriptions you can filter and group by.
 01 Fact tables hold measurements
 Each row records a business event — a sale, a shipment, a class booking — with its numbers: quantity, amount, duration. Fact tables are long and narrow: many rows, few columns.
 02 Dimension tables hold descriptions
 Each row describes a “who, what, where, when”: a customer, a product, a date, a warehouse. Dimension tables are short and wide: fewer rows, many descriptive columns.
 03 Keys connect them
 Every fact row stores a key for each dimension that describes it. To answer a question you join the fact table to the dimensions you need, then group and sum.

 The approach was popularised by Ralph Kimball in The Data Warehouse Toolkit (1996, third edition 2013) and is still the most common way analytics data is organised — in warehouses such as Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks and Fabric, and in BI tools such as Power BI and Tableau.

 The main idea measurements in the middle, descriptions around the edge. Every technique in this course is a refinement of that one idea.
 05

passages.heading: Facts vs dimensions
passages.text:
Building blocks · measurements vs context
 Facts vs dimensions
 A fact is a measurement of an event
 Something happened in the business, and we measured it. Facts are almost always numbers, and usually you want to add them up.
 Leafy examples: quantity = 2, line_amount = 24.00, shipping_fee = 8.00.
 A dimension gives that event its context
 Dimensions answer who, what, where, when, how, and why. They are mostly text, and you use them to filter , group , and label results.
 Leafy examples: the product Ceramic Pot in category Accessories , the customer Maya in Austin , the date Monday 2 March 2026 .

 Sort each column from Leafy’s order lines:
 Column Fact or dimension? Why 
 line_amount Fact (measure) A number produced by the sale; summing it is meaningful. 
 quantity Fact (measure) A count of units; summing it gives units sold. 
 product name, category Dimension attribute Text that describes what was sold; you group by it. 
 customer city Dimension attribute Describes who / where ; you filter or group by it. 
 order_date Dimension (date) Describes when ; you group by month, weekday, quarter. 
 product weight in kg Dimension attribute A number, but it describes the product rather than measuring the sale. Test: does it change from sale to sale? 

 On the job In Fabric, Snowflake or a dbt project the same split appears as fct_ and dim_ tables. Power BI semantic models expect exactly this shape.

 The main idea ask “is this a measurement taken when the event happened, or a description of something involved in it?” Numbers that describe a thing (weight, list price) usually belong in the dimension.
 06

passages.heading: Hear the facts and dimensions in a question
passages.text:
Building blocks · a habit that makes design easy
 Hear the facts and dimensions in a question
 Business questions almost always follow the same shape: a number , then “by” one or more descriptions, sometimes with a filter. The number is a fact; the “by” words and filters are dimensions.
 Business question Fact (the number) Dimensions (by / for / where) 
 Revenue by category by month revenue = SUM(line_amount) product → category; date → month 
 Units sold in Denver last week SUM(quantity) customer → city; date → week 
 Average order value by marketing channel SUM(amount) ÷ COUNT(orders) order profile → channel 
 How many orders shipped late from each warehouse? COUNT of late orders warehouse; date (ship vs promised) 

 Why this matters
 When you interview stakeholders, write their questions down and underline the numbers and the “by” words. The numbers become columns in fact tables; the “by” words become dimension tables and their attributes.
 A useful rule of thumb
 If people say “ by X” or “ for each X” or “ only X”, then X belongs in a dimension. If they say “ how much ” or “ how many ”, that is a fact.

 On the job In requirement meetings, write down the questions word for word and underline the measures and the “by” words. That list becomes your first draft of the fact and dimension tables.

 The main idea a dimensional model is simply the shape of the questions people ask: measures to aggregate, descriptions to slice by.
 07

passages.heading: Anatomy of a fact table
passages.text:
Building blocks · what goes in, what stays out
 Anatomy of a fact table
 Leafy’s order-line fact table
 fact_order_line fact 
 date_key FK 
 customer_key FK 
 product_key FK 
 warehouse_key FK 
 order_number DD 
 line_number DD 
 quantity M 
 unit_price M 
 line_amount M 
 discount_amount M 
 One row per order line. Four rows for our sample orders.

 Three kinds of column
 Foreign keys (FK) — one per dimension that describes the event. Together they say who, what, where, when .
 Measures (M) — the numbers recorded by the event. These are what you SUM, COUNT, or AVG.
 Degenerate dimensions (DD) — transaction identifiers like the order number. The Dimension tables deck explains these.
 What stays out: descriptive text. The product name is not repeated on every sale row; it lives once in the product dimension and is reached through product_key .
 Fact tables are the biggest tables in a warehouse — often billions of rows — so they are kept narrow: integer keys and numbers.

 The main idea a fact row = keys to its context + the numbers measured. If you find yourself adding a text description to a fact table, it probably belongs in a dimension.
 08

passages.heading: Anatomy of a dimension table
passages.text:
Building blocks · wide, flat, and readable
 Anatomy of a dimension table
 Leafy’s product dimension
 dim_product dimension 
 product_key PK 
 product_id NK 
 product_name 
 subcategory 
 category 
 light_needs 
 is_pet_safe 
 pot_size_cm 
 supplier_name 

 product_key product_name subcategory category 
 1 Monstera Large plants Plants 
 2 Snake Plant Easy-care plants Plants 
 3 Ceramic Pot Pots Accessories 
 4 Fertilizer Plant care Accessories 

 Design habits
 Surrogate key (PK) — a warehouse-made number such as 1, 2, 3. The Dimension tables deck explains why.
 Natural key (NK) — the ID from the source system, kept so you can trace a row back.
 Flattened hierarchies — product → subcategory → category all sit in one row, even though “Plants” repeats. Repeating short text is cheap; extra joins are not.
 Readable labels, not codes — store “Yes / No” or “Pet safe / Not pet safe” instead of 1 / 0, and “Shipped” instead of status code 3. Report labels come straight from these columns.
 Many attributes — dimensions often have dozens of columns. Each one is a new way to slice the facts.

 The main idea a good dimension reads like a well-labelled spreadsheet: one row per thing, every useful description as its own column, nothing hidden behind codes or extra joins.
 09

passages.heading: The star schema
passages.text:
Building blocks · fact in the centre, dimensions around it
 The star schema
 Put the fact table in the middle and connect each dimension to it with a single key. Drawn on a page, it looks like a star — hence the name. Compare this with the eight-table source model from lesson 4.
 Leafy sales star fact_order_line fact 
 date_key FK 
 customer_key FK 
 product_key FK 
 warehouse_key FK 
 order_number DD 
 quantity M 
 line_amount M 

 dim_date dimension 
 date_key PK 
 full_date 
 month_name 
 quarter 
 is_weekend 

 dim_customer dimension 
 customer_key PK 
 customer_id NK 
 name 
 city 
 state 

 dim_product dimension 
 product_key PK 
 product_id NK 
 product_name 
 subcategory 
 category 

 dim_warehouse dimension 
 warehouse_key PK 
 warehouse_name 
 city 
 region 

 Every dimension joins directly to the fact table with one key. Tags: PK primary key · FK foreign key · DD degenerate dimension · NK natural key · M measure. 
 Each dimension is exactly one join away from the facts. Dimensions do not join to each other; every path goes through the centre.
 On the job Gold-layer marts and BI semantic models are almost always stars: one fact per business process, joined to shared dimensions by surrogate keys.

 The main idea one fact table + one join per dimension. That predictability is what makes star schemas easy to query, easy to explain, and fast.
 10

passages.heading: Why analytics prefers a star
passages.text:
Building blocks · star vs snowflake vs source model
 Why analytics prefers a star
 Compare two ways to store the product hierarchy 

 dim_product dimension 
 product_key PK 
 product_name 
 subcategory 
 category 

 One table. “Revenue by category” is one join from the fact table. “Plants” repeats on several rows — that is fine.

 dim_product dimension 
 product_key PK 
 product_name 
 subcategory_key FK 

 dim_subcategory dimension 
 subcategory_key PK 
 subcategory 
 category_key FK 

 dim_category dimension 
 category_key PK 
 category 

 Three tables. Less repetition, but “revenue by category” now needs three joins, and every user must know the chain.

 Simple to understand
 Business users can see the whole model on one page. Table names match how people talk: sales, products, customers, dates.
 Simple to query
 Every question has the same shape: join the fact to a few dimensions, filter, group, sum. Fewer joins also means fewer ways to make mistakes.
 Fast
 Engines and BI tools are optimised for this shape (“star join” plans, columnar compression of repeated text). Power BI’s own guidance recommends star schemas.

 A snowflake schema normalizes dimensions into sub-tables. It is not wrong, and sometimes useful for very large shared hierarchies, but it gives up simplicity for storage savings that rarely matter today. A one big table (everything flattened into the fact) is easy to query, but repeats descriptions on every row and makes history and reuse hard; teams often build it from a star.
 On the job A recurring design review question is “why not one big table?” or “why not keep it normalised?”. The answers on this slide (fewer, predictable joins; consistent attributes; BI-friendly) are the ones teams use.

 The main idea prefer a star by default: flatten hierarchies into the dimension and keep every dimension one join from the facts.
 11

passages.heading: Every star query has the same shape
passages.text:
Building blocks · join, filter, group, aggregate
 Every star query has the same shape
 Revenue by category for March 2026
 SQL 
 SELECT
 p.category,
 SUM(f.line_amount) AS revenue,
 SUM(f.quantity) AS units
FROM fact_order_line AS f
JOIN dim_product AS p ON p.product_key = f.product_key
JOIN dim_date AS d ON d.date_key = f.date_key
WHERE d.year = 2026
 AND d.month_name = 'March'
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

 category revenue units 
 Plants 65.00 2 
 Accessories 42.00 5 

 Read it as a recipe
 FROM the fact table — start from the measurements.
 JOIN each dimension you need, on its key.
 WHERE on dimension attributes — the filters.
 GROUP BY dimension attributes — the “by” words.
 SUM / COUNT the measures.
 Check it: Plants = Monstera 40 + Snake Plant 25 = 65. Accessories = Ceramic Pot 24 + Fertilizer 18 = 42. Total 107, matching lesson 3.
 BI tools such as Power BI generate exactly this query when someone drags “category” and “revenue” onto a chart.

 On the job Once the model is a star, every report and ad-hoc question is the same shape of SQL. That is what makes self-service BI and semantic layers possible.

 The main idea if your model is a proper star, every business question becomes the same five-step query. That consistency is the real payoff.
 12

passages.heading: Grain: the most important decision
passages.text:
Grain · what does one row represent?
 Grain: the most important decision
 The grain of a fact table is a precise statement of what one row represents.
 Grain statement Example fact table Rows for Leafy’s sample 
 One row per order fact_order 3 (SO-5001, SO-5002, SO-5003) 
 One row per order line (product within an order) fact_order_line 4 
 One row per product per warehouse per day fact_inventory_daily products × warehouses × days 
 One row per customer per day fact_customer_daily_activity customers × active days 
 One row per website session fact_web_session one per visit 

 Why it comes first
 The grain decides which dimensions can attach to a row and which measures make sense on it. A product can describe an order line , but not a whole order that contains three products.
 How to say it well
 Write it in business words, as a sentence, before choosing any columns: “One row per product on a customer order.” If two people read it and imagine different rows, it is not precise enough.

 On the job The grain statement goes into the model’s documentation (a dbt model description, for example) and is enforced with a uniqueness test on the grain columns.

 The main idea if you remember one thing from this course: before designing a fact table, finish the sentence “one row in this table represents one …”. Interviewers ask this constantly.
 13

passages.heading: The same sales at three different grains
passages.text:
Grain · what each grain can and cannot answer
 The same sales at three different grains
 Choose a grain 

 order_number order_date customer order_amount line_count 
 SO-5001 03-02 Maya 64.00 2 
 SO-5002 03-02 Leo 25.00 1 
 SO-5003 03-09 Maya 18.00 1 

 Can answer: average order value (107 ÷ 3 = 35.67), orders per customer. Cannot answer: revenue by product or category — SO-5001 contains two products and its 64 cannot be split.

 order_number line product customer qty line_amount 
 SO-5001 1 Monstera Maya 1 40.00 
 SO-5001 2 Ceramic Pot Maya 2 24.00 
 SO-5002 1 Snake Plant Leo 1 25.00 
 SO-5003 1 Fertilizer Maya 3 18.00 

 Can answer everything the order grain can (group lines by order_number), plus revenue by product and category. This is the most detailed — atomic — grain for sales.

 order_date product units revenue 
 03-02 Monstera 1 40.00 
 03-02 Ceramic Pot 2 24.00 
 03-02 Snake Plant 1 25.00 
 03-09 Fertilizer 3 18.00 

 A summary. Small and fast for daily product trends, but the customer and order are gone: you can no longer ask “revenue by city” or “average order value”.

 Moving from a fine grain to a coarser one is easy (GROUP BY). Moving the other way is impossible — the detail has been thrown away.

 The main idea finer grain = more questions answerable. A summary table can always be built from atomic data, never the other way round.
 14

passages.heading: Three rules for grain, and the classic mistake
passages.text:
Grain · atomic, declared first, never mixed
 Three rules for grain, and the classic mistake
 01 Prefer the atomic grain
 Store the most detailed level the source provides (order line, not order; individual event, not daily total). It answers the widest range of questions and survives new requirements. Build summaries on top if speed is needed.
 02 Declare it before columns
 Write the grain sentence first. Then a dimension is allowed only if it has a single value for that row; a measure only if it is true for exactly that row.
 03 Never mix grains
 Every row in one fact table must represent the same kind of thing. Facts recorded at a different level go in a different fact table.

 The mistake: order-level shipping on line rows
 order_number line line_amount shipping_fee 
 SO-5001 1 40.00 8.00 
 SO-5001 2 24.00 8.00 
 SO-5002 1 25.00 5.00 
 SO-5003 1 18.00 0.00 

 The shipping fee belongs to the order , but it was copied onto each line . SUM(shipping_fee) returns 21 ; the true total is 13 (8 + 5 + 0).
 Two correct fixes
 Allocate it down to the line grain, for example by each line’s share of the order amount: Monstera gets 8 × 40/64 = 5.00 , Ceramic Pot 8 × 24/64 = 3.00 . Now every column is true for its row, and sums are correct.
 Or keep a separate order-grain fact table ( fact_order ) for order-level measures such as shipping fee and order-level discounts.
 Either way, document the choice so nobody adds the order-level number back onto lines later.

 On the job The classic production bug is a header-level amount (shipping fee, order discount) copied onto every line row. Totals look fine for single-line orders and are wrong for the rest, so it can go unnoticed for weeks.

 The main idea double counting almost always comes from a measure stored at the wrong grain. Ask “is this number true for exactly one row?”
 15

passages.heading: The four-step design process
passages.text:
Grain · how every dimensional model is designed
 The four-step design process
 Kimball’s four steps give you an order to make decisions in. They work for a one-table project and for an enterprise warehouse, and they are a great structure for answering “design a data model for…” interview questions.
 01 Choose the business process a verb: take orders, ship parcels, book classes 
 An operational activity that generates events you can measure. One process → (usually) one fact table.

 02 Declare the grain “one row per order line” 
 The precise meaning of one row. Decided before anything else; it constrains the next two steps.

 03 Identify the dimensions who, what, where, when, how, why 
 Descriptions that have exactly one value for a row at this grain: date, customer, product, warehouse.

 04 Identify the facts the numbers measured 
 Measurements true at this grain: quantity, line amount, discount. Anything at another grain goes elsewhere.

 Leafy, worked through
 Process: customer orders . Grain: one row per product on an order . Dimensions: order date, customer, product, warehouse, promotion . Facts: quantity, unit price, line amount, discount amount .
 Start from requirements and data together
 Collect the business questions (lesson 7) and look at what the source systems actually record. The best design satisfies the questions using data that really exists.

 On the job Use the four steps as the agenda for a modeling workshop: process, grain, dimensions, facts. It keeps the conversation on business questions instead of source table names.

 The main idea process → grain → dimensions → facts. Say these four steps out loud in any modeling interview and you will already sound structured.
 16

passages.heading: A glossary to come back to
passages.text:
Quick reference · every term in this deck
 A glossary to come back to
 Term Meaning 
 Fact / measure A numeric measurement of a business event, stored in a fact table 
 Dimension / attribute A table of descriptive context (who, what, where, when) / one of its columns 
 OLTP / OLAP Systems built for many small writes (apps) / for reading and aggregating many rows (analytics) 
 Normalised / denormalised Data split into many tables to avoid repetition / combined into fewer, wider tables for reading 
 Grain What one row of a fact table represents; declared first 
 Star / snowflake schema Fact surrounded by flat dimensions / dimensions normalized into sub-tables 
 Four-step design process Business process → grain → dimensions → facts 
 Natural / surrogate key Source-system ID / warehouse-generated row ID 

 17

passages.heading: Recap: what to remember when you close this deck
passages.text:
Recap · the ideas that carry everything else
 Recap: what to remember when you close this deck
 App databases are built for writing ; analytics needs a shape built for reading and aggregating.
 Measurements in the centre, descriptions around them. Facts measure events; dimensions give context.
 A star keeps every dimension one join away from the fact, so every report query has the same simple shape.
 Grain first, always. Say what one row is before choosing columns. Prefer atomic grain; never mix grains.
 Design with four steps : business process, grain, dimensions, facts.

 The main idea when in doubt, return to the questions the business asks: the measures are the numbers, the dimensions are the “by” words, and the grain is what one answer row is built from.
 18

passages.heading: Fact tables
passages.text:
Data engineering · dimensional modeling · lesson deck
 Know how
 every number adds up. 
 Fact tables: additive, semi-additive and non-additive measures; transaction, periodic snapshot, accumulating snapshot and factless facts.
 A fact table is where the numbers live. Two decisions shape it: how each measure may be added up, and which rhythm the table follows (one row per event, per period, or per process).
 Leafy, the small plant shop from the first deck, is reused so every number can be checked by hand. It builds on Why dimensional modeling (facts, dimensions, grain).
 Meet Leafy again → 13 short lessons 

 The route through the deck Part A · measures Additive, semi-additive, non-additive Which numbers can be summed, and along which dimensions

 Part B · fact table types Transaction, periodic snapshot, accumulating snapshot Match the table to the rhythm of the process

 Part C · no numbers Factless fact tables Record that something happened, or could have

 Wrap-up Glossary, recap, references Practice with these ideas in the FitHub project deck

 Part of a split series. This deck is one lesson of the former “Dimensional modeling” course. Sibling decks, in order: Why dimensional modeling , Fact tables , Dimension tables , Model a business end to end (bus matrix and the FitHub project).

passages.heading: Why this matters on the job
passages.text:
Why this matters · the need behind the topic
 Why this matters on the job
 Most wrong numbers on dashboards come from facts that are aggregated the wrong way: twelve month-end balances summed into a “yearly balance”, averages of averages, or snapshot rows treated like events. Knowing measure additivity and the three fact table types prevents these errors and is a standard interview topic.
 Where you will use it
 Designing sales, inventory, subscription and fulfilment marts.
 Defining measures in semantic models (Power BI, dbt metrics) with the right aggregation.
 Choosing how a pipeline loads a table: append events, write snapshots, or update milestones.
 What goes wrong without it
 Balances summed over time; ratios averaged instead of recomputed.
 Daily snapshots missing days when nothing changed, so trends break.
 Process durations calculated from scattered event rows with fragile self-joins.
 Who expects you to know it
 Analytics engineers and BI developers defining measures.
 Data engineers loading facts on a schedule.
 Interviewers: “give an example of each fact table type”, “why is a balance semi-additive?”.

 On the job Operations wants “average days from order to delivery, by warehouse”. You choose an accumulating snapshot: one row per order, a date key per milestone, lag measures between them, updated as each milestone arrives. The average is then one GROUP BY.

 The main idea measures must be aggregated the way their meaning allows, and the fact table type must match the rhythm of the process.
 why

passages.heading: When to reach for it, and when not to
passages.text:
Why this matters · choosing the right tool
 When to reach for it, and when not to
 Situation Reach for Why 
 Each event or transaction Transaction fact table Most detailed; any roll-up possible 
 Level measured at regular intervals (stock, balance) Periodic snapshot One row per thing per period, even without change 
 Process with milestones (order → ship → deliver) Accumulating snapshot One row per instance; lags between dates 
 Event with no number (attendance, coverage) Factless fact table Count rows; compare coverage with events 
 Ratio or percentage Store numerator and denominator Recompute at every level; never average ratios 

 How interviews test it
 “Give an example of transaction, periodic and accumulating snapshot facts.”
 “How should a balance be totalled for a year?”
 “Which students enrolled but never attended?” (factless facts).
 Where it sits in your learning path
 Builds on: Why dimensional modeling (facts, dimensions, grain).
 Next: Dimension tables (keys, SCDs, special dimensions).
 Practice: the FitHub project in Model a business end to end.

 The main idea pick the fact type from how the business process happens, and store measures so every report can aggregate them correctly.
 why

passages.heading: Meet Leafy, our example business
passages.text:
Start here · one example used throughout the course
 Meet Leafy, our example business
 Leafy is a small online plant shop. Customers order plants and accessories; warehouses in Austin and Denver ship them. The owner wants answers such as “Which product categories sell best each month?” and “Did customers who moved cities change what they buy?” 
 Here are Leafy’s first three orders. We will reuse these exact numbers in almost every lesson, so it is worth a careful look.
 order_number order_date customer line product qty unit_price line_amount 
 SO-5001 2026-03-02 Maya (Austin) 1 Monstera 1 40.00 40.00 
 SO-5001 2026-03-02 Maya (Austin) 2 Ceramic Pot 2 12.00 24.00 
 SO-5002 2026-03-02 Leo (Denver) 1 Snake Plant 1 25.00 25.00 
 SO-5003 2026-03-09 Maya (Denver) 1 Fertilizer 3 6.00 18.00 

 Numbers to remember
 Order totals: SO-5001 = 64 , SO-5002 = 25 , SO-5003 = 18 . All sales = 107 . Shipping fees (charged per order): 8, 5, and 0.
 Notice the details
 One order can contain several lines (products). Maya moved from Austin to Denver between her two orders — that will matter a lot when we talk about history.

 The main idea learning works best with a small example you can check by hand. Whenever a query result appears in this course, try to predict it from this table first.
 02

passages.heading: Three kinds of measures
passages.text:
Measures · which numbers can be added up, and along which dimensions
 Three kinds of measures
 Not every number in a fact table can simply be summed. Classify each measure by whether SUM gives a meaningful answer across all , some , or none of the dimensions.
 Kind Can be summed across… Leafy examples How to aggregate 
 Additive every dimension (products, customers, dates…) quantity, line_amount, discount_amount, shipping_fee (at the right grain) SUM, freely 
 Semi-additive some dimensions, but not time units on hand in a warehouse; a customer’s gift-card balance SUM across products or warehouses; across time use the period-end value, or an average 
 Non-additive no dimension unit_price, discount %, margin %, conversion rate, distinct customer counts Store the additive parts; compute the ratio after summing 

 Why it matters
 A BI tool will happily SUM any number column. If a measure is semi- or non-additive, the default total on a report is wrong unless the model or the measure definition prevents it.
 Best practice
 Prefer additive measures. Store numerators and denominators ( margin_amount , sales_amount ) rather than ratios. Document semi-additive measures and define their aggregation explicitly in the semantic layer.

 On the job Semantic models (Power BI, dbt metrics, Fabric) need to know how each measure aggregates. Marking a balance as semi-additive is how dashboards avoid summing twelve month-end balances into one meaningless number.

 The main idea additive: sum anything. Semi-additive: sum anything except time. Non-additive: never sum — rebuild from additive parts.
 03

passages.heading: Semi-additive measures in action
passages.text:
Measures · stock levels and balances
 Semi-additive measures in action
 Leafy records how many Monsteras are on the shelf at the end of each day in each warehouse. That number is a level (a state at a moment), not an activity (something that happened during the period).
 date warehouse units_on_hand units_sold 
 03-01 Austin 10 0 
 03-01 Denver 4 0 
 03-02 Austin 9 1 
 03-02 Denver 4 0 
 03-03 Austin 9 0 
 03-03 Denver 3 1 

 Ask a question 

 “How many Monsteras did we have on 3 March?” Austin 9 + Denver 3 = 12 . Summing a level across warehouses (or products) on the same day is correct.

 “How many Monsteras did Austin have in the first three days of March?” SUM gives 10 + 9 + 9 = 28 . Nonsense: there were never 28 plants. Use the last value (9, the closing stock) or the average (9.33).

 units_sold is an activity, so it is fully additive: Austin sold 1 and Denver sold 1 → 2 over the three days. Snapshots often carry both kinds of measure side by side.

 SQL 
 -- Closing stock per warehouse for March: take the last day of the period
SELECT w.warehouse_name, SUM(f.units_on_hand) AS closing_units
FROM fact_inventory_daily AS f
JOIN dim_warehouse AS w ON w.warehouse_key = f.warehouse_key
JOIN dim_date AS d ON d.date_key = f.date_key
WHERE d.full_date = DATE '2026-03-31' -- one day only: no summing over time
GROUP BY w.warehouse_name;

 On the job Inventory levels, account balances, open tickets and subscriber counts are all semi-additive; finance and operations reports use the closing or average value over time.

 The main idea balances, stock levels, headcounts and queue lengths are semi-additive: sum them across things, but pick one point in time (or average) across time.
 04

passages.heading: Non-additive measures: store the parts
passages.text:
Measures · ratios, percentages, prices, and distinct counts
 Non-additive measures: store the parts
 The trap: averaging percentages
 order sales_amount margin_amount margin_% 
 A 100.00 50.00 50% 
 B 10.00 1.00 10% 

 AVG(margin_%) = (50% + 10%) ÷ 2 = 30% . But the business earned 51 on 110 of sales: the true margin is 46.4% . A small order counted as much as a large one.
 The fix: sum, then divide
 SQL 
 SELECT
 SUM(margin_amount) * 100.0
 / NULLIF(SUM(sales_amount), 0) AS margin_pct
FROM fact_order_line; -- 46.4

 Store the additive numerator and denominator in the fact table. Compute the ratio at query time, at whatever level the report needs.

 Non-additive measure Store instead 
 unit_price line_amount and quantity (price = amount ÷ quantity) 
 discount % discount_amount and gross_amount 
 conversion rate sessions and orders 
 count of distinct customers keep customer_key on the fact and COUNT(DISTINCT) at query time — daily distinct counts cannot be added into a monthly one 

 On the job Conversion rates, margins and averages are stored as their parts (numerator and denominator) so any report can recompute the ratio at its own level. Averaging stored ratios is a frequent review finding.

 The main idea if a number is a ratio or a distinct count, do not sum or average it. Keep its additive ingredients and recompute.
 05

passages.heading: Three types of fact table
passages.text:
Fact table types · a map before the details
 Three types of fact table
 Business processes measure things in different rhythms. Some record each event; some take a regular picture of a level; some follow one item through a series of steps. Each rhythm gets its own kind of fact table.
 Transaction Periodic snapshot Accumulating snapshot 
 Grain One row per event One row per thing per period One row per process instance, for its whole life 
 Leafy example fact_order_line fact_inventory_daily fact_order_fulfillment 
 Rows appear When an event happens Every period, even with no activity Once, when the process starts 
 Rows change? Never (insert only) Never (new set each period) Yes — updated as milestones happen 
 Dates One event date One snapshot date Several milestone dates (role-playing) 
 Typical measures Additive amounts and counts Semi-additive levels + period activity Durations between steps, milestone counts 
 Answers “What happened?” “What was the level at the end of each period?” “How long does each step take? Where are things stuck?” 

 A fourth, the factless fact table (lesson 10), has no numeric measure at all. It can follow any of these rhythms.
 On the job Picking the fact table type is part of every new mart design. Orders and clicks are transactions; daily inventory and month-end balances are periodic snapshots; order fulfilment and loan applications are accumulating snapshots.

 The main idea events → transaction fact; regular measurements of a level → periodic snapshot; a pipeline with milestones → accumulating snapshot. This comparison is a very common interview question.
 06

passages.heading: Transaction fact tables
passages.text:
Fact table types · one row per event
 Transaction fact tables
 Leafy’s order lines
 fact_order_line fact 
 date_key FK 
 customer_key FK 
 product_key FK 
 warehouse_key FK 
 promotion_key FK 
 order_number DD 
 line_number DD 
 quantity M 
 line_amount M 
 discount_amount M 
 Grain: one row per product on a customer order.

 Characteristics
 Most common and most detailed. Sales, payments, clicks, log-ins, sensor readings.
 Insert-only. An event that happened does not change. Corrections arrive as new rows (e.g., a return or a reversal).
 Sparse. Rows exist only when something happens. Leafy had no orders from 3 to 8 March, so there are no rows for those days — to show zeros, join from dim_date .
 Additive measures , so almost any roll-up works.
 Limitation: to know a level (“how much stock on 31 March?”) you would have to replay every event since the beginning. That is what snapshots solve.

 The main idea transaction facts record what happened, one event per row, and never change. Start here for most business processes.
 07

passages.heading: Periodic snapshot fact tables
passages.text:
Fact table types · a regular picture of a level
 Periodic snapshot fact tables
 Leafy’s daily inventory
 fact_inventory_daily fact 
 snapshot_date_key FK 
 product_key FK 
 warehouse_key FK 
 units_on_hand M 
 units_received M 
 units_sold M 
 inventory_value M 
 Grain: one row per product per warehouse per day.

 date product warehouse on_hand sold 
 03-02 Monstera Austin 9 1 
 03-03 Monstera Austin 9 0 
 03-04 Monstera Austin 9 0 

 Characteristics
 Dense. A row exists for every product × warehouse × day, even when nothing happened (highlighted rows). “No activity” is itself information.
 Predictable size : products × warehouses × days. 2,000 products × 2 warehouses × 365 days ≈ 1.5 million rows a year.
 Semi-additive levels (on hand, balance) sit next to additive activity for the period (received, sold).
 Common periods: daily inventory, monthly account balances, month-end subscription status, weekly headcount.
 Built by taking the current state at the end of each period, or by aggregating transactions — a snapshot complements a transaction fact table; it does not replace it.

 On the job Daily or monthly snapshots (stock on hand, account balances, active subscriptions) are built by a scheduled job that writes one row per thing per period, even when nothing changed.

 The main idea periodic snapshots answer “what was the level at the end of each period?” cheaply. Remember: their level measures cannot be summed across time.
 08

passages.heading: Accumulating snapshot fact tables
passages.text:
Fact table types · one row that follows a process to the end
 Accumulating snapshot fact tables
 Leafy wants to know how long fulfilment takes. An order passes through milestones: placed → shipped → delivered . An accumulating snapshot has one row per order and a date column for each milestone, filled in as the order progresses. Step through SO-5001:
 Timeline for SO-5001 

 order_number order_date shipped_date delivered_date days_to_ship days_ship_to_deliver is_delivered 
 SO-5001 2026-03-02 Not yet Not yet NULL NULL No 

 Row inserted when the order is placed. Future milestones point at a special date row meaning “not yet happened” (the Dimension tables deck).

 order_number order_date shipped_date delivered_date days_to_ship days_ship_to_deliver is_delivered 
 SO-5001 2026-03-02 2026-03-03 Not yet 1 NULL No 

 The same row is updated : shipped date filled, days_to_ship = 1.

 order_number order_date shipped_date delivered_date days_to_ship days_ship_to_deliver is_delivered 
 SO-5001 2026-03-02 2026-03-03 2026-03-06 1 3 Yes 

 Updated again. The row is now complete; total order-to-door time = 4 days.

 Characteristics
 The only fact type whose rows are routinely updated .
 Several dates, all pointing at dim_date in different roles (the Dimension tables deck).
 Measures are usually lags (durations between milestones) and milestone counts.
 Questions it answers
 “Average days from order to delivery by warehouse.” “How many orders are shipped but not delivered right now?” ( shipped_date known AND is_delivered = 'No' ). “Which step is the bottleneck this month?”
 Other examples: insurance claims, loan applications, hiring pipelines, support tickets.

 On the job Fulfilment pipelines, claims processing and hiring funnels are modelled as accumulating snapshots; the row is updated as each milestone happens, which is why these tables are often loaded with MERGE.

 The main idea accumulating snapshots model a pipeline with a clear start, defined milestones, and an end. One row per item, updated in place.
 09

passages.heading: Factless fact tables
passages.text:
Fact table types · recording that something happened, or could have
 Factless fact tables
 Some events have nothing to measure except that they happened. A factless fact table has foreign keys (and maybe degenerate dimensions) but no numeric measure . You analyse it by counting rows.
 01 Event tracking: workshop attendance
 fact_workshop_attendance fact 
 date_key FK 
 customer_key FK 
 workshop_key FK 
 store_key FK 
 Grain: one row per customer attending a workshop.

 SQL 
 SELECT w.workshop_name, COUNT(*) AS attendees
FROM fact_workshop_attendance AS f
JOIN dim_workshop AS w ON w.workshop_key = f.workshop_key
GROUP BY w.workshop_name;

 Leafy runs repotting workshops. Each attendance is an event with no amount; COUNT(*) is the measure.
 02 Coverage: what was possible
 fact_promotion_coverage fact 
 date_key FK 
 product_key FK 
 promotion_key FK 
 Grain: one row per product per day it is on promotion.

 SQL 
 -- Promoted products that did NOT sell during the promotion
SELECT DISTINCT p.product_name
FROM fact_promotion_coverage AS c
JOIN dim_product AS p ON p.product_key = c.product_key
WHERE c.promotion_key = 12 -- Spring Sale
 AND NOT EXISTS (
 SELECT 1 FROM fact_order_line AS f
 WHERE f.product_key = c.product_key
 AND f.date_key = c.date_key);

 A sales table only records what did sell. To find what did not happen, you need a record of what could have — eligibility, schedules, assignments.

 On the job Attendance, sign-ins, product views without a price and “promotion coverage” are factless facts. They answer “what happened” and, with a coverage table, “what could have happened but did not”.

 The main idea no measure does not mean no value: factless facts record events (attendance, registrations) or coverage (eligibility, schedules) so you can count them and find what is missing.
 10

passages.heading: A glossary to come back to
passages.text:
Quick reference · every term in this deck
 A glossary to come back to
 Term Meaning 
 Fact / measure A numeric measurement of a business event, stored in a fact table 
 Grain What one row of a fact table represents; declared first 
 Additive / semi-additive / non-additive Summable across all / all but time / no dimensions 
 Transaction / periodic / accumulating Fact per event / per thing per period / per process instance, updated through milestones 
 Factless fact table Fact table with no measures, recording events or coverage 

 11

passages.heading: Recap: what to remember when you close this deck
passages.text:
Recap · the ideas that carry everything else
 Recap: what to remember when you close this deck
 Know how each number adds up. Additive sums everywhere; semi-additive not over time; non-additive never: store the parts.
 A balance or stock level is semi-additive : sum across products or accounts, but over time take the closing value or the average.
 Match the fact type to the rhythm. Events → transaction; levels per period → periodic snapshot; pipelines with milestones → accumulating snapshot.
 An accumulating snapshot is updated as milestones happen and carries one date key per milestone.
 A factless fact records events or coverage with no measure; count its rows.

 The main idea every fact table has a declared grain, a rhythm, and a known way each measure aggregates.
 12

passages.heading: Dimension tables
passages.text:
Data engineering · dimensional modeling · lesson deck
 Keep the context
 right, and its history. 
 Dimension tables: surrogate keys, slowly changing dimensions, date, role-playing, degenerate, junk, unknown members, bridges and conformed dimensions.
 Dimensions hold the descriptive context behind every “by” in a report. This deck covers how the warehouse keys them, how it keeps history when descriptions change, and the special dimensions that solve recurring design problems.
 Leafy, the small plant shop from the first deck, is reused so every number can be checked by hand. It builds on Why dimensional modeling and Fact tables .
