passages.heading: Why this matters on the job
passages.text:
Why this matters · the need behind the topic
 Why this matters on the job
 Dimensions are what users filter and group by, so their mistakes show up everywhere: last year’s sales move to a customer’s new city, a NULL key drops rows from totals, a customer in two segments doubles revenue. Surrogate keys, SCDs and the special dimension techniques prevent these problems, and interviewers ask about them in almost every modeling round.
 Where you will use it
 Customer, product and employee dimensions with history (dbt snapshots, MERGE loads).
 Shared dim_date and conformed dimensions used by every mart.
 BI semantic models with role-playing dates and many-to-many relationships.
 What goes wrong without it
 History overwritten: past reports change when a description changes.
 NULL foreign keys silently drop facts from inner-joined reports.
 Many-to-many relationships double count without a bridge.
 Who expects you to know it
 Data and analytics engineers who load and maintain dimensions.
 BI developers wiring relationships in semantic models.
 Interviewers: “SCD Type 1 vs 2?”, “why surrogate keys?”, “order date, ship date, delivery date?”.

 On the job Marketing asks for “revenue by customer city, as it was when they bought”. You keep city as a Type 2 attribute in dim_customer , the fact load looks up the customer version valid on the order date, and the report needs no special logic.

 The main idea well-designed dimensions keep context correct over time and make every fact easy to slice.
 why

passages.heading: When to reach for it, and when not to
passages.text:
Why this matters · choosing the right tool
 When to reach for it, and when not to
 Situation Reach for Why 
 Corrections where history should change SCD Type 1 (overwrite) Past reports show the corrected value 
 Changes where “as was” matters SCD Type 2 (new row, valid dates) Old facts keep old descriptions 
 Several dates on one fact Role-playing date dimension One dim_date, several foreign keys 
 Missing or late dimension values Unknown / inferred member rows Never a NULL key; totals stay complete 
 One fact row relates to many dimension rows Bridge table with weights Avoids double counting 

 How interviews test it
 “How do you track a customer changing address?” (Type 2 plus the as-of lookup).
 “Why not use the source system’s ID?” (surrogate keys).
 “Where does the order number go?”, “how do you model a customer in many segments?”.
 Where it sits in your learning path
 Builds on: Why dimensional modeling and Fact tables.
 Next: Model a business end to end (bus matrix, full model, FitHub project).
 Later: dbt snapshots implement Type 2; SQL correctness covers bridge-table fan-out in queries.

 The main idea decide history per attribute, key everything with surrogate keys, and reach for the special dimensions when their problem appears.
 why

passages.heading: Meet Leafy, our example business
passages.text:
Start here · one example used throughout the course
 Meet Leafy, our example business
 Leafy is a small online plant shop. Customers order plants and accessories; warehouses in Austin and Denver ship them. The owner wants answers such as “Which product categories sell best each month?” and “Did customers who moved cities change what they buy?” 
 Here are Leafy’s first three orders. We will reuse these exact numbers in almost every lesson, so it is worth a careful look.
 order_number order_date customer line product qty unit_price line_amount 
 SO-5001 2026-03-02 Maya (Austin) 1 Monstera 1 40.00 40.00 
 SO-5001 2026-03-02 Maya (Austin) 2 Ceramic Pot 2 12.00 24.00 
 SO-5002 2026-03-02 Leo (Denver) 1 Snake Plant 1 25.00 25.00 
 SO-5003 2026-03-09 Maya (Denver) 1 Fertilizer 3 6.00 18.00 

 Numbers to remember
 Order totals: SO-5001 = 64 , SO-5002 = 25 , SO-5003 = 18 . All sales = 107 . Shipping fees (charged per order): 8, 5, and 0.
 Notice the details
 One order can contain several lines (products). Maya moved from Austin to Denver between her two orders — that will matter a lot when we talk about history.

 The main idea learning works best with a small example you can check by hand. Whenever a query result appears in this course, try to predict it from this table first.
 02

passages.heading: Surrogate keys: why the warehouse makes its own IDs
passages.text:
Keys · surrogate vs natural keys
 Surrogate keys: why the warehouse makes its own IDs
 A natural key (also called business key) is the ID that comes from the source system, such as customer_id = C-101 . A surrogate key is a meaningless integer the warehouse assigns itself (1, 2, 3…). Dimensions use the surrogate key as their primary key and keep the natural key as an ordinary column.
 Five problems surrogate keys solve 

 source customer_id name 
 web shop 1001 Maya 
 market stall POS 1001 Raj 

 Leafy also sells at a weekend market with its own till system. Both systems use 1001 for different people. A warehouse-generated key gives Maya and Raj different keys (1 and 7); the natural key is kept alongside with its source.

 customer_key customer_id name city 
 1 C-101 Maya Austin 
 4 C-101 Maya Denver 

 To keep Maya’s old and new city (SCD Type 2, lesson 6) the dimension needs two rows for one customer. The natural key C-101 is no longer unique; the surrogate key is.

 Source systems get migrated, IDs get reformatted (C-101 → CUST-000101), emails used as IDs change, and deleted IDs are sometimes reused. Surrogate keys insulate every fact row from these events: only the dimension’s mapping needs updating.

 A sale with no known customer can point at a special row with key −1 “Unknown” (lesson 15). There is no natural key for “unknown”, but a surrogate key can represent it.

 A 4-byte integer is smaller than a 36-character text ID. On a billion-row fact table, narrow integer keys save storage and make joins faster.

 In practice
 Generate them with an identity / sequence column, or a deterministic hash of natural key + source (common in dbt and lakehouse pipelines). Fact tables store only surrogate keys.
 One exception: dates
 Date dimensions commonly use a readable key such as 20260302 . Dates never change meaning and never collide, so a “smart” key is safe and convenient.

 On the job Surrogate keys are generated in the dimension load (identity columns, sequences, or a hash of the natural key and version in dbt). They make Type 2 history and “Unknown” rows possible.

 The main idea natural keys identify things in a source system; surrogate keys identify rows in the warehouse. Keep both, but join on the surrogate.
 03

passages.heading: Descriptions change. What should history show?
passages.text:
Slowly changing dimensions · the question behind every SCD type
 Descriptions change. What should history show?
 On 5 March 2026 Maya moved from Austin to Denver . Her first order (SO-5001, 64.00) was placed while she lived in Austin; her third (SO-5003, 18.00) after she moved. The source system simply overwrote her city — it only knows where she lives now .
 The business question
 “What were our sales by customer city in March?”
 Two different answers are both reasonable, depending on what the business means:
 Two possible answers
 Meaning Austin Denver 
 Where the customer lived at the time of each sale (“as was”) 64 43 
 Where the customer lives today (“as is”) 0 107 

 Dimension attributes that change occasionally — a customer’s city, a product’s category, an employee’s department — are called slowly changing dimensions (SCDs). The SCD “type” is the rule you choose for how the warehouse reacts to a change. It is decided per attribute , not per table.
 On the job Ask the business per attribute: “if a customer moves, should last year’s sales move with them?”. The answer decides Type 1 or Type 2 and belongs in the model’s documentation.

 The main idea an SCD type is an answer to “when this description changes, should old facts keep the old description or show the new one?”
 04

passages.heading: SCD Type 1: overwrite
passages.text:
Slowly changing dimensions · Type 1 · keep only the current value
 SCD Type 1: overwrite
 Maya’s dimension row 

 customer_key customer_id name city 
 1 C-101 Maya Austin 

 customer_key customer_id name city 
 1 C-101 Maya Denver 

 Same row, same key, city updated in place. All of Maya’s sales — past and future — now show Denver.

 How it works
 UPDATE dim_customer SET city = 'Denver' WHERE customer_id = 'C-101'; 
 Simple and cheap: one row per customer, nothing else changes. Fact rows keep pointing at key 1.
 Consequence
 History is restated . Last month’s “Austin sales” report would now show 0 for Maya, and a report run before the change can no longer be reproduced.
 Use it when
 The old value was a mistake (a typo in a name), or nobody needs the old value for analysis (an email address, a phone number). Many attributes in real dimensions are Type 1.

 The main idea Type 1 = overwrite. Simple, but it rewrites the past. Use it for corrections and for attributes whose history does not matter.
 05

passages.heading: SCD Type 2: add a new row
passages.text:
Slowly changing dimensions · Type 2 · preserve full history
 SCD Type 2: add a new row
 Instead of overwriting, close Maya’s old row and add a new row with a new surrogate key . Each row is a version of the customer, valid for a date range.
 customer_key customer_id name city valid_from valid_to is_current 
 1 C-101 Maya Austin 2025-01-10 2026-03-04 false 
 2 C-102 Leo Denver 2025-06-01 9999-12-31 true 
 3 C-103 Ana Seattle 2025-11-20 9999-12-31 true 
 4 C-101 Maya Denver 2026-03-05 9999-12-31 true 

 Facts point to the version that was true at the time
 order_number order_date customer_key line_amount 
 SO-5001 03-02 1 (Maya, Austin) 64.00 
 SO-5002 03-02 2 (Leo, Denver) 25.00 
 SO-5003 03-09 4 (Maya, Denver) 18.00 

 Sales by city now gives Austin 64 , Denver 43 — the “as was” answer — with an ordinary join on customer_key .
 The housekeeping columns
 valid_from / valid_to — the date range this version was true. The open-ended current row uses a far-future date such as 9999-12-31 rather than NULL, so range checks stay simple.
 is_current — a flag for quickly finding the latest version.
 The natural key customer_id repeats across versions — this is exactly why dimensions need surrogate keys (lesson 3).

 On the job Type 2 dimensions are how warehouses keep “as was” history for customers, products and org structures. In dbt, snapshots generate exactly these valid_from / valid_to rows.

 The main idea Type 2 = new row per change, new surrogate key, effective dates. Old facts keep the old description automatically. It is the most important SCD type to understand.
 06

passages.heading: How a Type 2 load works
passages.text:
Slowly changing dimensions · Type 2 · the two steps, and the fact lookup
 How a Type 2 load works
 Step 1 and 2: maintain the dimension
 SQL 
 -- 1. Expire current rows whose tracked attributes changed
UPDATE dim_customer AS d
SET valid_to = CURRENT_DATE - 1,
 is_current = FALSE
FROM stg_customer AS s
WHERE d.customer_id = s.customer_id
 AND d.is_current
 AND d.city IS DISTINCT FROM s.city; -- tracked attribute(s)

-- 2. Insert a new current row for anyone without one
-- (brand-new customers, and the ones just expired)
INSERT INTO dim_customer
 (customer_id, name, city, valid_from, valid_to, is_current)
SELECT s.customer_id, s.name, s.city,
 CURRENT_DATE, DATE '9999-12-31', TRUE
FROM stg_customer AS s
LEFT JOIN dim_customer AS d
 ON d.customer_id = s.customer_id AND d.is_current
WHERE d.customer_id IS NULL;

 customer_key is an identity column, so each insert gets a new key automatically. Many tools package this logic: MERGE statements, dbt snapshots, or Delta / Databricks change-data-feed patterns.
 Step 3: load facts with an “as of” lookup
 SQL 
 INSERT INTO fact_order_line (date_key, customer_key, …)
SELECT d.date_key,
 COALESCE(c.customer_key, -1), -- unknown member
 …
FROM stg_order_lines AS s
JOIN dim_date AS d ON d.full_date = s.order_date
LEFT JOIN dim_customer AS c
 ON c.customer_id = s.customer_id
 AND s.order_date BETWEEN c.valid_from
 AND c.valid_to;

 Match on the natural key and the date range, so each sale picks up the version that was valid on its order date. SO-5001 (2 March) finds key 1; SO-5003 (9 March) finds key 4.
 This uses inclusive dates: the old row ends the day before the new one starts. If you track changes with timestamps, use a half-open range ( valid_from <= t AND t < valid_to ) instead.

 On the job A Type 2 load is usually a MERGE or a dbt snapshot that closes the current row and inserts a new version. Loading the fact must then look up the version that was valid on the event date.

 The main idea Type 2 loading is: detect change → expire old row → insert new row → look up facts by natural key and date. Load dimensions before facts.
 07

passages.heading: Querying a Type 2 dimension correctly
passages.text:
Slowly changing dimensions · counting, “as was”, and “as is”
 Querying a Type 2 dimension correctly
 Three common questions 

 SQL 
 SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_in_dim, -- 4 ✗ counts versions
 COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers, -- 3 ✓
 COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE is_current) AS current_rows -- 3 ✓
FROM dim_customer;

 A Type 2 dimension has one row per version , not per customer. Count distinct natural keys, or filter to current rows.

 SQL 
 SELECT c.city, SUM(f.line_amount) AS revenue
FROM fact_order_line AS f
JOIN dim_customer AS c ON c.customer_key = f.customer_key
GROUP BY c.city; -- Austin 64, Denver 43

 The normal join gives history as it was at the time of each sale. This is the default behaviour of a Type 2 model.

 SQL 
 SELECT cur.city, SUM(f.line_amount) AS revenue
FROM fact_order_line AS f
JOIN dim_customer AS hist ON hist.customer_key = f.customer_key
JOIN dim_customer AS cur ON cur.customer_id = hist.customer_id
 AND cur.is_current
GROUP BY cur.city; -- Denver 107

 Hop from the historical version to the current version through the natural (or a durable) key. Some teams add “current_city” columns to every version (a Type 6 hybrid, next lesson) to make this a single join.

 Point-in-time questions
 “How many customers lived in Austin on 1 March?” → WHERE DATE '2026-03-01' BETWEEN valid_from AND valid_to AND city = 'Austin' .
 Interview phrasing
 Be ready to explain “as was” vs “as is” reporting, and why COUNT(*) on a Type 2 dimension over-counts.

 On the job The most common Type 2 query bug is counting rows instead of distinct natural keys, so one moved customer counts twice. Reviewers check for this.

 The main idea Type 2 makes “as was” the default and “as is” possible. Always count entities by natural key, not by dimension rows.
 08

passages.heading: The other SCD types, and choosing per attribute
passages.text:
Slowly changing dimensions · Types 0, 3, 4, 6 and a decision table
 The other SCD types, and choosing per attribute
 Type What happens on change Use when Example 
 Type 0 Nothing — the original value is kept forever The value is defined as “original” first_order_date, original_signup_channel 
 Type 1 Overwrite Corrections; history not needed name typo, email, phone 
 Type 2 New row, new key, effective dates History matters for analysis city, customer segment, product category 
 Type 3 Add a previous_… column next to the current one One planned change where people compare “old vs new” previous_sales_region after a re-organisation 
 Type 4 (mini-dimension) Move fast-changing attributes to a small separate dimension with its own key on the fact Attributes change so often Type 2 would explode the row count loyalty_tier, age_band, income_band 
 Type 6 (1 + 2 + 3) Type 2 rows, plus a current_… column overwritten on every version Need “as was” and “as is” in one easy join city (historic) + current_city 

 Decide per attribute: Leafy’s dim_customer
 Attribute Type Reason 
 name 1 Changes are corrections 
 email 1 Contact detail; no analytic history 
 city, state 2 “Sales by region” must not move history 
 loyalty_tier 4 or 2 Changes monthly → mini-dimension if volume grows 
 first_order_date 0 Defined as the original value 

 Questions to ask the business
 “If this changes, should last year’s report change too?” If no → Type 2. If yes, or it was an error → Type 1.
 “How often does it change?” Daily changes on millions of customers → consider a mini-dimension (Type 4).
 In interviews, Types 1 and 2 are expected; knowing 0, 3, 4 and 6 exist (and why) is a bonus.

 The main idea SCD type is chosen per column. Most dimensions mix Type 1 and Type 2 attributes; the others solve specific problems.
 09

passages.heading: Type 3: keep two views of the same sales
passages.text:
Slowly changing dimensions · 9A · worked example
 Type 3: keep two views of the same sales
 Leafy redraws its sales regions. Maya’s assignment changes from South to Central; Leo stays in West. Management wants to compare the same orders under both maps. Type 3 keeps an alternate assignment beside the main value, so a report can choose its lens.

 Before and after the reorganisation
 State customer_key customer_id sales_region previous_sales_region 
 Before 1 C-101 South NULL 
 After 1 C-101 Central South 
 After 2 C-102 West NULL 

 The key stays 1. Both Maya orders still reference that row: 64 + 18 = 82. Grouping by sales_region puts all 82 in Central. Grouping by COALESCE(previous_sales_region, sales_region) puts all 82 in South. Leo’s 25 stays in West.

 The important distinction The old-map query also puts Maya’s newer order in South. This is an alternate classification of the same facts, rather than a reconstruction of the region at each order date.

 Use it for a small, agreed set of comparisons: the old organisation versus the new one, or an original category versus today’s category. If every historical assignment and its dates must remain queryable, choose a versioned design such as Type 2.

 The main idea Type 3 preserves a limited set of alternative descriptions. Choose the column that matches the report’s business question.
 9A

passages.heading: Type 3: update safely and name the comparison
passages.text:
Slowly changing dimensions · 9B · worked example
 Type 3: update safely and name the comparison
 This rolling-previous implementation moves the old assignment into previous_sales_region only when the incoming assignment differs. The guard matters: replaying the same Central update should leave South in the previous column. The examples use DuckDB, a local analytical SQL database; the downloadable lab creates its tables in memory.

 SQL · DuckDB 
 UPDATE dim_customer3
SET previous_sales_region = sales_region,
 sales_region = 'Central'
WHERE customer_id = 'C-101'
 AND sales_region IS DISTINCT FROM 'Central'; 

 Compare the same 107 of sales under both maps SQL · DuckDB 
 SELECT 'new_map' AS perspective,
 d.sales_region AS region, SUM(f.amount) AS sales
FROM fact_order3 AS f
JOIN dim_customer3 AS d USING (customer_key)
GROUP BY d.sales_region
UNION ALL
SELECT 'old_map',
 COALESCE(d.previous_sales_region, d.sales_region),
 SUM(f.amount)
FROM fact_order3 AS f
JOIN dim_customer3 AS d USING (customer_key)
GROUP BY COALESCE(d.previous_sales_region, d.sales_region)
ORDER BY perspective, region; 

 Expected result
 perspective region sales 
 new_map Central 82.00 
 new_map West 25.00 
 old_map South 82.00 
 old_map West 25.00 

 A later move to East would leave Central as previous and erase South from this two-slot representation. If the requirement is specifically “before the 2026 reorganisation,” preserve a named baseline such as sales_region_before_2026_reorg once. Agree whether a column means original, previous, or a particular approved map.

 In this fixture, the original assignments are known and an empty previous slot means unchanged. If an old assignment can itself be unknown, distinguish that state explicitly; blindly falling back to the current region would misrepresent the old map.

 Load assumptions The example applies one authoritative assignment per customer. Deduplicate incoming changes and define effective order before rotating values. Replaying an older source snapshot must not be treated as a new business change.

 Try it: a replay, then a second change Run the Central update twice. Maya must still be Central / South. Change the incoming value to East and run it: expect East / Central. Explain why neither version of the report can now reconstruct all historical assignments.

passages.heading: Type 3: update safely and name the comparison
passages.text:
Change the incoming value to East and run it: expect East / Central. Explain why neither version of the report can now reconstruct all historical assignments.

 The main idea A previous-value slot is limited history. A replay guard protects it, and precise column names protect its meaning.
 9B

passages.heading: Type 4: separate a reusable customer profile
passages.text:
Slowly changing dimensions · 9C · worked example
 Type 4: separate a reusable customer profile
 Suppose Leafy’s large customer dimension also carries loyalty tier, age band and income band. Creating a full customer version whenever this profile changes can duplicate many stable attributes. A mini-dimension holds the distinct profile combinations separately. This deck uses Kimball’s Type 4 terminology.

 Customer dimension One row per base customer here customer_key 
 Order fact One row per order customer_key + profile_key 
 Profile mini-dimension One row per attribute combination profile_key 

 dim_profile4: one row per combination, shared by customers
 profile_key loyalty_tier age_band income_band 
 10 Bronze 25-34 40k-60k 
 11 Silver 25-34 40k-60k 

 fact_order4: one row per order, with two foreign keys
 order_number customer_key profile_key amount 
 SO-5001 1 · Maya 10 64.00 
 SO-5002 2 · Leo 10 25.00 
 SO-5003 1 · Maya 11 18.00 

 Maya’s customer key remains 1 in this simplified base dimension; the later order records profile 11. Leo shares profile 10. A profile row represents a combination, rather than one person or a customer-specific version.

 Keep the old combinations stable When a profile changes, reuse or create its combination and put that key on the new fact. Editing profile 10 from Bronze to Silver would relabel every old fact that references it.

 The main idea Type 4 stores the customer and the event-time profile as separate dimensions. The fact captures which combination applied.
 9C

passages.heading: Type 4: capture the profile at the event time
passages.text:
Slowly changing dimensions · 9D · worked example
 Type 4: capture the profile at the event time
 Prepare the event. Resolve the customer and the profile that applied when the order occurred. A historical backfill needs historical profile evidence.
 Find or add the combination. Look up the complete tuple. Insert an observed combination only when absent; enforce uniqueness.
 Write the fact. Store both keys. Validate unmatched lookups and reconcile row counts before publishing.

 SQL · DuckDB 
 SELECT p.loyalty_tier, SUM(f.amount) AS sales
FROM fact_order4 AS f
JOIN dim_customer4 AS c USING (customer_key)
JOIN dim_profile4 AS p USING (profile_key)
GROUP BY p.loyalty_tier
ORDER BY p.loyalty_tier; 

 Expected sales by the profile on each order
 loyalty_tier sales 
 Bronze 89.00 
 Silver 18.00 

 See the complete profile lookup and fact load The lab provides three unique staged orders, non-null profile bands and a sequence that generates surrogate keys. It validates customer lookups before these statements. Run both inside one transaction.

 SQL · DuckDB 
 INSERT INTO dim_profile4 (loyalty_tier, age_band, income_band)
SELECT DISTINCT s.loyalty_tier, s.age_band, s.income_band
FROM stg_order4 AS s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
 SELECT 1 FROM dim_profile4 AS p
 WHERE p.loyalty_tier = s.loyalty_tier
 AND p.age_band = s.age_band
 AND p.income_band = s.income_band
)
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3; 

 SQL · DuckDB 
 INSERT INTO fact_order4
SELECT s.order_number, s.order_date,
 c.customer_key, p.profile_key, s.amount
FROM stg_order4 AS s
JOIN dim_customer4 AS c USING (customer_id)
JOIN dim_profile4 AS p
 ON p.loyalty_tier = s.loyalty_tier
 AND p.age_band = s.age_band
 AND p.income_band = s.income_band
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
 SELECT 1 FROM fact_order4 AS f
 WHERE f.order_number = s.order_number
); 

 The replay guard assumes an identical replay. If the same order ID arrives with different values, validate and apply an explicit correction policy rather than silently ignoring it.

 Choose bounded bands deliberately. Three tiers × eight age bands × six income bands permits 144 combinations in this toy design; exact balances or timestamps could make combinations nearly unique per customer. Store observed tuples rather than eagerly generating every possible tuple.

passages.heading: Type 4: capture the profile at the event time
passages.text:
exact balances or timestamps could make combinations nearly unique per customer. Store observed tuples rather than eagerly generating every possible tuple.

 What facts cannot tell you If a profile changes between purchases, an order fact alone does not record that change. A dated customer–profile assignment history, such as a factless fact table, is needed for questions about every interval between events.

 Try it: a shared profile and a backfill Give Ana a new order with the same Silver profile: reuse key 11. Then backfill a Maya order from before the tier change: its profile must be 10, even if her current tier is Silver. Explain how you would resolve it if the source supplies only today’s profile.

 The main idea A mini-dimension stays useful when combinations are reusable and facts carry the correct event-time key.
 9D

passages.heading: Type 6: historical city and current city together
passages.text:
Slowly changing dimensions · 9E · worked example
 Type 6: historical city and current city together
 Return to Maya’s move from Austin to Denver on 5 March. Type 2 keeps Austin on the old row and Denver on the new one. Type 6 additionally carries current_city on every version, allowing both historical and current rollups through the fact’s existing surrogate-key join.

 After the move: two versions, one current perspective
 customer_key customer_id city current_city valid_from valid_to is_current 
 1 C-101 Austin Denver 2025-01-10 2026-03-04 false 
 4 C-101 Denver Denver 2026-03-05 9999-12-31 true 
 2 C-102 Denver Denver 2025-06-01 9999-12-31 true 

 SO-5001 still points to key 1. Its historical city is Austin, but its current city is Denver. SO-5003 points to key 4. These examples retain the earlier slides’ inclusive dates: the old version ends on 4 March and the new one starts on 5 March.

 SQL · DuckDB 
 SELECT 'as_was' AS perspective,
 d.city, SUM(f.amount) AS sales
FROM fact_order6 AS f
JOIN dim_customer6 AS d USING (customer_key)
GROUP BY d.city
UNION ALL
SELECT 'as_is', d.current_city, SUM(f.amount)
FROM fact_order6 AS f
JOIN dim_customer6 AS d USING (customer_key)
GROUP BY d.current_city
ORDER BY perspective, city; 

 Same three orders; both views total 107
 perspective city sales 
 as_is Denver 107.00 
 as_was Austin 64.00 
 as_was Denver 43.00 

 Why “1 + 2 + 3”? Type 2 supplies versioned rows; the extra alternate-view column is the Type 3 idea; its values are overwritten using Type 1 behaviour. This Kimball hybrid does not require a separate previous_city column.

 The main idea The fact key preserves its historical version. Choosing city or current_city changes the analytical perspective without a second dimension join.
 9E

passages.heading: Type 6: update every version, then prove both views
passages.text:
Slowly changing dimensions · 9F · worked example
 Type 6: update every version, then prove both views
 For an ordered, effective-dated change, detect the real difference before modifying rows. Close the old version, insert the new one, and overwrite current_city for every version of the same customer. A transaction publishes those steps together.

 Keep the historical column. Expired rows retain their city and surrogate key.
 Propagate the current column. Every C-101 row receives Denver, including key 1.
 Keep fact keys stable. Existing facts retain their historical keys; new or late facts use an event-date lookup.

 The transactional update used in the lab DuckDB SQL. The fixture provides a surrogate-key sequence and one deduplicated change per customer, with an effective date strictly after the existing version’s start. Detecting only changed values makes an identical replay a no-op. For multiple changes within a day, use timestamp intervals and a consistent half-open boundary rule.

 SQL · DuckDB 
 BEGIN TRANSACTION;
-- Freeze the actual changes before expiring any rows.
CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP TABLE changed6 AS
SELECT s.*
FROM stg_city6 AS s
JOIN dim_customer6 AS d USING (customer_id)
WHERE d.is_current AND d.city IS DISTINCT FROM s.city;

UPDATE dim_customer6 AS d
SET valid_to = s.effective_date - 1, is_current = FALSE
FROM changed6 AS s
WHERE d.customer_id = s.customer_id AND d.is_current;

INSERT INTO dim_customer6
 (customer_id, name, city, current_city,
 valid_from, valid_to, is_current)
SELECT customer_id, name, city, city,
 effective_date, DATE '9999-12-31', TRUE
FROM changed6;

-- Deliberately update EVERY version of the customer.
UPDATE dim_customer6 AS d
SET current_city = s.city
FROM changed6 AS s
WHERE d.customer_id = s.customer_id;
COMMIT; 

 Two easy mistakes Updating current_city only WHERE is_current leaves old facts grouped under stale “current” values. Conversely, filtering WHERE is_current after joining facts by their historical key drops Maya’s old 64 of sales: the remaining total is only 43.

 Use a durable identity to group all versions. In this example customer_id is assumed stable; if a source can reassign or replace it, resolve a warehouse-managed durable identity first. Test one current row, no overlapping intervals, and a single current-city value across each customer’s versions.

passages.heading: Type 6: update every version, then prove both views
passages.text:
a warehouse-managed durable identity first. Test one current row, no overlapping intervals, and a single current-city value across each customer’s versions.

 The trade-off is deliberate: the historical city remains reproducible, while yesterday’s “as is” report may change after another move. Many versions also mean more rows to update. Type 2 plus a separate current-row join can be simpler when the combined view is rarely needed.

 Try it: replay, failure and a third city Replay the Denver change: no extra version should appear. Roll back a deliberately interrupted update: readers should retain the previous state. Then apply a later Seattle move: historical cities must remain Austin / Denver / Seattle, while every current_city becomes Seattle. Retroactive corrections need interval repair; do not run them blindly through this forward-change example.

 Download runnable SCD lab ↗ Lab instructions · Worked notes (Markdown) 

 The main idea Type 6 is useful when both perspectives are common enough to justify maintaining a current attribute on all historical rows.
 9F

passages.heading: Date dimensions: why not just use a date column?
passages.text:
Dimension techniques · dim_date · the most-used dimension in any warehouse
 Date dimensions: why not just use a date column?
 Databases already have a DATE type and functions such as EXTRACT(MONTH …) . So why does almost every dimensional model have a dim_date table with one row per calendar day? Because the business calendar contains far more than the computer calendar.
 01 Things SQL cannot calculate
 Fiscal periods (Leafy’s year starts 1 July), holidays and observed holidays, retail 4-4-5 calendars, promotional seasons (“Spring Sale week”), company shutdown days. These are business decisions, stored as data.
 02 One definition for everyone
 Without a date table, each analyst writes their own “week”, “quarter” or “weekend” logic — and they will not agree. A shared dim_date gives every report the same calendar.
 03 Easier and faster to use
 Report builders filter on readable columns (“March”, “Weekend”, “FY26 Q3”) instead of writing date functions. BI tools need it too: Power BI’s time intelligence expects a marked date table.

 It also fills gaps
 Transaction facts are sparse: Leafy had no orders 3–8 March. Starting a query from dim_date and LEFT JOINing the facts shows those days as zero instead of hiding them.
 Separate time of day
 If you need hours or minutes, use a separate dim_time_of_day (1,440 rows for minutes) rather than one row per timestamp. Combining them would create 525,600 rows per year for no benefit.

 On the job Almost every warehouse has a shared dim_date generated once for many years. Fiscal calendars and holidays live there, not in each report.

 The main idea dim_date turns the company calendar into data: one row per day, dozens of ready-made labels, shared by every fact table.
 10

passages.heading: What a date dimension contains
passages.text:
Dimension techniques · dim_date · columns, rows, and how to build it
 What a date dimension contains
 date_key full_date day_name weekday_flag iso_week month quarter fiscal_period holiday_flag holiday_name 
 20260302 2026-03-02 Monday Weekday 10 March Q1 FY26 Q3 Not holiday — 
 20260307 2026-03-07 Saturday Weekend 10 March Q1 FY26 Q3 Not holiday — 
 20260703 2026-07-03 Friday Weekday 27 July Q3 FY27 Q1 Holiday Independence Day (observed) 
 20260704 2026-07-04 Saturday Weekend 27 July Q3 FY27 Q1 Not holiday — 
 20261126 2026-11-26 Thursday Weekday 48 November Q4 FY27 Q2 Holiday Thanksgiving 

 Generate it once, for many years
 SQL 
 SELECT
 CAST(TO_CHAR(d, 'YYYYMMDD') AS INT) AS date_key,
 d::date AS full_date,
 TO_CHAR(d, 'FMDay') AS day_name,
 CASE WHEN EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM d) IN (6, 7)
 THEN 'Weekend' ELSE 'Weekday' END AS weekday_flag,
 EXTRACT(WEEK FROM d) AS iso_week,
 TO_CHAR(d, 'FMMonth') AS month_name,
 'Q' || EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM d) AS quarter,
 -- fiscal year starts 1 July: shift the date forward 6 months
 'FY' || TO_CHAR(d + INTERVAL '6 months', 'YY')
 || ' Q' || EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM d + INTERVAL '6 months')
 AS fiscal_period
FROM generate_series(DATE '2015-01-01', DATE '2035-12-31',
 INTERVAL '1 day') AS g(d);

 Design notes
 Key: a readable integer such as 20260302 is standard for dates (lesson 3).
 Holidays come from a small business-maintained list joined in after generation. Note the observed holiday on Friday 3 July.
 Labels and numbers: keep month_name for display and month_number for sorting.
 Special rows for unknown or not-yet-happened dates (lesson 15).
 20 years is only about 7,300 rows — tiny. Build it far into the future so loads never fail on a missing date.
 PostgreSQL syntax shown; other engines use a recursive CTE or a sequence generator.

 The main idea generate dim_date once with every calendar label the business uses, including fiscal periods and holidays. It is small, static, and used everywhere.
 11

passages.heading: Role-playing dimensions
passages.text:
Dimension techniques · one dimension, several meanings
 Role-playing dimensions
 Leafy’s fulfilment fact has three dates: when the order was placed , shipped , and delivered . We do not build three date tables. One dim_date plays three roles , through three different foreign keys.
 One physical dim_date, three roles fact_order_fulfillment fact 
 order_date_key FK 
 shipped_date_key FK 
 delivered_date_key FK 
 customer_key FK 
 warehouse_key FK 
 order_number DD 
 days_to_ship M 
 days_ship_to_deliver M 

 dim_date AS order_date dimension 
 date_key PK 
 month_name 

 dim_date AS shipped_date dimension 
 date_key PK 
 day_name 

 dim_date AS delivered_date dimension 
 date_key PK 
 weekday_flag 

 dim_warehouse dimension 
 warehouse_key PK 
 city 

 Every dimension joins directly to the fact table with one key. Tags: PK primary key · FK foreign key · DD degenerate dimension · NK natural key · M measure. 
 Query it with one alias per role
 SQL 
 SELECT od.month_name AS order_month,
 dd.weekday_flag AS delivered_on,
 COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM fact_order_fulfillment AS f
JOIN dim_date AS od ON od.date_key = f.order_date_key
JOIN dim_date AS dd ON dd.date_key = f.delivered_date_key
GROUP BY od.month_name, dd.weekday_flag;

 Make roles friendly
 Create a view per role with renamed columns ( dim_order_date with order_month , dim_delivery_date with delivery_month ), so report users never see three identical “month_name” fields. In Power BI, import one role-playing table per role, or use inactive relationships with USERELATIONSHIP.
 Other examples: dim_customer as buyer and gift recipient; dim_airport as origin and destination; dim_employee as sales rep and approving manager.

 On the job Order date, ship date and delivery date on one fact are modelled as three foreign keys to one date dimension. In Power BI the same idea appears as role-playing date tables or inactive relationships.

 The main idea role-playing = the same physical dimension joined several times for different meanings. Store one table; give each role its own key, alias, or view.
 12

passages.heading: Degenerate dimensions
passages.text:
Dimension techniques · an identifier with no table of its own
 Degenerate dimensions
 Look again at the order number SO-5001. Its date went to dim_date, its customer to dim_customer, its products to dim_product. What is left about “the order” itself? Just the number. A dim_order table would contain only that one column — and have as many rows as the fact table.
 So the order number is stored directly in the fact table , as a dimension with no dimension table. Kimball calls this a degenerate dimension (DD).
 What it is useful for
 SQL 
 -- Orders and average order value
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_number) AS orders, -- 3
 SUM(line_amount)
 / COUNT(DISTINCT order_number) AS avg_order_value -- 35.67
FROM fact_order_line;

-- Group lines back into baskets: which products are bought together?
SELECT order_number, STRING_AGG(p.product_name, ' + ') AS basket
FROM fact_order_line AS f
JOIN dim_product AS p ON p.product_key = f.product_key
GROUP BY order_number; -- SO-5001: Monstera + Ceramic Pot

 Recognise one
 A transaction or document identifier: order number, invoice number, receipt number, ticket ID, booking ID, payment ID.
 Has no descriptive attributes left after the other dimensions are modelled.
 Lives in the fact table, typically as text or a large integer. It is not a foreign key — there is nothing to join to.
 Also valuable for tracing : support staff can look up an order in the source system using the number they see in a report.
 If the order header does have descriptive attributes (channel, payment method, gift flag), those go into other dimensions — often a junk dimension (next lesson).

 The main idea a degenerate dimension is a transaction ID kept on the fact row. Use it to count transactions, group lines into baskets, and trace back to the source.
 13

passages.heading: Junk dimensions
passages.text:
Dimension techniques · tidy up the leftover flags
 Junk dimensions
 Leafy orders also carry small descriptive fields: sales channel (Web, App), payment method (Card, PayPal, Gift card), whether it is a gift , and whether a coupon was used. Each has only a few possible values. Where should they go?
 Three options 

 Four text columns repeated on every fact row. The fact table gets wide, descriptive text mixes with measures, and labels are inconsistent (“Y”, “yes”, “1”).

 dim_channel (2 rows), dim_payment_method (3), dim_gift_flag (2), dim_coupon_flag (2). Correct, but four extra keys on the fact and four extra boxes cluttering the model.

 dim_order_profile dimension 
 order_profile_key PK 
 channel 
 payment_method 
 gift_flag 
 coupon_flag 

 order_profile_key channel payment_method gift_flag coupon_flag 
 1 Web Card Not a gift No coupon 
 2 Web Card Not a gift Coupon used 
 3 Web Card Gift No coupon 
 … … … … … 
 17 App PayPal Gift No coupon 
 … … … … … 
 24 App Gift card Gift Coupon used 

 All combinations: 2 × 3 × 2 × 2 = 24 rows . The fact needs one key. SO-5002 (App, PayPal, a gift, no coupon) points at key 17.

 How to build and load it
 Small sets: generate every combination up front (a cross join of the value lists). Larger sets: add a row the first time a new combination appears. During the fact load, look up the key by matching all the columns.
 What not to junk
 Only low-cardinality attributes (few distinct values) that do not belong to an existing dimension. A free-text delivery note or a customer email is not junk; it belongs elsewhere or nowhere.

 On the job Junk dimensions keep facts narrow when sources send many yes/no flags (gift wrap, express, coupon used). They are typically built as the distinct combinations seen in the data.

 The main idea a junk dimension groups miscellaneous low-cardinality flags and codes into one small table of their combinations, with one key on the fact.
 14

passages.heading: Never leave a foreign key NULL
passages.text:
Dimension techniques · unknown and not-applicable members
 Never leave a foreign key NULL
 A fourth order arrives from Leafy’s weekend market stall: SO-5004, 30.00, no customer recorded . It is tempting to leave customer_key NULL. Watch what happens.
 Compare 

 SQL 
 SELECT c.city, SUM(f.line_amount) AS revenue
FROM fact_order_line AS f
JOIN dim_customer AS c ON c.customer_key = f.customer_key
GROUP BY c.city;
-- Austin 64, Denver 43 → total 107. The 30.00 sale vanished.

 An inner join drops the row: revenue silently disappears from every report joined to customers. A LEFT JOIN keeps it, but shows a blank group — and every user must remember to use LEFT JOIN.

 customer_key customer_id name city 
 -1 N/A Unknown customer Unknown 
 -2 N/A Not applicable Not applicable 
 1 C-101 Maya Austin 
 … … … … 

 SO-5004 is loaded with customer_key = -1 . The same query now returns Austin 64, Denver 43, Unknown 30 → total 137. Every join is safe, and the gap is visible and labelled.

 Special row Meaning Leafy example 
 −1 Unknown The value should exist, but is missing or could not be matched Market-stall sale without a customer; a customer ID not yet in the dimension 
 −2 Not applicable The dimension does not apply to this row promotion_key on a full-price sale (“No promotion”) 
 −3 Not yet happened (dates) A milestone in the future delivered_date_key for an order still in transit (the Fact tables deck) 

 Late-arriving dimensions: if a sale references customer C-200 before C-200 reaches the warehouse, insert an inferred row (key, natural key, “Unknown” attributes) and update it when the real data arrives — the fact keeps its key. Measures, by contrast, may be NULL when genuinely unknown; aggregates ignore NULLs.
 On the job Facts that arrive before their dimension rows (late-arriving dimensions) are common with event streams. Pointing them at an Unknown or inferred member keeps totals complete and the load re-runnable.

 The main idea every fact foreign key should point at a real dimension row. Use labelled special members (Unknown, Not applicable, Not yet) instead of NULL.
 15

passages.heading: Bridge tables for many-to-many relationships
passages.text:
Dimension techniques · when one row relates to several dimension members
 Bridge tables for many-to-many relationships
 Leafy groups customers into marketing segments, and a customer can belong to several. Maya is in Plant Parent Club and Newsletter ; Leo is in Newsletter . A sale has one customer, but that customer has many segments — the fact table cannot hold one segment_key . A bridge table sits between them.
 fact_order_line fact 
 customer_key FK 
 line_amount M 

 dim_customer dimension 
 customer_key PK 
 name 
 segment_group_key FK 

 bridge_customer_segment bridge 
 segment_group_key FK 
 segment_key FK 
 weight M 

 dim_segment dimension 
 segment_key PK 
 segment_name 

 The bridge rows
 segment_group_key customer segment weight 
 G1 Maya Plant Parent Club 0.5 
 G1 Maya Newsletter 0.5 
 G2 Leo Newsletter 1.0 

 SQL 
 SELECT s.segment_name,
 SUM(f.line_amount) AS revenue_from_members,
 SUM(f.line_amount * b.weight) AS revenue_allocated
FROM fact_order_line AS f
JOIN dim_customer AS c ON c.customer_key = f.customer_key
JOIN bridge_customer_segment AS b ON b.segment_group_key = c.segment_group_key
JOIN dim_segment AS s ON s.segment_key = b.segment_key
GROUP BY s.segment_name;

 Two correct answers — and one wrong total
 segment from members allocated 
 Plant Parent Club 82.00 41.00 
 Newsletter 107.00 66.00 
 Sum of rows 189.00 ✗ 107.00 ✓ 

 From members : “how much did customers in this segment spend?” Each row is right, but Maya’s 82 is counted in both segments, so the rows must not be added up .
 Allocated : weights for each group sum to 1, so totals reconcile to 107. Use it when the business wants credit shared out.
 Other bridges: patients with several diagnoses, bank accounts with several holders, products with many tags, classes taught by two instructors.

 On the job Customers in several segments, accounts with several owners, and patients with several diagnoses all need a bridge. Reports that ignore it double count; reports that use weights reconcile.

 The main idea use a bridge table when one fact row relates to many members of a dimension. Decide whether you want overlapping totals or weighted allocation, and label the result clearly.
 16

passages.heading: Conformed dimensions
passages.text:
Dimension techniques · one shared definition across fact tables
 Conformed dimensions
 Leafy now has several fact tables: order lines, returns, daily inventory, website sessions. If each team builds its own product table, “Accessories” in the sales report may not mean the same as “Accessories” in the inventory report. A conformed dimension is one dimension — same keys, same attribute names, same values — shared by every fact table that needs it.
 One product dimension shared by four fact tables dim_product (conformed) dimension 
 product_key PK 
 product_name 
 category 

 fact_order_line fact 
 product_key FK 
 line_amount M 

 fact_returns fact 
 product_key FK 
 return_amount M 

 fact_inventory_daily fact 
 product_key FK 
 units_on_hand M 

 fact_promotion_coverage fact 
 product_key FK 

 Every dimension joins directly to the fact table with one key. Tags: PK primary key · FK foreign key · DD degenerate dimension · NK natural key · M measure. 
 Drill across: combine facts through conformed dimensions
 SQL 
 WITH sales AS (
 SELECT p.category, SUM(f.line_amount) AS sales
 FROM fact_order_line AS f
 JOIN dim_product AS p ON p.product_key = f.product_key
 GROUP BY p.category
), returns AS (
 SELECT p.category, SUM(r.return_amount) AS returns
 FROM fact_returns AS r
 JOIN dim_product AS p ON p.product_key = r.product_key
 GROUP BY p.category
)
SELECT COALESCE(s.category, r.category) AS category,
 s.sales, COALESCE(r.returns, 0) AS returns,
 ROUND(100.0 * COALESCE(r.returns, 0) / NULLIF(s.sales, 0), 1) AS return_rate_pct
FROM sales AS s
FULL OUTER JOIN returns AS r ON r.category = s.category;

 Why it matters
 Aggregate each fact separately to the same conformed attribute, then join the small results. If one Ceramic Pot (12.00) is returned: Accessories return rate = 12 ÷ 42 = 28.6% , Plants = 0%.
 Never join two fact tables row to row : one order line matched to several return rows multiplies amounts (fan-out).
 Typical conformed dimensions: dim_date , dim_customer , dim_product , dim_store , dim_employee . A shrunken version (e.g., dim_month , or category-only) conforms too, as long as its values match.

 On the job Conformed dimensions are what make numbers comparable across teams: one dim_customer and one dim_date shared by every fact. Platform teams often own them centrally.

passages.heading: Conformed dimensions
passages.text:
dimensions are what make numbers comparable across teams: one dim_customer and one dim_date shared by every fact. Platform teams often own them centrally.

 The main idea conformed dimensions are what make separate fact tables comparable. They are the glue of an enterprise warehouse.
 17

passages.heading: A glossary to come back to
passages.text:
Quick reference · every term in this deck
 A glossary to come back to
 Term Meaning 
 Dimension / attribute A table of descriptive context (who, what, where, when) / one of its columns 
 Normalised / denormalised Data split into many tables to avoid repetition / combined into fewer, wider tables for reading 
 Natural / surrogate key Source-system ID / warehouse-generated row ID 
 SCD Type 1 / Type 2 Overwrite the value / add a new versioned row with effective dates 
 Date dimension One row per calendar day with readable attributes (month name, fiscal year, holiday) 
 Conformed dimension One dimension shared consistently by several fact tables 
 Role-playing dimension One dimension used in several roles via different foreign keys 
 Degenerate dimension A transaction ID stored on the fact with no dimension table 
 Junk dimension A table of combinations of low-cardinality flags 
 Bridge table Resolves a many-to-many between a fact (or dimension) and a dimension 
 Unknown member A special dimension row (−1, −2…) used instead of a NULL key 

 18

passages.heading: Recap: what to remember when you close this deck
passages.text:
Recap · the ideas that carry everything else
 Recap: what to remember when you close this deck
 The warehouse owns its keys. Surrogate keys make history, multiple sources and unknown members possible.
 Decide how history behaves, per attribute. Type 1 overwrites; Type 2 adds a version so old facts keep old descriptions.
 Load Type 2 by closing the current row and inserting a new one ; load facts by looking up the version valid on the event date.
 Count Type 2 entities with distinct natural keys , and filter is_current only when you want today’s view.
 Use the toolbox: a shared date dimension, role-playing keys, degenerate IDs, junk dimensions for flags, and Unknown rows instead of NULL keys.
 Bridges resolve many-to-many (with weights to reconcile); conformed dimensions make facts comparable.

 The main idea good dimensions are wide, readable, keyed by the warehouse, and explicit about how history is kept.
 19

passages.heading: Why this matters on the job
passages.text:
Why this matters · the need behind the topic
 Why this matters on the job
 Knowing each technique is not the same as designing a warehouse. Real work, and the modeling round of an interview, starts from vague requirements: you have to find the business processes, decide what to build first, choose every grain, and prove the numbers. This deck practises that end to end.
 Where you will use it
 Kick-off workshops for a new mart or Gold layer.
 Architecture reviews, where the bus matrix is the one-page plan.
 Take-home and whiteboard modeling cases in interviews.
 What goes wrong without it
 Teams build facts one dashboard at a time, with dimensions that do not conform.
 Loads run facts before dimensions and leave orphan keys.
 Mistakes (mixed grain, summed snapshots, NULL keys) are found by finance, not by tests.
 Who expects you to know it
 Senior data and analytics engineers leading model design.
 Stakeholders who sign off what gets built first.
 Interviewers: “design a data model for X” is a standard round.

 On the job A new studio chain asks for revenue, attendance and membership reporting. You list processes (payments, bookings, memberships), draw the bus matrix, agree the grain of each fact, and deliver the first star with tests that reconcile to the source totals.

 The main idea planning with a bus matrix and proving the model with numbers is what turns techniques into a warehouse people trust.
 why

passages.heading: When to reach for it, and when not to
passages.text:
Why this matters · choosing the right tool
 When to reach for it, and when not to
 Situation Reach for Why 
 Several processes share customers, products, dates Bus matrix before any SQL Shows what must be conformed and the build order 
 A vague request (“a dashboard for the studios”) Ask for the questions; apply the four steps Turns the request into grains and measures 
 A design case in an interview Clarify, list processes, four steps, sketch, traps Shows structure, not just syntax 
 Checking a finished model Grain tests, orphan checks, control totals Finds mistakes before users do 
 A single, one-off report A focused query or a small mart A full bus matrix is overkill 

 How interviews test it
 “Design a data model for a ride-sharing / e-commerce / fitness app.”
 “What would you build first, and why?” (the bus matrix).
 “How do you know the model is right?” (grain tests and reconciliation).
 Where it sits in your learning path
 Builds on: Why dimensional modeling, Fact tables, Dimension tables.
 Next: SQL correctness (fan-out and reconciliation in queries) and dbt (building and testing the model).
 Interview prep: modeling, metrics and dbt cases.

 The main idea plan with a bus matrix, design each process with the four steps, and prove the result with numbers that match the source.

passages.heading: Meet Leafy, our example business
passages.text:
Start here · one example used throughout the course
 Meet Leafy, our example business
 Leafy is a small online plant shop. Customers order plants and accessories; warehouses in Austin and Denver ship them. The owner wants answers such as “Which product categories sell best each month?” and “Did customers who moved cities change what they buy?” 
 Here are Leafy’s first three orders. We will reuse these exact numbers in almost every lesson, so it is worth a careful look.
 order_number order_date customer line product qty unit_price line_amount 
 SO-5001 2026-03-02 Maya (Austin) 1 Monstera 1 40.00 40.00 
 SO-5001 2026-03-02 Maya (Austin) 2 Ceramic Pot 2 12.00 24.00 
 SO-5002 2026-03-02 Leo (Denver) 1 Snake Plant 1 25.00 25.00 
 SO-5003 2026-03-09 Maya (Denver) 1 Fertilizer 3 6.00 18.00 

 Numbers to remember
 Order totals: SO-5001 = 64 , SO-5002 = 25 , SO-5003 = 18 . All sales = 107 . Shipping fees (charged per order): 8, 5, and 0.
 Notice the details
 One order can contain several lines (products). Maya moved from Austin to Denver between her two orders — that will matter a lot when we talk about history.

 The main idea learning works best with a small example you can check by hand. Whenever a query result appears in this course, try to predict it from this table first.
 02

passages.heading: Plan with a bus matrix
passages.text:
Dimension techniques · the one-page plan of a warehouse
 Plan with a bus matrix
 A bus matrix lists business processes (future fact tables) as rows and dimensions as columns. A dot means “this process uses this dimension”. Columns with many dots are the dimensions to conform first, because they connect the most processes.
 Business process (fact table) Date Customer Product Warehouse Promotion Order profile Workshop 
 Orders · fact_order_line ● ● ● ● ● ● 
 Fulfilment · fact_order_fulfillment ● ×3 ● ● ● 
 Returns · fact_returns ● ● ● ● 
 Inventory · fact_inventory_daily ● ● ● 
 Promotion coverage · fact_promotion_coverage ● ● ● 
 Workshops · fact_workshop_attendance ● ● ● 

 How to read it
 Read across a row to see a star schema. Read down a column to see every process a dimension must serve — and everyone who must agree on its definition. “×3” marks a role-playing dimension (the Dimension tables deck).
 How to use it
 Build the warehouse one row (one business process) at a time, but design the shared columns once. It is also the best artefact to bring to an interview whiteboard or a stakeholder meeting.

 On the job The bus matrix is the one-page plan you bring to a stakeholder or an architecture review: rows are business processes, columns are shared dimensions. It shows what to build first and what must be conformed.

 The main idea the bus matrix turns many separate stars into one coherent warehouse: incremental delivery, shared conformed dimensions.

 Every dimension joins directly to the fact table with one key. Tags: PK primary key · FK foreign key · DD degenerate dimension · NK natural key · M measure. 
 Concept Where it appears in this model 
 Grain One row per order line; shipping allocated down to the line so every measure is true for its row (the Why dimensional modeling deck) 
 Measures quantity, line_amount, discount_amount, allocated_shipping — all additive; unit price is derived

 The main idea a real model is just these techniques combined. Each one answers a specific question: what is a row, what can be summed, what happens on change, how to describe things cleanly.

passages.heading: How a dimensional model is loaded
passages.text:
Put it together · dimensions first, then facts, then tests
 How a dimensional model is loaded
 01 Land raw data in staging copy source tables as-is 
 Keep the original rows so loads can be re-run and audited.

 02 Load dimensions apply SCD rules 
 Insert new members, overwrite Type 1 attributes, version Type 2 attributes. Make sure the special −1 / −2 rows exist.

 03 Load facts look up surrogate keys 
 For each natural key find the dimension key (by natural key + date for Type 2). If no match: −1 Unknown, or insert an inferred member.

 04 Build snapshots and summaries from atomic facts 
 Periodic snapshots at period end; update accumulating snapshots as milestones arrive; aggregates for speed.

 05 Test before anyone sees the numbers 
 Grain is unique, no NULL foreign keys, totals reconcile with the source.

 Three tests worth automating
 SQL 
 -- 1. Grain: no duplicate rows for the declared grain (expect 0 rows)
SELECT order_number, line_number, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM fact_order_line
GROUP BY order_number, line_number
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- 2. No NULL foreign keys (expect 0)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM fact_order_line
WHERE customer_key IS NULL OR product_key IS NULL OR date_key IS NULL;

-- 3. Reconcile with the source (expect equal totals)
SELECT (SELECT SUM(line_amount) FROM fact_order_line) AS warehouse_total,
 (SELECT SUM(qty * price) FROM stg_order_items) AS source_total;

 Why dimensions go first
 A fact row needs the dimension’s surrogate key at load time. If the dimension has not been refreshed, new customers and new versions are missing and facts would fall back to Unknown.
 Tools such as dbt express this order automatically through dependencies, and provide built-in tests for uniqueness, not-null and relationships.

 On the job The load order (dimensions first, then facts with key lookups, then tests) is how dbt DAGs and orchestrated pipelines are arranged; tests on grain and orphan keys run after every load.

 The main idea staging → dimensions → facts → snapshots → tests. The grain-uniqueness test is the single most valuable check on any fact table.
 05

passages.heading: Common modeling mistakes
passages.text:
Put it together · and how to spot them
 Common modeling mistakes
 Mistake Symptom Fix 
 Grain never declared, or mixed Totals double-count; nobody can say what a row is Write the grain sentence; one grain per fact table; allocate or split 
 Summing a semi-additive measure over time Stock or balances that grow every day in a monthly report Period-end or average across time; define the measure in the semantic layer 
 Storing ratios and averages Report totals that do not match the detail Store numerator and denominator; compute after summing 
 Natural keys as dimension keys Collisions between sources; Type 2 impossible Surrogate keys; keep the natural key as an attribute 
 NULL foreign keys Revenue disappears from joined reports Unknown / Not applicable members 
 Joining two fact tables directly Inflated numbers (fan-out) Drill across: aggregate each fact, join on conformed attributes 
 Every team builds its own dimensions Same KPI, different answers Conformed dimensions planned with a bus matrix 
 Codes instead of labels Reports full of “3”, “Y”, “ST_02” Decode into readable attributes in the dimension 
 Snowflaking everything Long join chains, slow and confusing BI models Flatten hierarchies into the dimension 
 Too many tiny flag dimensions Fact tables with 30 keys (a “centipede”) Junk dimension; question whether each attribute is needed 

 On the job These mistakes are the checklist for reviewing someone else’s model or pull request: ask for the grain statement, look for header amounts on line rows, summed snapshots, and NULL foreign keys.

 The main idea nearly every modeling bug shows up as a wrong total. When a number looks off, check grain, additivity, joins, and NULL keys — in that order.
 06

passages.heading: Interview cheat-sheet
passages.text:
Put it together · what is asked, and what a strong answer includes
 Interview cheat-sheet
 If you are asked… A strong answer covers 
 “Design a data model for X .” Clarify questions → list business processes → four steps per process (process, grain, dimensions, facts) → sketch the star → mention SCDs, conformed dims, unknowns 
 “What is grain? Why does it matter?” What one row represents; declared first; atomic preferred; mixing grains causes double counting (give the shipping-fee example) 
 “Fact vs dimension?” Measurements of events vs descriptive context; numbers that describe a thing go in the dimension 
 “Why a star schema?” Simple, few predictable joins, fast, BI-friendly; compare with snowflake and normalized OLTP 
 “Additive vs semi-additive vs non-additive?” Revenue / account balance / percentage; how each should be aggregated 
 “Why surrogate keys?” Source collisions, key changes, Type 2 history, unknown members, join performance 
 “How do you track address changes?” SCD Type 2: new row, new key, valid_from/to, is_current; as-of lookup when loading facts; contrast with Type 1 
 “Types of fact tables?” Transaction, periodic snapshot, accumulating snapshot (+ factless) with an example and grain for each 
 “Order date, ship date, delivery date — how?” Role-playing dim_date with three foreign keys and aliases or views 
 “Where does order number go?” Degenerate dimension on the fact table 
 “Customer in many segments?” Bridge table; weighting factor; warn about double counting 
 “Missing dimension values?” Unknown / Not applicable rows, never NULL keys; inferred members for late arrivals 

 On the job The same questions come up in design reviews at work, not only in interviews. Having a one-sentence answer and a concrete example for each makes those discussions short.

 The main idea interviewers reward structure: state the grain, name the technique, give a concrete example, and mention the trap it avoids.
 07

passages.heading: Quick checks before the project
passages.text:
Try it · decide, then reveal
 Quick checks before the project
 A table has one row per customer per month with the column loyalty_points_balance . What kind of fact table is it, and how should balances be totalled for a year? Periodic snapshot. The balance is semi-additive : sum across customers for one month, but for a year take the December (closing) value or the average — never the sum of 12 months.
 A support ticket moves from opened → assigned → resolved → closed, and managers want time spent in each step. Which fact table type? Accumulating snapshot : one row per ticket, a role-playing date key per milestone, lag measures between them, updated as the ticket progresses.
 A product’s category was wrong for a month because of a data-entry typo. Type 1 or Type 2? Type 1. It is a correction; history should show the right category everywhere. Type 2 would preserve a mistake.
 Every sale has an invoice number and nothing else about the invoice is descriptive. Where does invoice_number go? On the fact table as a degenerate dimension .
 A hospital visit can have several diagnoses. Revenue by diagnosis adds up to more than total revenue. Is something broken? Not necessarily: this is a bridge table (many-to-many) and overlapping totals are expected. Either label it “revenue from visits with this diagnosis” and do not total it, or use a weighting factor so allocated revenue reconciles.
 Which students were enrolled in a course but never attended a lecture? What two fact tables do you need? A coverage factless fact (enrolment: student × course × term) and an event factless fact (attendance). Enrolled minus attended = the answer.

 The main idea if you can answer all six with a reason, you are ready to model a business from scratch.
 08

passages.heading: Project: model FitHub’s studios
passages.text:
Practice project · the brief
 Project: model FitHub’s studios
 FitHub runs fitness studios in Austin and Denver. Members buy a monthly plan (Basic, Plus, Premium) after a free trial, and book group classes — yoga, spin, HIIT — through the app, the website, or the front desk. Some classes are co-taught by two instructors. Walk-in visitors can pay for a single class without being members. FitHub’s financial year starts on 1 July .
 Leadership wants a dimensional model that answers these questions. Your job is to design it, build it on the sample data, and answer them:
 Revenue in March 2026 by member home city (as it was at the time of payment) and by payment type — walk-ins included.
 Attendance rate by class type: attended bookings ÷ bookings that were not cancelled in advance.
 Attended visits credited to instructors , with co-taught classes shared fairly so the total matches attended bookings.
 Active paying members by plan on 31 January 2026 , as they were on that date (not as they are today).
 Scheduled classes that received no bookings at all. 
 Days from trial start to paid conversion for each member, and the average for those who converted.

 What you will practise
 Business processes and a bus matrix, grain statements, all three fact table types plus a factless fact, additivity, surrogate keys, SCD Type 1 and 2, role-playing dates, degenerate IDs, a junk dimension, unknown members, a bridge table, conformed dimensions, and a date dimension with a fiscal calendar.
 Tools
 Pen and paper for the design. To build it, any SQL engine works; DuckDB is ideal because it is free, needs no server, and reads CSV files directly. Expect 3–5 hours for the full project.

 On the job This is the shape of a real first assignment on an analytics team: a short brief, a handful of source extracts, and questions the business wants answered by the end of the week.

 The main idea this is a realistic, small-scale version of a real modeling assignment. The sample data is tiny on purpose, so you can check every number by hand.

passages.heading: Project: your tasks, step by step
passages.text:
Practice project · work through these in order
 Project: your tasks, step by step
 Find the business processes. List the events FitHub records (hint: there are at least five). Draw a bus matrix of processes × dimensions.
 Declare the grain of each fact table in one sentence, and name its type: transaction, periodic snapshot, accumulating snapshot, or factless.
 Design the dimensions. List attributes, flatten hierarchies, replace codes with labels, and assign surrogate keys. Decide which dimensions are conformed.
 Choose SCD types for every member attribute. Rebuild dim_member as Type 2 from members.csv + member_changes.csv (trial counts as its own “plan”).
 Classify every measure as additive, semi-additive or non-additive, and decide how each should be aggregated.
 Handle the special cases: the several dates on a booking, booking and payment IDs, the small booking flags, the walk-in payment, the co-taught class, and the class nobody booked.
 Build it in SQL: dim_date with a July fiscal year, then the dimensions (with −1 / −2 rows), then the facts with surrogate-key lookups.
 Answer the six questions from the brief with SQL against your model — not against the staging tables.
 Write three tests: grain uniqueness for each fact, no NULL foreign keys, and payments reconciling to the source total.

 Deliverables
 A one-page diagram (bus matrix + stars), a short document with grain sentences and design decisions, the SQL scripts, and your six answers.
 Stretch goals
 Add dim_time_of_day and report attendance by morning / lunchtime / evening. Build a month-end membership snapshot for January–March. Expose the model in Power BI and check the relationships are all one-to-many from dimensions to facts.

 The main idea do steps 1–6 on paper before writing any SQL. Most of the learning — and most interview credit — is in the design decisions.
 11

passages.heading: Project: hints if you get stuck
passages.text:
Practice project · open only the hint you need
 Project: hints if you get stuck
 Hint 1 · Which business processes are there? Think in verbs: members book classes; FitHub schedules classes; people pay ; members hold a plan each month ; trials convert (or not). Each verb is a candidate fact table.
 Hint 2 · Is a scheduled class a dimension or a fact? Both views are defensible. A class session has descriptive attributes (studio, type, start time) — those become dimensions on the booking fact, with class_id as a degenerate dimension. The schedule itself is a coverage-style factless fact (one row per scheduled class, optionally with capacity), which is exactly what you need for “classes with no bookings”.
 Hint 3 · How do I rebuild member history? Each member starts with a TRIAL version from trial_start until the day before converted_on . Then a paid version begins. For members in member_changes.csv , the first paid version uses the old values and ends the day before changed_on ; a new version with the new values starts on changed_on . Everyone’s last version is current, valid to 9999-12-31.
 Hint 4 · Where do channel, status, waitlisted and guest pass go? They are low-cardinality booking flags: a junk dimension ( dim_booking_profile ). Also add 0/1 measures such as attended_count and no_show_count on the fact so rates are easy sums.
 Hint 5 · Which dates does a booking have? Booked date, class date, and cancellation date — three roles of one dim_date . Bookings that were never cancelled use the −2 “Not applicable” date row, not NULL.
 Hint 6 · How do I share credit for C901? Create instructor groups: each class points at a group, and bridge_instructor_group lists the instructors in it with weights summing to 1 (0.5 and 0.5 for Dev and Kim).
 Hint 7 · What member does the walk-in payment get? P703 has no member by design, so it is not “unknown” — use the −2 Not applicable member (label it “Walk-in / non-member”). Reserve −1 Unknown for member IDs that are missing by mistake or do not match.

 The main idea every hint maps to a lesson: processes (16), factless (31), Type 2 (23–24), junk (36), role-playing (34), bridge (38), unknown members (37).

passages.heading: Recap: what to remember when you close this deck
passages.text:
Recap · the ideas that carry everything else
 Recap: what to remember when you close this deck
 Start a warehouse with a bus matrix : one row per business process, one column per shared dimension.
 Apply the four steps to each process: process, grain, dimensions, facts.
 Load dimensions first , then facts with key lookups (and Unknown rows), then test grain, keys and totals.
 Most modeling bugs show up as a wrong total : check grain, additivity, joins and NULL keys, in that order.
 In interviews, state the grain, name the technique, give a concrete example, and mention the trap it avoids .

 The main idea a good model is planned on one page, built in a fixed order, and proven with numbers that reconcile.

passages.text:
Companion to python-foundations.html: same lessons, same numbering, same code. Hints and solutions are in Appendices A and B.

Lesson: Python for data engineering, deck 1 of 2. This deck covers the in-memory core (values, collections and their costs, functions, errors, copies, Counter/defaultdict/deque, type hints, dataclasses); deck 2 of 2, Python files, generators, and practical data scripts, covers files, streams, datetimes at the edges, databases, scripts and concurrency.

Audience: you already program (comparisons use C#) and are learning Python for analytics and data engineering. New terms are defined on first use and collected in the glossary (section 46).

Scope: everything happens in memory. Files, I/O, databases and concurrency are covered in the files-and-streams deck; HTTP APIs in the reliable-ingestion deck.

passages.heading: 1. Python foundations for data engineering
passages.text:
This deck teaches the plain Python you need to transform data before you use DataFrame libraries. It assumes you already program (comparisons use C#) and are new to Python and data engineering.

- Lessons 2–10, values: types, None, truthiness, strings, numbers, dates and times.
- Lessons 11–16, control and code: branching, loops, functions, scope, imports, exceptions.
- Lessons 17–32, collections: lists, tuples, dicts, sets, comprehensions, sorting, copies, Counter, defaultdict, deque, time and memory costs, type hints, dataclasses.
- Lessons 33–48, practice: parsing, validating, deduplicating, grouping and counting events; a bug clinic; 10 exercises; an in-memory event-cleaning mini-project; a cheat sheet.

Out of scope: files, databases, async and threads (the second deck of this lesson, Python files, generators, and practical data scripts), DataFrames (the pandas & Polars deck) and HTTP (the reliable-ingestion deck).

passages.heading: Why this matters · Why this matters on the job
passages.text:
Why this matters · the need behind the topic

Python is the glue language of data engineering. Before you use DataFrames or Spark you write plain Python to parse records, validate fields, deduplicate, and count, and when a DataFrame job misbehaves, you debug it with the same mental model: names, objects, collections, copies.

Where you will use it

- Fabric and Databricks notebooks: validation and small transforms around Spark/pandas code.
- Azure Functions and scripts that receive JSON events or API responses.
- Data-quality checks, reconciliation scripts, and test fixtures.
- Coding interviews: dicts, sets, Counter, sorting with keys, dedupe rules.

What goes wrong without it

- Zero amounts treated as missing (truthiness), float money that doesn’t reconcile.
- Shared mutable defaults and shallow copies that corrupt “unrelated” records.
- O(n²) loops (list membership inside loops) that take hours on real volumes.
- One bad record crashes the job, or vanishes silently.

Who expects you to know it

- Data engineers (Python is in almost every job description).
- Analytics engineers writing dbt Python models or utilities.
- Interviewers in Python rounds: clean, correct code on small data problems.

> On the job: A typical ticket: “the nightly job crashed on a record with a null user, fix it and stop it happening again”. The fix is plain Python: parse at the edge, validate every field, quarantine bad rows with reasons, and add an invariant so counts always add up.

> The main idea: plain Python is the foundation under every data library. Getting values, collections and copies right prevents the bugs that silently change numbers.

Read more: The Python tutorial.

passages.heading: Why this matters · When to reach for it, and when not to
passages.text:
Why this matters · choosing the right tool

| Situation | Reach for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Small or record-by-record logic, glue, validation | Plain Python | Clear, testable, no dependencies |
| Tables of thousands to millions of rows | pandas / Polars / DuckDB | Vectorised, columnar, far less memory per row |
| Data in a warehouse already | SQL | Push work to the engine instead of pulling rows out |
| Billions of rows or many files in a lake | Spark | Distributed processing |
| Counting, grouping, dedupe in memory | Counter, defaultdict, sets, dicts | O(1) lookups; built for exactly this |

How interviews test it

- Live coding: “count events per user”, “deduplicate keeping the latest”, “group by day”.
- Follow-ups: complexity (why a set, not a list?), edge cases (None, 0, duplicates, time zones).
- Reading code: spotting mutable defaults, aliasing, truthiness bugs.

Where it sits in your learning path

- First of the two decks for the lesson Python for data engineering; assumes only general programming experience (C#).
- Next: the files-and-streams deck completes the lesson (files, generators, databases, scripts, concurrency); then the pandas & Polars deck and the reliable-ingestion deck.

> The main idea: use plain Python for glue, validation and per-record logic; move to DataFrame engines or SQL when the work becomes table-shaped or large.
