passages.heading: 29. dbt test: reading a failure
passages.text:
Trust · the accepted_values test fails, on purpose

Run every test. Expect one failure (refund is not in the accepted list) and one warning (e7).

Terminal (PASS lines removed):

$ dbt test
2 of 32 WARN 1 assert_no_unparseable_amounts ................................... [WARN 1 in x.xxs]
1 of 32 FAIL 1 accepted_values_stg_events_event_type__page_view__add_to_cart__purchase  [FAIL 1 in x.xxs]
Completed with 1 error, 0 partial successes, and 1 warning:
[ERROR]: in test accepted_values_stg_events_event_type__page_view__add_to_cart__purchase (models\staging\_staging.yml)
  Got 1 result, configured to fail if != 0
  compiled code at target\compiled\leafy\models\staging\_staging.yml\accepted_values_stg_events_2ed8c44c503f537c31b00e985e4153d8.sql
[WARNING]: in test assert_no_unparseable_amounts (tests\assert_no_unparseable_amounts.sql)
[WARNING]: Got 1 result, configured to warn if != 0
  compiled code at target\compiled\leafy\tests\assert_no_unparseable_amounts.sql
Done. PASS=30 WARN=1 ERROR=1 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=32
[exit code 1]

How to read it

- FAIL 1: the test query returned 1 row. For accepted_values that means one distinct bad value.
- The test name tells you the model, column and rule: accepted_values_stg_events_….
- “compiled code at …” is the exact SQL that ran. Open it, run it, look at the rows.
- Summary: ERROR=1 counts failed error-severity tests; WARN=1 is the singular test. The exit code is 1.

The failing query

-- target/compiled/leafy/models/staging/_staging.yml/accepted_values_stg_events_2ed8c44c503f537c31b00e985e4153d8.sql (generated by dbt)
with all_values as (
    select
        event_type as value_field,
        count(*) as n_records
    from "leafy"."main_staging"."stg_events"
    group by event_type
)
select *
from all_values
where value_field not in (
    'page_view','add_to_cart','purchase'
)

The generic test is a macro: dbt filled in the model, the column and the list.

> On the job: In an on-call rotation, a failed test is an alert. The first three questions are always the same: which rows (run the compiled SQL), since when (which load introduced them), and is the data wrong or is the rule out of date? Here the rule is out of date: refunds are a real new event type.

> The main idea: a test failure names the model, column and rule, gives the number of failing rows, and points to the compiled SQL. Run that SQL to see the rows, then decide whether the data or the rule is wrong.

passages.heading: 30. dbt build: a failed test protects everything downstream
passages.text:
Trust · seeds, models and tests interleaved in DAG order added

dbt build runs each node, then its tests, before moving downstream. When an error-severity test fails, every node that depends on the tested model is skipped, so bad data does not flow into marts. Run it now, with the failing test still in place:

Terminal (only the interesting lines):

$ dbt build
12 of 42 FAIL 1 accepted_values_stg_events_event_type__page_view__add_to_cart__purchase  [FAIL 1 in x.xxs]
13 of 42 WARN 1 assert_no_unparseable_amounts .................................. [WARN 1 in x.xxs]

21 of 42 SKIP test relationships_fct_daily_funnel_date_key__date_key__ref_dim_date_  [SKIP]
22 of 42 SKIP test unique_fct_daily_funnel_date_key ............................ [SKIP]
33 of 42 SKIP relation main_marts.fct_orders due to ephemeral model status 'skipped'  [ERROR SKIP]
34 of 42 SKIP test not_null_fct_orders_amount .................................. [SKIP]
35 of 42 SKIP test not_null_fct_orders_customer_key ............................ [SKIP]
36 of 42 SKIP test not_null_fct_orders_date_key ................................ [SKIP]
37 of 42 SKIP test not_null_fct_orders_order_id ................................ [SKIP]
38 of 42 SKIP test not_null_fct_orders_product_key ............................. [SKIP]
39 of 42 SKIP test relationships_fct_orders_customer_key__customer_key__ref_dim_customer_  [SKIP]
40 of 42 SKIP test relationships_fct_orders_date_key__date_key__ref_dim_date_ .. [SKIP]
41 of 42 SKIP test relationships_fct_orders_product_key__product_key__ref_dim_product_  [SKIP]
42 of 42 SKIP test unique_fct_orders_order_id .................................. [SKIP]
[ERROR]: in test accepted_values_stg_events_event_type__page_view__add_to_cart__purchase (models\staging\_staging.yml)
[WARNING]: in test assert_no_unparseable_amounts (tests\assert_no_unparseable_amounts.sql)
[WARNING]: Got 1 result, configured to warn if != 0
Done. PASS=26 WARN=1 ERROR=1 SKIP=14 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=42
[exit code 1]

What happened

- Seeds, staging views and the three dimensions were built and tested.
- accepted_values on stg_events failed, so both facts (which depend on stg_events) and all of their tests were skipped: 14 skipped nodes.

passages.heading: 30. dbt build: a failed test protects everything downstream
passages.text:
built and tested.
- accepted_values on stg_events failed, so both facts (which depend on stg_events) and all of their tests were skipped: 14 skipped nodes.
- fct_orders says “due to ephemeral model status ‘skipped’”: its direct parent is the ephemeral int_purchases, which was skipped first.
- With 4 threads, lines can appear in a slightly different order on every run; the numbers (12 of 42) identify the nodes.
- The previous versions of fct_orders and fct_daily_funnel are still in the database, untouched: consumers keep yesterday’s good data rather than today’s suspect data.

run + test vs build

|  | dbt run then dbt test | dbt build |
|---|---|---|
| order | all models, then all tests | per node: build, test, then children |
| bad data in marts? | yes, until someone reacts | no: children are skipped |
| use | quick local loops | production and CI |

> On the job: Production schedules run dbt build, not run followed by test: by the time a separate test step fails, dashboards have already refreshed with bad data.

> The main idea: dbt build tests each node before building its children and skips descendants of a failed test, so marts keep their last good data.

Read more: dbt build.

passages.heading: 31. Fix the rule, store failures, and go green
passages.text:
Trust · --store-failures, then update the accepted values

--store-failures added saves each failing test’s rows in a table (schema main_dbt_testaudit) so you can query them after the run, from a notebook or a dashboard.

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt test --select stg_events --store-failures
2 of 5 WARN 1 assert_no_unparseable_amounts .................................... [WARN 1 in x.xxs]
1 of 5 FAIL 1 accepted_values_stg_events_event_type__page_view__add_to_cart__purchase  [FAIL 1 in x.xxs]
[WARNING]: in test assert_no_unparseable_amounts (tests\assert_no_unparseable_amounts.sql)
[WARNING]: Got 1 result, configured to warn if != 0
Done. PASS=3 WARN=1 ERROR=1 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=5
[exit code 1]

import duckdb
with duckdb.connect("leafy.duckdb", read_only=True) as con:
    (name,) = con.sql("""select table_name from information_schema.tables
                         where table_schema = 'main_dbt_test__audit'
                           and table_name like 'accepted_values%'""").fetchone()
    print(name)
    print(con.sql(f'select * from main_dbt_test__audit."{name}"'))

Output:

accepted_values_stg_events_2ed8c44c503f537c31b00e985e4153d8
┌─────────────┬───────────┐
│ value_field │ n_records │
│   varchar   │   int64   │
├─────────────┼───────────┤
│ refund      │         1 │
└─────────────┴───────────┘

The fix

The data is right; the rule was out of date. Add refund to the list in models/staging/_staging.yml:

-                values: ["page_view", "add_to_cart", "purchase"]

passages.heading: 32. Documentation: descriptions, doc blocks, dbt docs
passages.text:
Trust · documentation lives next to the code

Every description: you wrote in YAML is documentation. For longer text, a doc block is a named piece of Markdown in a .md file under models/, referenced with {{ doc("name") }}. dbt docs generate combines the project (descriptions, tests, SQL, lineage) with the catalog (column names and types read from the database) into a static website.

A doc block for the fact

# models/docs.md
{% docs fct_orders %}
**Orders fact.** One row per purchase event with a parseable amount.

- **Grain:** `order_id` (the purchase `event_id`), tested with `unique` and `not_null`.
- **Excluded:** purchases whose amount text cannot be parsed; the
  `assert_no_unparseable_amounts` test warns about each one.
- **Unknown members:** a missing or unknown customer or product maps to the
  dimension row with natural key `-1`.
- **Time:** `ordered_at_utc` and `date_key` are in UTC.
{% enddocs %}

…referenced from models/marts/_marts.yml:

   - name: fct_orders
-    description: Orders fact. One row per purchase event with a valid amount.
+    description: '{{ doc("fct_orders") }}'

Generate the site

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt docs generate --static
Building catalog
Catalog written to <project>\target\catalog.json

from pathlib import Path
for name in ["index.html", "static_index.html", "manifest.json", "catalog.json", "run_results.json"]:
    print(f"{name:<18} exists: {Path('target', name).exists()}")

Output:

index.html         exists: True
static_index.html  exists: True
manifest.json      exists: True
catalog.json       exists: True
run_results.json   exists: True

--static also writes static_index.html, one self-contained file you can open in a browser or attach to a ticket.

dbt docs serve

dbt docs serve starts a small local web server (default port 8080) and opens the site in your browser: model and column descriptions, tests, the compiled SQL, and an interactive lineage graph. It keeps running until you press Ctrl+C, so it is not run in this build. Teams publish target/ to internal static hosting after each production run instead.

Good descriptions

- Models: the grain, the business meaning, what is excluded.
- Columns: units (USD, UTC), meaning of special values (-1), source of truth.
- persist_docs can also write descriptions into the warehouse as table and column comments, so they show up in other tools.

passages.heading: 33. Lineage: the DAG, drawn from manifest.json
passages.text:
Trust · every ref() and source() is an edge

Lineage is the record of where each table’s data comes from. dbt knows it exactly, because every ref() and source() is an edge. target/manifest.json stores the whole project as JSON, including a parent_map: for each node, the nodes it reads from. The diagram below was drawn by this deck’s build script from that file (tests omitted).

Lineage edges from target/manifest.json parent_map (parent → child; tests omitted):

- dim_customer → fct_orders
- dim_product → fct_orders
- int_purchases → fct_orders
- stg_customers → dim_customer
- stg_events → fct_daily_funnel
- stg_events → int_purchases
- stg_products → dim_product
- customers → stg_customers
- products → stg_products
- shop_raw.events → stg_events

Read it yourself

import json
manifest = json.load(open("target/manifest.json", encoding="utf-8"))
print("dbt", manifest["metadata"]["dbt_version"], "| nodes:", len(manifest["nodes"]), "| sources:", len(manifest["sources"]))
for child in ["model.leafy.fct_orders", "model.leafy.int_purchases", "model.leafy.stg_events"]:
    print(child.split(".")[-1], "<-", sorted(p.split(".")[-1] for p in manifest["parent_map"][child]))
print("children of stg_events:", sorted(manifest["nodes"][c]["name"] for c in manifest["child_map"]["model.leafy.stg_events"]))

Output:

dbt 1.12.5 | nodes: 43 | sources: 1
fct_orders <- ['dim_customer', 'dim_product', 'int_purchases']
int_purchases <- ['stg_events']
stg_events <- ['events']
children of stg_events: ['accepted_values_stg_events_event_type__page_view__add_to_cart__purchase__refund', 'assert_no_unparseable_amounts', 'fct_daily_funnel', 'int_purchases', 'not_null_stg_events_event_at_utc', 'not_null_stg_events_event_id', 'unique_stg_events_event_id']

Tests are children too: child_map lists the tests on stg_events next to the models that read it.

What lineage is for

- Impact analysis: “if I change stg_events, what breaks?” is dbt ls --select stg_events+.
- Root cause: a wrong number in fct_orders can only come from its ancestors (+fct_orders).
- Governance: catalogs such as Microsoft Purview, DataHub or the dbt platform’s explorer import manifest.json to show lineage across tools.

passages.heading: 35. Bug clinic: what goes wrong in dbt projects
passages.text:
Practice · symptom → cause → fix

| # | Symptom | Cause | Fix | Lesson |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | On a fresh database a model fails with “table does not exist”; it works on your laptop | Hard-coded table name instead of ref()/source(), so dbt doesn’t know the order | Always ref/source; check with dbt ls --select +model | 13, ex. 7 |
| 2 | Tables appear in main_marts, not marts | Default custom-schema naming: <target schema>_<custom> | Expected; override generate_schema_name only if your team agrees | 10 |
| 3 | “Configuration paths exist … which do not apply to any resources” | Folder renamed, typo in dbt_project.yml, or no models yet | Fix the path; never ignore this warning after a rename | 10 |
| 4 | “Column types specified for non-existent columns … 2)” and a seed load error | Unquoted decimal(10,2) in a YAML {…} mapping: YAML splits at the comma (this happened while building the deck) | Quote it: "decimal(10,2)" | 10 |
| 5 | Seed IDs lose leading zeros | Type inference turns 007 into 7 | column_types: {id: varchar} | 10 |
| 6 | unique fails on a fact, revenue too high | Fan-out join or missing dedupe; grain not preserved | Dedupe in staging; check every join against the grain | 12, 19 |
| 7 | relationships fails after new data arrives | Late-arriving or missing dimension member | Unknown member + coalesce in the fact; monitor unknown counts | 17, ex. 4 |
| 8 | relationships passes but facts have NULL keys | relationships ignores NULLs | Add not_null to every foreign key | 27 |
| 9 | Orders silently missing from a mart | Inner join to a dimension | Left join + unknown member; reconciliation test | 19, ex. 5 |
| 10 | accepted_values fails after a source change | A new legitimate value, or bad data | Decide rule vs data; store failures to see rows | 29, 31 |
| 11 | Times or dates off by hours; orders on the wrong day | Offsets ignored or session time zone used | Parse as TIMESTAMPTZ, convert to UTC in staging | 12 |
| 12 | Dashboards showed bad data before the test failed | dbt run then dbt test | dbt build in production | 30 |
| 13 | Deprecation warning: “Arguments to generic tests should be nested under the arguments property” | Pre-1.10 test syntax (values: directly under the test) | Move parameters under arguments: | 27 |

> On the job: Many dbt bugs leave every test green: a filter in the wrong layer, a join that drops rows, a hard-coded name that works in dev. Reconciliation tests, unknown-member counts, and reading compiled SQL catch them. Mention all three when you describe how you keep a pipeline trustworthy.

> The main idea: most dbt problems are about dependencies (ref), naming (schemas, paths), grain (joins, dedupe), and rules that drift from reality (tests). Each has a cheap, standard fix.

passages.heading: 36. Interview questions you should now be able to answer
passages.text:
Practice · short answers, then say them in your own words added

Q: What does dbt do, and what doesn’t it do?  
It is the T in ELT: it compiles templated SELECT statements to SQL, runs them on the warehouse in dependency order, tests the results and documents them. It does not extract or load data, does not store data itself, and (Core) does not schedule runs.

Q: Why use ref() instead of a table name?  
Build order from the DAG, environment-specific names (dev vs prod schemas), graph selection (+model), and lineage in docs and manifest.json. A hard-coded name breaks all four silently.

Q: Source vs seed vs model?  
A source is a raw table loaded by another tool and declared in YAML; a seed is a small CSV in the repository loaded by dbt seed; a model is a SELECT that dbt builds.

Q: View, table, ephemeral, incremental: how do you choose?  
Views for light staging logic (cheap to build, cost on every query); tables for marts people query; ephemeral for small reusable steps you don’t need as objects; incremental when a table is too large to rebuild every run.

Q: What are the four built-in generic tests, and what do you test first?  
unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships. First: the grain (unique + not_null on keys), then fact-to-dimension relationships plus not_null, then columns that drive logic.

Q: What happens in dbt build when a test fails?  
Nodes downstream of the tested model are skipped; already-built objects keep their previous data; the run exits with code 1. With severity: warn the run continues and the warning is recorded.

Q: How would you handle a fact row whose customer isn’t in the dimension yet?  
Keep the row: left join, map to an unknown (or inferred) member key, monitor the count of unknown keys with a test, and re-process once the dimension catches up.

Q: Explain dbt build --select state:modified+.  
Compare the project with a saved manifest (usually production’s), select changed nodes and everything downstream, and build only those, often with --defer so unchanged parents are read from production. This is slim CI.

Q: Where do you look when a model fails?  
The error message, then target/compiled/… (the SELECT) or target/run/… (the DDL); run that SQL directly in the warehouse. For test failures, run the compiled test SQL or use --store-failures.

passages.heading: 40. Cheat sheet
passages.text:
Reference · the deck on one page

Commands

| Need | Run |
|---|---|
| check setup | dbt debug |
| load CSV seeds | dbt seed |
| build models | dbt run --select … |
| run data tests | dbt test --select … |
| everything, safely | dbt build (tests between nodes; skips children of failures) |
| see the SQL | dbt compile --select m → target/compiled/ |
| preview rows | dbt show --select m / --inline "select …" |
| what would run? | dbt ls --select … |
| keep failing rows | dbt test --store-failures |
| override a variable | --vars '{key: value}' |
| docs | dbt docs generate, then dbt docs serve |
| start again | dbt clean, then dbt build |

Selectors

| Write | Means |
|---|---|
| m | just m |
| m+ / +m | m and descendants / ancestors |
| 1+m | m and direct parents |
| @m | descendants of m and all their ancestors |
| tag:mart | by tag |
| path:models/staging | by folder |
| resource_type:test | by type |
| a b | a OR b |
| a,b | a AND b |
| --exclude x | minus x |
| state:modified+ | changed + children (CI) |

Jinja in models

| Need | Write |
|---|---|
| another model or seed | {{ ref("stg_events") }} |
| a raw table | {{ source("shop_raw", "events") }} |
| per-model config | {{ config(materialized="view", tags=["x"]) }} |
| variable with default | {{ var("name", "default") }} |
| secret / setting | {{ env_var("NAME", "default") }} |
| comment | {# not sent to the database #} |

Tests and layout

| Need | Write |
|---|---|
| grain | data_tests: [unique, not_null] on the key |
| allowed values | accepted_values: {arguments: {values: [...]}} |
| foreign key | relationships: {arguments: {to: ref('dim'), field: key}} + not_null |
| custom rule | SELECT of bad rows in tests/*.sql |
| known, accepted issue | {{ config(severity="warn") }} |
| layers | sources → stg_ (views) → int_ (ephemeral) → fct_/dim_ (tables) |
| staging does | rename, cast, clean, UTC, dedupe; no joins |
| marts do | declared grain, surrogate keys, unknown members, left joins |
| schemas | custom marts → <target>_marts |

> The main idea: ref and source for every dependency, layers with clear jobs, tests on every grain and key, dbt build with selectors, and compiled SQL whenever something is unclear.

passages.heading: 41. Glossary
passages.text:
Reference · every new term in this deck

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ETL / ELT | Transform before loading / load raw data first, then transform inside the warehouse |
| Analytics engineering | Building tested, documented transformations that turn raw data into trusted models |
| dbt Core / dbt platform | The open-source CLI / the hosted product (formerly dbt Cloud) with scheduler and IDE |
| Adapter | Plug-in that lets dbt connect to and generate SQL for one database (dbt-duckdb, dbt-fabric) |
| Project | A folder with dbt_project.yml, models, seeds, macros and tests |
| YAML / property file | Indented key: value text format / a .yml file describing resources (descriptions, tests) |
| Profile / target | Connection settings outside the project / one named connection (dev, ci, prod) |
| Threads | How many nodes dbt builds in parallel |
| Config | A setting that changes how a resource is built (materialized, schema, tags, severity) |
| Custom schema | A schema set with +schema; by default named <target schema>_<custom> |
| Model | One .sql file with one SELECT; dbt creates the object |
| Materialization | How a model is built: view, table, ephemeral, incremental |
| Ephemeral model | A model inlined as a CTE (dbtctename) into the models that use it |
| Incremental model | A table that processes only new or changed rows after the first run |
| Seed | Small CSV in the repository loaded as a table by dbt seed |
| Source | A raw table loaded by another tool and declared in YAML; referenced with source() |
| Source freshness | A check that the newest row of a source is recent enough |
| Bronze / silver / gold | Medallion layers ≈ sources / staging (+ intermediate) / marts |
| Staging / intermediate / marts | Clean one source / reusable logic / business-facing facts and dimensions |
| CTE / import CTE | A named subquery in WITH / a CTE at the top that selects from one ref or source |
| QUALIFY | Filter on a window-function result (used for dedupe) |
| ref() | Reference to a dbt resource; resolves its name and adds a DAG edge |
| DAG | Directed acyclic graph of dependencies between nodes |
| Node | Anything in the DAG: model, seed, source, test, snapshot |
| Template / compile | SQL with Jinja / render it to plain SQL (target/compiled) |
| DDL | SQL that creates or changes objects (CREATE, ALTER, DROP); in target/run |

passages.heading: 41. Glossary
passages.text:
/ compile | SQL with Jinja / render it to plain SQL (target/compiled) |
| DDL | SQL that creates or changes objects (CREATE, ALTER, DROP); in target/run |
| Jinja | The template language in dbt: {{ expression }}, {% statement %}, {# comment #} |
| Variable (var) | A project setting read in models; overridable with --vars |
| Grain | What one row of a table means |
| Surrogate key / hashed key | A warehouse key for a dimension row / one computed as a hash of the natural key |
| Natural key | The identifier from the source system (customer_id) |
| Unknown member | A dimension row (key -1) that facts use when the real member is missing |
| Late-arriving dimension | A fact that arrives before its dimension member exists |
| Degenerate dimension | An identifier kept on the fact with no dimension table (order_id) |
| Conformed dimension | One dimension shared, with the same keys, by several facts |
| Periodic snapshot fact | A fact with one row per period (per day) |
| Fan-out | A join that multiplies rows and inflates totals |
| Data test | A query returning rows that break a rule; zero rows = pass |
| Generic / singular test | Reusable parameterised test attached in YAML / one-off SELECT in tests/ |
| Severity | Whether a failing test errors (stops) or warns (continues) |
| Store failures | Saving failing rows of a test in a table for investigation |
| Reconciliation test | Compares counts or totals between layers or with the source |
| Unit test | Tests a model’s logic on hand-made input rows (dbt 1.8+) |
| Selector / graph operator / set operator | Picks nodes / + and @ walk the DAG / space = OR, comma = AND |
| Skip | A node not run because something it depends on failed |
| Exit code | 0 success, 1 failures, 2 dbt error; read by schedulers and CI |
| manifest.json / catalog.json | The project as JSON (nodes, parent_map, child_map) / column metadata read from the database |
| Doc block | Named Markdown in a .md file, used with {{ doc("name") }} |
| Lineage | Where each table’s data comes from, as edges between nodes |
| Snapshot (dbt) | Records changes of a mutable source as SCD type 2 rows |
| Package | A reusable dbt project installed with dbt deps (dbt_utils) |
| Slim CI / defer | Build only state:modified+ in CI / read unchanged parents from production |
| Idempotent | Running twice gives the same result as running once |

passages.heading: 42. What to remember, and what comes next
passages.text:
Reference · recap

1. dbt is the T in ELT. It compiles templated SELECTs, runs them in DAG order on the warehouse, tests and documents them. Loading and scheduling are elsewhere.
2. The project is code. dbt_project.yml sets folder defaults; profiles.yml holds targets outside the code; secrets via env_var.
3. Every dependency goes through source() or ref(). That gives order, environment-safe names, selection and lineage.
4. Layers have jobs. Staging cleans one source (cast, UTC, dedupe); intermediate holds reusable logic; marts are facts and conformed dimensions at a declared grain, with unknown members.
5. Materialization is a choice per layer. Views for staging, ephemeral for small steps, tables for marts; incremental later.
6. Models are templates. ref, source, var and config are Jinja; dbt compiles them to plain SQL, so read the compiled SQL whenever in doubt.
7. Tests encode expectations. unique + not_null on every grain, relationships + not_null on keys, accepted_values on logic columns, singular tests for reconciliations; choose severity on purpose.
8. Build, select, document. dbt build stops bad data; selectors keep work focused; docs and manifest.json give lineage for free.

Practise this week

- Rebuild the project from an empty folder from memory, checking against dbt-fundamentals-project/.
- Do exercises 4, 5 and 7 again without hints.
- Add a second source (for example a refunds table) with its own staging model, tests and a fact.
- Explain the lineage diagram out loud, layer by layer, in two minutes.

Coming up

Deck 2, dbt Jinja and macros, starts from this project: Jinja expressions and statements, a loop that rebuilds fct_daily_funnel from a variable, a macro for the UTC conversion, then a preview of incremental models, snapshots, unit tests, packages and contracts. Later lessons cover deployment, slim CI and the same project on a cloud warehouse such as Fabric Data Warehouse.

> The main idea: ref and source for dependencies, layers with clear jobs, tests at every grain and key, dbt build with selectors, and docs from the same files: that is a trustworthy dbt project.

Read more: What is dbt?, How we structure our dbt projects.

passages.text: Every solution below was applied to a scratch copy of the project and run with dbt during the build; the outputs shown are real (timestamps and durations normalised).

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 1 · Test the grain and the categories of stg_products

# models/staging/_staging.yml (stg_products entry)
  - name: stg_products
    description: One row per product from the catalogue seed.
    columns:
      - name: product_id
        data_tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: category
        data_tests:
          - not_null
          - accepted_values:
              arguments:
                values: ["Plants", "Accessories", "Plant care"]

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt test --select stg_products
2 of 4 PASS not_null_stg_products_category ..................................... [PASS in x.xxs]
1 of 4 PASS accepted_values_stg_products_category__Plants__Accessories__Plant_care  [PASS in x.xxs]
3 of 4 PASS not_null_stg_products_product_id ................................... [PASS in x.xxs]
4 of 4 PASS unique_stg_products_product_id ..................................... [PASS in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=4 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=4

Why it works. Four generic tests attach to two columns; dbt test --select stg_products runs every test whose parent is stg_products. Values in accepted_values are case-sensitive: plants would fail.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 2 · Write selectors, check them with dbt ls

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt ls --select products+ --resource-type model
leafy.marts.dim_product
leafy.marts.fct_orders
leafy.staging.stg_products

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt ls --select 1+fct_daily_funnel --resource-type model
leafy.marts.fct_daily_funnel
leafy.staging.stg_events

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt ls --select tag:mart --exclude fct_orders fct_daily_funnel --resource-type model
leafy.marts.dim_customer
leafy.marts.dim_date
leafy.marts.dim_product

Why it works. + after a name walks down the DAG to children; a number limits the depth; --exclude is applied after selection. Seeds are nodes too, so products+ starts at the seed. In practice you would run dbt build --select products+ after editing the CSV.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 3 · Override a materialization in one model

# models/marts/dim_product.sql (first line added)
{{ config(materialized='view') }}
-- dim_product: one row per product, plus one unknown member.
…

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt run --select dim_product
1 of 1 OK created sql view model main_marts.dim_product ........................ [OK in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1

import duckdb
with duckdb.connect("leafy.duckdb", read_only=True) as con:
    print(con.sql("""select table_name, table_type from information_schema.tables
                     where table_schema = 'main_marts' and table_name like 'dim_%' order by 1"""))

Output:

┌──────────────┬────────────┐
│  table_name  │ table_type │
│   varchar    │  varchar   │
├──────────────┼────────────┤
│ dim_customer │ BASE TABLE │
│ dim_date     │ BASE TABLE │
│ dim_product  │ VIEW       │
└──────────────┴────────────┘

Why it works. Config precedence: model file > property file > dbt_project.yml. dbt sees an existing table called dim_product, drops it, and creates the view. The schema is still main_marts because the folder’s +schema still applies.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 4 · Debug failing relationships and not_null tests

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt build --select fct_orders   # with the teammate’s change
3 of 10 FAIL 1 not_null_fct_orders_customer_key ................................ [FAIL 1 in x.xxs]
7 of 10 FAIL 1 relationships_fct_orders_customer_key__customer_key__ref_dim_customer_  [FAIL 1 in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=8 WARN=0 ERROR=2 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=10
[exit code 1]

import duckdb
with duckdb.connect("leafy.duckdb", read_only=True) as con:
    print(con.sql("""select f.order_id, f.customer_key is null as key_is_null
                     from main_marts.fct_orders f
                     left join main_marts.dim_customer c using (customer_key)
                     where c.customer_key is null order by 1"""))

Output:

┌──────────┬─────────────┐
│ order_id │ key_is_null │
│ varchar  │   boolean   │
├──────────┼─────────────┤
│ e13      │ false       │
│ e6       │ true        │
└──────────┴─────────────┘

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt build --select fct_orders   # after restoring the lookup
Done. PASS=10 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=10

Why it fails. e6 has no user: md5(NULL) is NULL, so not_null fails (and relationships ignores it). e13’s user u6 is not in the CRM: its hash exists nowhere in dim_customer, so relationships fails. The hash alone is not enough; the lookup decides whether the member exists and maps misses to the unknown member. dbt build --select fct_orders builds the model and runs its 9 tests, which is why the fixed run shows PASS=10.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 5 · A reconciliation test that catches silent row loss

# tests/assert_orders_reconcile_to_staging.sql
-- Reconciliation: fct_orders must hold exactly the valid purchases from staging.
with mart as (
    select count(*) as n, sum(amount) as total
    from {{ ref('fct_orders') }}
),
staging as (
    select count(*) as n, sum(amount) as total
    from {{ ref('stg_events') }}
    where event_type = 'purchase' and amount is not null
)
select
    mart.n as mart_orders, staging.n as staging_orders,
    mart.total as mart_total, staging.total as staging_total
from mart cross join staging
where mart.n <> staging.n or mart.total <> staging.total

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt test --select assert_orders_reconcile_to_staging
1 of 1 PASS assert_orders_reconcile_to_staging ................................. [PASS in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt build --select fct_orders   # after changing left join to join
2 of 11 FAIL 1 assert_orders_reconcile_to_staging .............................. [FAIL 1 in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=10 WARN=0 ERROR=1 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=11
[exit code 1]

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt show --inline "select order_id from {{ ref('fct_orders') }} order by order_id"
Previewing inline node:
| order_id |
| -------- |
| e10      |
| e12      |
| e3       |
| e5       |
| e8       |

Why it works. The inner join drops e6 and e13 (no matching customer). Every remaining row is still unique, not null and has valid relationships, so the nine generic tests pass; only the reconciliation sees that 2 orders and 27.99 are missing. Reconciliation tests are the safety net for joins and filters.

# data/raw/events_2026-03-05.jsonl
{"event_id":"e14","user_id":"u3","event_type":"purchase","ts":"2026-03-05T08:00:00Z","amount":"30.00","product_id":"P5"}

events_2026-03-02.jsonl: 9 rows
events_2026-03-03.jsonl: 4 rows
events_2026-03-04.jsonl: 2 rows
events_2026-03-05.jsonl: 2 rows
total: 17

$ dbt build
Done. PASS=41 WARN=1 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=42

import duckdb
with duckdb.connect("leafy.duckdb", read_only=True) as con:
    print(con.sql("select count(*) as orders, sum(amount) as revenue from main_marts.fct_orders"))
    print(con.sql("""select f.order_id, c.customer_name, p.product_name, f.amount
                     from main_marts.fct_orders f
                     join main_marts.dim_customer c using (customer_key)
                     join main_marts.dim_product p using (product_key)
                     where p.product_id = '-1' or c.customer_id = '-1' order by 1"""))

Output:

┌────────┬───────────────┐
│ orders │    revenue    │
│ int64  │ decimal(38,2) │
├────────┼───────────────┤
│      8 │        205.99 │
└────────┴───────────────┘

┌──────────┬──────────────────┬─────────────────┬───────────────┐
│ order_id │  customer_name   │  product_name   │    amount     │
│ varchar  │     varchar      │     varchar     │ decimal(10,2) │
├──────────┼──────────────────┼─────────────────┼───────────────┤
│ e13      │ Unknown customer │ Fertilizer      │          9.99 │
│ e14      │ Ana Ruiz         │ Unknown product │         30.00 │
│ e6       │ Unknown customer │ Ceramic Pot     │         18.00 │
└──────────┴──────────────────┴─────────────────┴───────────────┘

Why it works. Staging dedupes the third e3, so only e14 is new: 8 orders, 175.99 + 30.00 = 205.99. P5 maps to the unknown product, so relationships passes and the order is kept; the second query is the monitoring query you would schedule to find unknown members. If the date had been outside the dim_date range, the relationships test on date_key would have failed: a good reason for a generous date range.

Why it fails. Without ref() the model has no parents, so dbt runs it in the first wave, before fct_orders exists. On your laptop yesterday’s tables hid the bug (and it would read dev tables even when deploying to prod). With ref() the model gets its ancestors, runs last, and is correct in every environment. passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 8 · From ephemeral to view: where does it land?

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt run --select int_purchases fct_orders
1 of 2 OK created sql view model main.int_purchases ............................ [OK in x.xxs]
2 of 2 OK created sql table model main_marts.fct_orders ........................ [OK in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=2 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=2

Terminal (lines mentioning int_purchases):

$ dbt compile --select fct_orders
    select * from "leafy"."main"."int_purchases"

Why it works. The intermediate folder sets a materialization but no custom schema, so the view goes to the target schema, main. The compiled fact no longer contains the dbtcteint_purchases CTE; it selects from the view instead. If you want it in its own schema, add +schema: intermediate (giving main_intermediate). Making an ephemeral model a view temporarily is also the standard way to debug it.

passages.heading: dbt Jinja and macros: templates, loops, reusable SQL
passages.text: Companion to dbt-jinja-macros.html: same lessons, same numbering, same code. Hints and solutions are in Appendices A and B. Tested with: dbt-core 1.12.5 and the dbt-duckdb adapter 1.11.0 (DuckDB 1.5.6) on CPython 3.12.10, Windows 11 (64-bit), in one virtual environment. SQL dialect: DuckDB. Every dbt command shown was executed while building this document, in a real project folder, and its real output is shown. Output was normalised in three ways only: the leading clock time on each dbt log line was removed, per-node and total durations were replaced by x.xx, and absolute folder paths were replaced by , or ~. Some long outputs are trimmed (marked). Series: this is deck 2 of 2 on dbt. It starts from the finished project of deck 1, dbt fundamentals (folder dbt-fundamentals-project/ next to that deck), and refactors it with a Jinja loop and a macro. The refactored project is in the folder dbt-jinja-macros-project/ next to this file; lesson 6 rebuilds it from scratch. Lessons 7–8 preview incremental models, snapshots, unit tests, packages and contracts in a scratch copy. Prerequisites: deck 1, dbt fundamentals (sources, ref, layers, materializations, tests, selectors), and the Python decks (functions, string formatting). New terms are defined on first use, collected in the glossary, and most lessons end with an On the job note. Interview focus: the interview questions and exercises follow common dbt interview patterns (research done in October 2026: how dbt uses Jinja, writing and calling macros, debugging templates, is_incremental() and unique_key, snapshot strategies, packages). All questions are original and use the Leafy project. Additions beyond the original brief are marked (added): a setup that starts from the dbt fundamentals project and keeps a copy of the old output; proving a refactor safe by comparing output rows before and after (EXCEPT both ways); a bug clinic for Jinja, macros, incremental models and snapshots; interview questions with model answers.

passages.heading: 1. dbt Jinja and macros: templates, loops, reusable SQL
passages.text:
Deck 1 built a tested star schema with dbt. Some of its SQL is repetitive: four nearly identical lines in a pivot, a time-zone conversion that every future source will need. This deck turns that SQL into templates with Jinja, proves the refactor changed nothing, and then previews what Jinja makes possible next: incremental models, snapshots, and unit tests. Every dbt command ran while the deck was built, against a local DuckDB file.

- Start here: the dbt fundamentals project, built and checked, with a copy of its output.
- Part A, Jinja: expressions, statements, comments, whitespace control, and dbt’s built-in functions.
- Part B, refactor: a loop over a project variable, a macro with an argument, and the refactored project rebuilt from scratch.
- Part C, next steps: incremental models, snapshots, unit tests, packages, contracts, CI (preview, in a scratch copy).
- Then: a bug clinic, interview questions, 2 exercises, a cheat sheet, a glossary and references.

passages.heading: Why this matters · Why this matters on the job
passages.text:
Why this matters · the need behind the topic

Real dbt projects repeat themselves: the same pivot for every new category, the same time-zone or currency conversion in every staging model, the same union for every country’s copy of a source. Copy-pasted SQL drifts, and a fix made in one place is forgotten in four others. Jinja and macros let you write such SQL once and generate the rest, and they are also the machinery behind incremental models, snapshots, and most dbt packages. Used with restraint, they make a project shorter and safer; used carelessly, they make it unreadable.

Where you will use it

- Pivots and column lists driven by a variable or seed.
- Shared expressions (UTC, currency, safe casts) in a small macros folder.
- Environment-specific SQL with target.name.
- Incremental models (is_incremental(), {{ this }}) and packages such as dbt_utils.

What goes wrong without it

- The same rule copied into many models and fixed in only some of them.
- A new category added in the data but not in the hand-written pivot.
- A refactor that silently changes dashboard numbers.
- Templates so clever that nobody can review the SQL they produce.

Who expects you to know it

- Analytics engineers: macros, packages and refactoring are daily work.
- Reviewers: expect compiled SQL and evidence that outputs did not change.
- Interviewers: “how does dbt use Jinja?”, “write a macro”, “what does is_incremental() do?”, “snapshot or incremental?”.

> On the job: A teammate adds a fifth event type to the website. In a project with a hard-coded pivot, someone must find and edit every model that lists event types; in this deck’s project, they add one value to a variable, run dbt build, and a comparison query shows that the four existing columns did not move.

> The main idea: Jinja and macros remove repetition from SQL; the compiled output and an output comparison keep them honest.

Read more: dbt: Jinja and macros, Jinja template designer docs.

passages.heading: Why this matters · When to reach for it, and when not to
passages.text:
Why this matters · choosing the right tool

| Situation | Reach for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| The same SQL pattern repeated for a list of values | A Jinja loop over a variable or seed | One change point; the list is documented |
| The same expression in three or more models | A macro | One definition, one fix |
| SQL that differs per environment or database | target or adapter dispatch | One model, several targets |
| A large fact that is too slow to rebuild | An incremental model (Part C) | Processes only new rows |
| Logic that is clearer as plain SQL | Plain SQL | Reviewers read SQL faster than templates |
| Something that needs to look at data before writing SQL | Usually a model or a seed, not run_query | Jinja runs before the data is read |

How interviews test it

- “How does dbt use Jinja, and when does it run?”
- “Write a macro that …; how do you call it?” (column names as strings).
- “How do you debug a broken template?” (compile, read target/compiled).
- “What does is_incremental() do? Snapshot or incremental?”

Where it sits in your learning path

- Builds on: deck 1, dbt fundamentals (its project is the starting point here) and the Python decks (functions, default arguments).
- Next in your plan: incremental models, snapshots and unit tests in depth, then deployment and CI.

> The main idea: reach for a loop or macro when it removes real repetition, and prove every refactor with compiled SQL and an output comparison; otherwise keep plain SQL.

passages.heading: 3. Jinja basics: the template language inside dbt
passages.text:
Part A · {{ expressions }}, {% statements %}, {# comments #}

Jinja is a Python templating language. dbt renders every model with Jinja before sending it to the database. You already used it in deck 1: {{ ref() }}, {{ source() }}, {{ var() }} and {{ config() }} are Jinja. Three kinds of delimiter:

| Syntax | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {{ … }} | expression: evaluate and insert the result as text | {{ ref("stg_events") }}, {{ var("dim_date_start") }} |
| {% … %} | statement: logic that inserts nothing by itself | {% for t in types %} … {% endfor %}, {% if target.name == "ci" %}, {% set x = 3 %} |
| {# … #} | comment: removed before the SQL reaches the database | {# explain a tricky filter #} |
| {%- … -%} | whitespace control: the dash trims spaces/newlines on that side | keeps compiled SQL tidy |

Terminal (startup lines removed):

$ dbt compile --inline "select {{ 40 + 2 }} as answer, '{{ var('dim_date_start') }}' as first_day, '{{ target.name }}' as target_name {# not sent #}"
Compiled inline node is:
select 42 as answer, '2026-03-01' as first_day, 'dev' as target_name 

dbt’s built-in Jinja

| Function / variable | Returns |
|---|---|
| ref("m"), source("s", "t") | a relation name, and a DAG edge |
| config(materialized="view", tags=[…]) | sets configs for this model |
| var("name", default) | a project variable |
| env_var("NAME", default) | an environment variable |
| target.name, target.schema | details of the active target |
| is_incremental(), this | used by incremental models (lesson 7) |

Golden rule

Jinja runs before the database sees anything. It can write SQL, but it cannot see data (except through special macros such as run_query). If a template is confusing, read the compiled SQL: that is what really runs.

> On the job: Most production dbt Jinja is simple: ref, source, config, a variable, an occasional loop or if target.name. Heavy Jinja makes models hard to review; reviewers often ask “could this be plain SQL?”

> The main idea: {{ }} inserts a value, {% %} runs logic, {# #} is a comment. Jinja runs first and produces plain SQL; read the compiled output whenever in doubt.

Read more: Jinja and macros, dbt Jinja functions, Jinja template designer docs, target.

passages.heading: 4. A Jinja loop: one column per event type
passages.text:
Part B · generate repetitive SQL from a list

In deck 1, fct_daily_funnel has four nearly identical count(*) filter (…) lines, one per event type. A pivot (one column per category) is repetitive SQL: perfect for a {% for %} loop. First move the list into a project variable, so adding an event type becomes a one-line change in dbt_project.yml:

vars:
   dim_date_start: "2026-03-01"
   dim_date_end: "2026-03-07"
+  funnel_event_types: ["page_view", "add_to_cart", "purchase", "refund"]

The template replaces the four lines

# models/marts/fct_daily_funnel.sql
{{ config(tags=["funnel"]) }}
-- fct_daily_funnel: one row per UTC day with event counts by type.
-- A periodic snapshot fact (grain: date). Event types come from a project variable.
select
    cast(strftime(cast(event_at_utc as date), '%Y%m%d') as integer) as date_key,
    {%- for event_type in var("funnel_event_types") %}
    count(*) filter (where event_type = '{{ event_type }}') as {{ event_type }}_events,
    {%- endfor %}
    count(distinct customer_id) as active_customers
from {{ ref("stg_events") }}
group by 1

Compiled: the same four lines as before

Terminal (startup lines removed):

$ dbt compile --select fct_daily_funnel
Unable to do partial parsing because a project config has changed
-- fct_daily_funnel: one row per UTC day with event counts by type.
-- A periodic snapshot fact (grain: date). Event types come from a project variable.
select
    cast(strftime(cast(event_at_utc as date), '%Y%m%d') as integer) as date_key,
    count(*) filter (where event_type = 'page_view') as page_view_events,
    count(*) filter (where event_type = 'add_to_cart') as add_to_cart_events,
    count(*) filter (where event_type = 'purchase') as purchase_events,
    count(*) filter (where event_type = 'refund') as refund_events,
    count(distinct customer_id) as active_customers
from "leafy"."main_staging"."stg_events"
group by 1

Terminal (summary lines):

$ dbt run --select fct_daily_funnel
1 of 1 OK created sql table model main_marts.fct_daily_funnel .................. [OK in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1

Prove the refactor changed nothing

import duckdb
with duckdb.connect("leafy.duckdb", read_only=True) as con:
    new_only = con.sql("""select * from main_marts.fct_daily_funnel
                          except select * from main.fct_daily_funnel_legacy""").fetchall()

passages.heading: 4. A Jinja loop: one column per event type
passages.text:
new_only = con.sql("""select * from main_marts.fct_daily_funnel
                          except select * from main.fct_daily_funnel_legacy""").fetchall()
    old_only = con.sql("""select * from main.fct_daily_funnel_legacy
                          except select * from main_marts.fct_daily_funnel""").fetchall()
    print("rows only in the new output:", len(new_only))
    print("rows only in the old output:", len(old_only))
    assert new_only == [] and old_only == []

Output:

rows only in the new output: 0
rows only in the old output: 0

EXCEPT returns the rows of the first query that are missing from the second. Empty in both directions means the new table has exactly the old rows. Column names are compared by position, so the order of the generated columns matters too.

Notes

- The trailing-comma problem is avoided by ending with a column outside the loop. Alternative: {% if not loop.last %},{% endif %}.
- {%- for … %}: the dash removes the newline before the tag, so the compiled SQL has no blank lines.
- The funnel tag still comes from {{ config() }} in the file, so --select tag:funnel keeps working.

> On the job: Loops generate pivots, unions of many similar sources (“one staging model per country, unioned”), and column lists. If a loop needs a hard-coded list of values found in the data, consider dbt_utils.get_column_values or keep the list in a variable or seed.

> The main idea: use {% for %} over a variable list to generate repetitive SQL; control commas and whitespace, check the compiled result, and prove the output did not change.

Read more: Jinja and macros, Jinja for loops, config(), Project variables.

passages.heading: 5. A simple macro: reusable SQL snippets
passages.text:
Part B · macros are Jinja functions

A macro is a Jinja function, defined in a .sql file under macros/, that returns SQL text. Every model can call it. Here the UTC conversion from stg_events becomes a macro, so any future source with offset timestamps converts them the same way.

Define it

# macros/to_utc.sql
{% macro to_utc(column_name) -%}
    timezone('UTC', cast({{ column_name }} as timestamptz))
{%- endmacro %}

Then edit one line of models/staging/stg_events.sql:

-        timezone('UTC', cast(ts as timestamptz))  as event_at_utc,
+        {{ to_utc('ts') }}                        as event_at_utc,

Same SQL as before

Terminal (only the line that changed):

$ dbt compile --select stg_events
        timezone('UTC', cast(ts as timestamptz))                        as event_at_utc,

Bugs and fixes

| Bug | Fix |
|---|---|
| {{ to_utc(ts) }}: Jinja looks for a Jinja variable called ts and finds none | Pass column names as strings: to_utc('ts') |
| Macro output has stray newlines | Whitespace control: {%- … -%} |
| Macro edited but models not rebuilt | Macros change compiled SQL; re-run the models that use them |
| A macro called ref or source | Don’t shadow built-ins; prefix your own macros if unsure |

Where macros are used

- Repeated expressions: currency conversion, UTC conversion, safe casts.
- Adapter differences: the same macro can produce DuckDB SQL or T-SQL.
- Overriding dbt behaviour, e.g. generate_schema_name to change the main_marts naming rule.
- Packages such as dbt_utils are mostly collections of macros (lesson 8).

> On the job: A small macros/ folder of well-named helpers is a sign of a mature project; a huge one full of clever Jinja is a warning sign. Write a macro when the same expression appears in three models.

> The main idea: macros are Jinja functions that return SQL. Pass column names as strings, control whitespace, and verify with dbt compile that the generated SQL is what you meant.

Read more: Jinja and macros, Adapter dispatch, Custom schemas and generate_schema_name.

passages.heading: 7. Next steps: incremental models and snapshots
passages.text:
Part C · introduced only, tried in a scratch copy of the project

Two features that build directly on Jinja, and that come next in your plan (incremental models, snapshots, unit tests). Both were run here in a copy of the refactored project; the final project does not include them.

Incremental models

An incremental model is a table that, after the first run, processes only new or changed rows and merges them in, instead of rebuilding everything. The Jinja {% if is_incremental() %} block adds a filter only on later runs; {{ this }} is the model’s own existing table; unique_key tells dbt which rows to update rather than append.

# models/marts/fct_events_incremental.sql
{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='event_id') }}
-- Sketch: an event fact that only processes new rows after the first run.
select event_id, event_type, event_at_utc, amount
from {{ ref('stg_events') }}
{% if is_incremental() %}
where event_at_utc > (select max(event_at_utc) from {{ this }})
{% endif %}

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt run --select fct_events_incremental   # first run: creates the table
1 of 1 OK created sql incremental model main_marts.fct_events_incremental ...... [OK in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt run --select fct_events_incremental   # later runs: only new rows
1 of 1 OK created sql incremental model main_marts.fct_events_incremental ...... [OK in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1

-- target/compiled/leafy/models/marts/fct_events_incremental.sql (generated by dbt)
-- Sketch: an event fact that only processes new rows after the first run.
select event_id, event_type, event_at_utc, amount
from "leafy"."main_staging"."stg_events"
where event_at_utc > (select max(event_at_utc) from "leafy"."main_marts"."fct_events_incremental")

Watch for: late-arriving rows older than the max timestamp (use a look-back window), schema changes (on_schema_change), and --full-refresh to rebuild from scratch.

Snapshots

A snapshot records how rows of a mutable source change over time: SCD type 2 from the dimensional modeling deck, with dbt_valid_from / dbt_valid_to columns. Defined in YAML since dbt 1.9; run with dbt snapshot (also part of dbt build).

# snapshots/customers_snapshot.yml
snapshots:
  - name: customers_snapshot
    relation: ref('stg_customers')
    config:

passages.heading: 8. Next steps: packages, contracts, unit tests, other warehouses, CI
passages.text:
Part C · where to go after Jinja and macros

Unit tests (dbt 1.8+)

A unit test checks a model’s logic on a few hand-made input rows, without real data: “given these two deliveries of e1, staging keeps the later one and cleans the text”. Data tests check the data; unit tests check the SQL. Tried here in a scratch copy:

# models/staging/_unit_tests.yml
unit_tests:
  - name: stg_events_keeps_latest_delivery
    model: stg_events
    given:
      - input: source('shop_raw', 'events')
        rows:
          - {event_id: e1, user_id: " U1 ", event_type: Purchase, ts: "2026-03-02T10:00:00+01:00", amount: "10", product_id: p1, _source_file: a.jsonl}
          - {event_id: e1, user_id: u1, event_type: purchase, ts: "2026-03-02T10:00:00+01:00", amount: "12.50", product_id: p1, _source_file: b.jsonl}
    expect:
      rows:
        - {event_id: e1, customer_id: u1, event_type: purchase, amount: 12.50, product_id: P1, _source_file: b.jsonl}

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt test --select test_type:unit

Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1

passages.heading: 9. Bug clinic: what goes wrong with Jinja and macros
passages.text:
Practice · symptom → cause → fix added

| # | Symptom | Cause | Fix | Lesson |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Compilation error: “… is undefined” when calling a macro | Column name passed without quotes, so Jinja looks for a variable | to_utc('ts'): pass column names as strings | 5 |
| 2 | Syntax error near from in a generated pivot | Trailing comma from a Jinja loop | End with a fixed column, or {% if not loop.last %},{% endif %} | 4 |
| 3 | Compiled SQL full of blank lines and odd indentation | No whitespace control on loop or macro tags | {%- … %} / {%- … -%}; read target/compiled/ | 3, 4 |
| 4 | A new event type appears in the data but never gets a column | The list of values is hard-coded in the model | Keep it in a variable (or a seed); add a test that flags unknown values | 4 |
| 5 | “… is undefined” for a variable in one environment only | var() without a default, and the variable is not defined there | Define it in dbt_project.yml or give var() a default | 4, ex. 2 |
| 6 | A macro was fixed, but the table still has the old values | Macros change compiled SQL only; tables are rebuilt only when their models run | dbt build --select stg_events+ after changing a macro used by stg_events | 5 |
| 7 | A “harmless” refactor changes dashboard numbers | Nobody compared the output before and after | Save the old output; compare with EXCEPT both ways | 2, 4 |
| 8 | An incremental model misses events that arrived late | The filter > max(event_at_utc) skips rows older than the newest one | A look-back window plus unique_key, or --full-refresh | 7 |
| 9 | A snapshot shows no history for a change everyone remembers | The value changed and changed back between two snapshot runs | Run snapshots on a schedule frequent enough for the source | 7 |

> On the job: Jinja bugs are cheap to catch before they reach the warehouse: dbt compile (or dbt parse) in CI fails on undefined names, and reviewing the compiled SQL catches commas and whitespace. Output comparisons catch the rest.

> The main idea: most Jinja problems are names (strings vs variables), punctuation (commas, whitespace), or stale builds. Compile, read the SQL, rebuild downstream, and compare outputs.

passages.heading: 10. Interview questions and model answers
passages.text:
Practice · say each answer aloud before revealing it added

These questions recur in dbt interview guides and candidates’ write-ups (research done in October 2026): how dbt uses Jinja, macros, is_incremental(), snapshots, and testing logic. Answer aloud in about a minute, then open the model answer.

“How does dbt use Jinja, and when does it run?” · checks: compile-time rendering, the three delimiters, debugging habit

Model answer (about 60 seconds): Every model is a template. Before anything is sent to the warehouse, dbt renders it with Jinja: expressions in double curly braces insert values such as ref(), source(), var() or config(); statements in curly-percent tags add logic such as loops and ifs; comments are dropped. The result is plain SQL in target/compiled. Jinja cannot see the data, except through special macros such as run_query, so when a template is confusing I read the compiled SQL, which is what actually runs.

Likely follow-up: “How would you debug a model whose generated SQL is wrong?” → Run dbt compile for that model, open target/compiled, run that SQL directly, and fix the template; dbt parse catches undefined names quickly in CI.

“What is a macro, and when would you write one?” · checks: reusable SQL, judgement about when not to, strings vs variables

Model answer (about 60 seconds): A macro is a Jinja function in the macros folder that returns SQL text. I write one when the same expression appears in several models, such as a UTC conversion or a safe cast, when SQL must differ by adapter, or to override dbt behaviour such as generate_schema_name. Column names go in as strings. I keep macros small, check the compiled output after a change, and rebuild the models that use them. If a macro makes a model harder to read than plain SQL, I don’t write it.

Likely follow-up: “How would you share macros across several dbt projects?” → Put them in a package (a separate dbt project), add it to packages.yml with a pinned version, and install it with dbt deps; dbt_utils is the best-known example.

“What does is_incremental() do, and why does an incremental model need a unique_key?” · checks: incremental mechanics, merges vs appends, late data

passages.heading: 10. Interview questions and model answers
passages.text:

“What does is_incremental() do, and why does an incremental model need a unique_key?” · checks: incremental mechanics, merges vs appends, late data

Model answer (about 60 seconds): is_incremental() is true when the model’s table already exists, the model is materialized as incremental, and the run is not a full refresh. Inside that block I filter the source to new rows, usually comparing a timestamp with the maximum already in {{ this }}, the existing table. Without a unique_key dbt appends, so a changed or redelivered row is duplicated; with it dbt merges, updating rows whose key already exists.

Likely follow-up: “Events can arrive two days late. What changes?” → Use a look-back window, for example max timestamp minus three days, together with unique_key so reprocessed rows are merged, not duplicated; schedule a periodic full refresh if the source can change further back.

“When would you use a snapshot instead of an incremental model?” · checks: SCD2, strategies, what each tool keeps

Model answer (about 60 seconds): A snapshot keeps history of a mutable source: every time a row changes, the old version is closed with dbt_valid_to and a new one opens, which is a type 2 slowly changing dimension. An incremental model processes new rows efficiently but keeps only the current state of each key. With the timestamp strategy dbt trusts an updated_at column; with the check strategy it compares column values, which works without a timestamp but costs more.

Likely follow-up: “What is the risk with snapshots?” → They only see changes at the moments they run: a value that changes and changes back between two runs leaves no trace, so the schedule must match how fast the source changes.

“What is the difference between a unit test and a data test?” · checks: testing logic vs testing data

Model answer (about 60 seconds): A data test runs on the real data after a model is built and returns failing rows: unique, not_null, relationships, or a custom SQL rule. A unit test checks the model’s logic on a few hand-made input rows and expected output rows, without real data, so it can run in CI before anything is built. I use unit tests for tricky logic such as dedupe or date handling, and data tests on every key and grain.

Likely follow-up: “Can a unit test replace data tests?” → No: a unit test proves the SQL is right for the cases you thought of; data tests catch what the real source actually sends.

> The main idea: strong answers explain when Jinja runs, keep macros small and justified, and know what is_incremental(), unique_key and snapshots each guarantee.

passages.heading: 12. Cheat sheet
passages.text:
Reference · the deck on one page

Jinja in models

| Need | Write |
|---|---|
| insert a value | {{ expression }} |
| logic | {% statement %} |
| comment (not sent) | {# … #} |
| trim whitespace | {%- … -%} |
| loop | {%- for x in xs %} … {%- endfor %} |
| comma between items | {% if not loop.last %},{% endif %} |
| branch | {% if target.name == "ci" %} … {% endif %} |
| local variable | {% set xs = var("list", ["a", "b"]) %} |
| filter | {{ name \| lower \| replace(" ", "_") }} |
| macro | {% macro f(col, n=2) -%} … {%- endmacro %} |
| call a macro | {{ f('column_name') }} (column names as strings) |

Commands and checks

| Need | Run |
|---|---|
| see generated SQL | dbt compile --select m → target/compiled/ |
| try a snippet | dbt compile --inline "select {{ … }}" |
| catch undefined names fast | dbt parse |
| rebuild after a macro change | dbt build --select m+ |
| prove a refactor | save old output; EXCEPT both ways = 0 rows |
| incremental from scratch | dbt run --select m --full-refresh |
| record history | dbt snapshot |
| logic tests | dbt test --select test_type:unit |
| install packages | dbt deps (from packages.yml) |

| Built-in | Returns | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| ref(), source() | a relation name and a DAG edge | 3 |
| var("name", default) | a project variable; --vars overrides it | 3, 4 |
| config(...) | per-model settings (materialized, tags, unique_key) | 3, 4, 7 |
| target.name | the active target (dev, ci, prod) | 3 |
| is_incremental(), this | true on later incremental runs / the model’s own table | 7 |

> The main idea: write a template only when it removes real repetition, read the compiled SQL every time, rebuild downstream after macro changes, and prove a refactor with an output comparison.

passages.heading: 13. Glossary
passages.text:
Reference · every new term in this deck

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Jinja | The template language in dbt: {{ expression }}, {% statement %}, {# comment #} |
| Template / compile | SQL with Jinja / render it to plain SQL (target/compiled) |
| Expression / statement | Jinja that inserts a value / Jinja that runs logic (loops, ifs, set) without inserting text by itself |
| Whitespace control | A dash inside a Jinja tag ({%- -%}) trims spaces and newlines |
| Jinja filter | A transformation applied with a pipe: {{ x \| lower }} |
| Macro | A Jinja function in macros/ that returns SQL text |
| Variable (var) | A project setting read in models; default in dbt_project.yml, overridable with --vars |
| target | Jinja object describing the active connection (target.name, target.schema) |
| Refactor | Changing how code is written without changing what it produces |
| EXCEPT | Set operator: rows of the first query that are not in the second |
| Periodic snapshot fact | A fact with one row per period (per day) |
| Adapter dispatch | A macro mechanism that picks an implementation per database |
| Incremental model | A table that processes only new or changed rows after the first run |
| is_incremental() / this | True on later incremental runs / the model’s own existing table |
| unique_key | The key an incremental model merges on, instead of appending |
| Look-back window | Reprocessing a few recent periods on every run to catch late rows |
| Full refresh | Rebuilding an incremental model from scratch (--full-refresh) |
| Snapshot (dbt) | Records changes of a mutable source as SCD type 2 rows (dbt_valid_from, dbt_valid_to) |
| Snapshot strategy | timestamp (trust an updated_at column) or check (compare column values) |
| Unit test | Tests a model’s logic on hand-made input rows (dbt 1.8+) |
| Package | A reusable dbt project installed with dbt deps (dbt_utils) |
| Model contract | An enforced declaration of a model’s columns and types |
| Slim CI / defer | Build only state:modified+ in CI / read unchanged parents from production |

passages.heading: 14. What to remember, and what comes next
passages.text:
Reference · recap

1. Jinja runs first. dbt renders every model to plain SQL before the warehouse sees it; Jinja cannot see data.
2. Three delimiters. {{ }} inserts, {% %} runs logic, {# #} comments; dashes trim whitespace.
3. Loops remove repetition. Drive them from a variable or seed, avoid trailing commas, and read the compiled SQL.
4. Macros are functions that return SQL. Pass column names as strings, keep them small, rebuild downstream after a change.
5. Refactor safely. Start from a green build, save the old output, compare with EXCEPT both ways, rebuild from an empty folder.
6. Next steps are Jinja too. Incremental models use is_incremental() and {{ this }}; snapshots keep SCD2 history; unit tests check logic on fixed rows.

Practise this week

- Redo lessons 4 and 5 on a fresh copy of dbt-fundamentals-project/, checking against dbt-jinja-macros-project/.
- Do exercises 1 and 2 again without hints.
- Write one more macro (for example a safe division with NULLIF) and use it in a new mart.
- Explain is_incremental(), unique_key and the two snapshot strategies aloud in two minutes.

Coming up

The next lessons in your plan go deeper on what Part C previewed: incremental models with look-back windows and merge strategies, snapshots, advanced data tests and unit tests; then deployment with dev and prod targets, slim CI, and governance features such as contracts and versions.

> The main idea: Jinja is a tool for removing repetition, not for cleverness: template, compile, read, rebuild, and prove that nothing changed.

Read more: Jinja and macros, How we structure our dbt projects.

passages.heading: Appendix A · Hints
passages.text:
Hint 1 · Your own macro with a default argument

Copy the shape of macros/to_utc.sql. Jinja macros accept default arguments like Python functions. Pass the column name as a string.

passages.heading: Appendix A · Hints
passages.text:
Hint 2 · A Jinja loop over product categories

{% set categories = var("revenue_categories", [...]) %} gives a default. Jinja filters transform values with a pipe: {{ x | lower | replace(" ", "_") }}. Join the fact to dim_product on product_key.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text: Every solution below was applied to a scratch copy of the project and run with dbt during the build; the outputs shown are real (timestamps and durations normalised).

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 1 · Your own macro with a default argument

# macros/parse_amount.sql
{% macro parse_amount(column_name, scale=2) -%}
    try_cast(trim({{ column_name }}) as decimal(10, {{ scale }}))
{%- endmacro %}

# models/staging/stg_events.sql (changed line)
-        try_cast(trim(amount) as decimal(10, 2))  as amount,
+        {{ parse_amount('amount') }}              as amount,

Terminal (only the changed line):

$ dbt compile --select stg_events
        try_cast(trim(amount) as decimal(10, 2))              as amount,

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt build --select stg_events
Done. PASS=5 WARN=1 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=6

Why it works. The macro returns text; with scale defaulting to 2 it renders exactly the old expression, so the model’s behaviour (and its WARN for e7) is unchanged. Comparing compiled SQL before and after is how you refactor Jinja safely.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 2 · A Jinja loop over product categories

# models/marts/fct_daily_category_revenue.sql
{% set categories = var("revenue_categories", ["Plants", "Accessories", "Plant care"]) %}
-- fct_daily_category_revenue: one row per UTC day, one revenue column per product category.
select
    f.date_key,
    {%- for category in categories %}
    sum(case when p.category = '{{ category }}' then f.amount else 0 end) as {{ category | lower | replace(" ", "_") }}_revenue,
    {%- endfor %}
    sum(f.amount) as total_revenue
from {{ ref("fct_orders") }} as f
join {{ ref("dim_product") }} as p using (product_key)
group by 1

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt run --select fct_daily_category_revenue
1 of 1 OK created sql table model main_marts.fct_daily_category_revenue ........ [OK in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt show --inline "select * from {{ ref('fct_daily_category_revenue') }} order by date_key"
Previewing inline node:
| date_key | plants_revenue | accessories_revenue | plant_care_revenue | total_revenue |
| -------- | -------------- | ------------------- | ------------------ | ------------- |
| 20260302 |             89 |                  18 |              12.50 |        119.50 |
| 20260303 |              0 |                   0 |               7.50 |          7.50 |
| 20260304 |             39 |                   0 |               9.99 |         48.99 |

Why it works. The loop writes one sum(case …) per category; filters turn “Plant care” into a safe column name. Unknown products would count only in total_revenue, which is a good reason to keep a total column next to any pivot. Without the default in var(), the model would fail to compile until the variable is defined.

Companion to business-metrics-models.html: same lessons, same numbering, same queries and results. Hints and solutions are in Appendices A and B.
