passages.heading: 31. Interview questions: contracts, versions and schema changes
passages.text:
Interview · say it in about 60 seconds, then open the answer

6 · What is a dbt model contract? How is it different from a test and from a constraint?

A model contract is a promise about the model’s shape: with contract enforced, every column is declared with a data type, and dbt checks the SQL’s output against it before building and fails if names or types differ. A data test runs after the build and checks values. A constraint is a rule in the table DDL, such as not null or check, that the database enforces row by row while inserting, but only where the platform enforces it: Snowflake enforces not null but not primary keys. So: contract for shape, constraints for cheap row rules, tests for everything else.

What the interviewer checks: precise mechanics and platform nuance.

Follow-up: “Where do you put contracts?” → only on public models other people depend on; elsewhere they slow refactoring.

7 · An upstream team changed a field and our revenue dropped. How would you have caught it before production?

Two places. Upstream, a data contract the producer tests in their CI on a sample of the new release: required fields, types, a rule like “every purchase has an amount”. At our boundary, checks on what arrives: volume, null rates of required fields, and a reconciliation against an independent system, because a model contract wouldn’t fire: our output shape didn’t change, only the values. And when we adapt our staging to the new field, the model contract on the mart catches type drift such as decimal becoming double in CI.

What the interviewer checks: that you know a model contract does not validate inputs.

Follow-up: “The producer won’t agree to a contract.” → test their output at ingestion anyway and quarantine bad batches; show the incident cost to get buy-in.

8 · You need to rename a column in a mart that three dashboards use. How do you ship it?

I don’t rename in place. I create a new model version with the new shape, keep v1 under the old table name, and test v2 as a prerelease. Then I bump latest_version so plain refs move to v2, migrate the models I own in the same pull request, and set a deprecation date on v1 that I announce to consumers. dbt warns everyone who still pins v1. After the date I remove v1 and, if needed, point the old table name at v2. In CI the breaking-change check stops anyone from doing the rename without a version.

passages.heading: 31. Interview questions: contracts, versions and schema changes
passages.text:
the date I remove v1 and, if needed, point the old table name at v2. In CI the breaking-change check stops anyone from doing the rename without a version.

What the interviewer checks: versions, deprecation, communication, CI enforcement.

Follow-up: “Isn’t that just a v2 table?” → mostly, but dbt tracks versions under one name, lets consumers pin, selects by version status and warns on deprecation.

9 · What is a data contract between teams, what is in it, and who owns it?

It is the producer’s written promise to its consumers: the schema with field meanings and units, quality rules, the delivery SLA, the owner and support channel, and the change policy with versions. The producer owns it and tests their output against it in their CI; the consumer helps write it and mirrors the important rules in their own checks. Formats like the Open Data Contract Standard make it machine-readable, so tools can lint it, test data against it and detect breaking changes between versions.

What the interviewer checks: ownership, contents beyond schema, enforcement.

Follow-up: “How is it different from a schema registry?” → a registry enforces schema compatibility for messages; a data contract also covers semantics, quality, SLAs and ownership.

10 · Which schema changes are breaking?

For consumers: removing or renaming a field, narrowing a type, making an optional field required, changing the grain, and changing the meaning without changing the type, like dollars to cents, which schema checks can’t see. Usually compatible: adding an optional field, widening a type. Adding an enum value is in between: it breaks accepted-values tests and CASE statements, so it needs notice. Breaking changes ship with expand–contract: add the new field, let consumers move, then remove the old one under a new major version.

What the interviewer checks: semantic vs structural compatibility; a migration pattern.

Follow-up: “How do you enforce it?” → a breaking-change check in CI: datacontract breaking for data contracts, the dbt state comparison for model contracts.

> The main idea: name the mechanism (contract, constraint, version, data contract), say where it runs and what it cannot catch, and end with how the change reaches consumers safely.

passages.heading: 36. Cheat sheet
passages.text:
Reference · the deck on one page

Test strategy and thresholds

| Need | Write |
|---|---|
| freshness SLA | config: {loaded_at_field: _loaded_at, freshness: {warn_after: {count: 26, period: hour}, error_after: {…}}} on the source |
| run it | dbt source freshness (not part of build) → target/sources.json |
| build only fresh parts | --select source_status:fresher+ --state prev-run |
| threshold on a measured value | config: {fail_calc: "coalesce(max(pct), 0)", warn_if: "> 5", error_if: "> 20"} |
| two-sided band | warn_if: "not between 50 and 200" |
| the gotcha | severity: warn ignores error_if |
| volume | newest batch vs trailing average (volume_vs_trailing) |
| reconciliation | rows in = rows out + rejected; system A vs system B per day, tolerance, known differences |
| strategy doc | TESTING.md + scripts/test_inventory.py --catalogue TESTING.md |

Contracts, versions, access

| Need | Write |
|---|---|
| enforce a contract | config: {contract: {enforced: true}} + data_type on every column |
| row rules | constraints: [{type: not_null}, {type: check, expression: "amount > 0"}] |
| breaking-change gate in CI | --select state:modified+ --state prod-artifacts --warn-error-options '{"error": ["UnversionedBreakingChange"]}' |
| versions | latest_version: 1, versions: [{v: 1, config: {alias: fct_orders}}, {v: 2, columns: [{include: all, exclude: [amount]}, …]}] |
| pin a version | ref('fct_orders', v=1) |
| deprecate | deprecation_date: "2026-12-31T00:00:00+00:00" on the old version |
| select by version | version:latest, version:prerelease, version:old |
| ownership and access | groups: with owner; +group; access: private \| protected \| public |
| data contract (Data Contract CLI 1.2.4) | datacontract lint · test --server X · breaking old new |

| Layer | Test there | Do not test there |
|---|---|---|
| sources | freshness, volume, keys present | what you cannot fix (typos) |
| staging | primary keys, accepted codes, parse failures, null rates | unchanged columns tested upstream |
| marts | relationships, business rules, conservation, reconciliation; contract on public models | columns that cannot fail (counts, coalesced keys, calendars) |

> The main idea: freshness and volume at the boundary, keys and codes in staging, rules and reconciliation in marts; contracts, versions and access for interfaces; data contracts upstream.

passages.heading: 37. Glossary
passages.text:
Reference · every new term in this deck

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Producer / consumer | The team or system that creates a dataset / the one that reads it |
| Test strategy | The decisions about which failures to guard against, where, how loudly, and who acts |
| Risk | Likelihood × impact of a failure; decides whether a test is worth its cost |
| Test bloat | Tests that grow faster than the risks they cover: slow builds, many alerts |
| Noise | A test that fails without anyone needing to act |
| Source freshness | How long ago data last landed in a source, compared with warn_after / error_after |
| loaded_at_field | The column dbt uses for freshness; should be the landing time |
| SLA | Service-level agreement: how stale or late data may get before someone must act |
| sources.json | The artifact written by dbt source freshness: status, age, criteria per source table |
| source_status:fresher | Selector for sources whose newest load is newer than in a saved state |
| fail_calc | The SQL that turns a test’s rows into the “failures” number (default count(*)) |
| warn_if / error_if | SQL comparisons on the failures number that decide warn and error |
| Volume test | A check on how many rows arrived; relative = compared with recent batches |
| Batch | One delivery (here one daily file), identified by _batch_date |
| Reconciliation test | A test that two independent numbers for the same thing agree |
| Row conservation | Rows in = rows out + rows rejected for a stated reason |
| Known difference | A documented, explained reconciliation gap with a ticket |
| TESTING.md | The written test strategy at the root of the project |
| Contract (general) | An explicit, checked promise from a producer to its consumers |
| Model contract | dbt’s enforced promise about a model’s column names and data types |
| Preflight check | dbt’s comparison of the SQL’s output columns with the contract before building |
| Constraint | A rule in the table DDL (not null, primary key, unique, check, foreign key) |
| Enforced / declared constraint | Checked by the database on insert / stored as metadata only |
| Breaking change | A change that can break consumers: removing, renaming or retyping a column |
| State (state:modified) | Comparison with a saved manifest.json from production |
| --warn-error-options | Turns chosen dbt warnings (such as UnversionedBreakingChange) into errors |

passages.heading: 37. Glossary
passages.text:
| Comparison with a saved manifest.json from production |
| --warn-error-options | Turns chosen dbt warnings (such as UnversionedBreakingChange) into errors |
| Model version | One numbered shape of a model; several can be live at once |
| latest_version | The version a plain ref() resolves to; newer = prerelease, older = old |
| deprecation_date | When an old version will be removed; dbt warns its consumers |
| Group / access | A set of models with an owner / who may ref a model: private, protected, public |
| Data contract | An agreement between teams: schema, meaning, quality, SLA, owner, change policy |
| ODCS | Open Data Contract Standard: a YAML format for data contracts (Bitol, LF AI & Data) |
| Schema-change policy | Rules for which changes are allowed, how they are versioned, and the notice period |
| Semantic versioning | major.minor.patch: major for breaking changes, minor for compatible ones |
| Expand–contract | Add the new field next to the old one, migrate consumers, then remove the old one |
| Incident drill | Replaying bad deliveries on purpose to check the right test fires |

passages.heading: 38. What to remember, and what comes next
passages.text:
Reference · recap

1. Test by risk and layer: freshness and volume at the source, keys and codes in staging, rules and reconciliation in marts; delete tests that cannot fail or that nobody acts on.
2. Freshness compares the landing time with warn/error SLAs; run it first and stop on error. Volume compares the newest batch with recent ones.
3. Thresholds are SQL: fail_calc measures, warn_if/error_if compare, and severity: warn disables error_if.
4. Reconcile rows through each step and money against an independent system, with a tolerance and documented known differences.
5. Write it down in TESTING.md, with owners and first actions, and generate the catalogue from the manifest.
6. Model contracts guarantee shape before building; constraints refuse bad rows where the platform enforces them; contracts do not validate inputs.
7. Breaking changes are caught against production state; ship them as versions with a deprecation date; use access to mark the interface.
8. Data contracts move the checks to the producer, with a schema-change policy and expand–contract migrations.

Practise this week

- Redo the lab from dbt-jinja-macros-project/ without looking, then compare with data-quality-contracts-lab/.
- Do exercises 3, 5 and 7 again without hints.
- Explain aloud in a minute each: what you test per layer, contract vs test vs constraint, how you ship a breaking change.
- Fuel Smart: write TESTING.md, add freshness and volume to the USDA and Open Food Facts loads, and put a contract on the mart your dashboard reads.

Coming up

Next in the dbt track: CI/CD and deployment (environments, state:modified+ with --defer, artifacts, scheduling) and orchestration. Packages, the project evaluator and SQL linting are in dbt packages and project quality; unit tests and incremental testing in dbt incremental models, snapshots and unit tests.

> The main idea: a few well-placed tests with owners beat many noisy ones; contracts, versions and data contracts turn tables into dependable interfaces.

Read more: dbt blog: Test smarter, not harder, Model contracts, Model versions.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text: Every solution below was applied to a scratch copy of the project and run during the build; the outputs shown are real (clock times and durations normalised), and the Python checks (assert) passed.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 1 · Predict the freshness status

Terminal:

$ python scripts/load_raw.py --lag-hours 40
raw.events     39 rows from 6 files, newest delivery 2026-03-07
raw.payments   19 rows from 6 files, newest delivery 2026-03-07
newest files landed 40 h ago

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt source freshness   # files landed 40 h ago
1 of 2 WARN freshness of payments_raw.payments ................................. [WARN in x.xxs]
2 of 2 WARN freshness of shop_raw.events ....................................... [WARN in x.xxs]

import json
expected = {20: ("pass", "pass"), 40: ("warn", "warn"), 70: ("error", "error")}   # (events, payments)
for lag, want in expected.items():
    results = json.load(open(f"fresh_{lag}.json", encoding="utf-8"))["results"]
    got = {r["unique_id"].split(".")[2]: r["status"] for r in results}
    print(f"{lag} h:", got)
    assert (got["shop_raw"], got["payments_raw"]) == want

Output:

20 h: {'payments_raw': 'pass', 'shop_raw': 'pass'}
40 h: {'shop_raw': 'warn', 'payments_raw': 'warn'}
70 h: {'payments_raw': 'error', 'shop_raw': 'error'}

Why. 20 h is under every threshold; 40 h is past both warnings but under both errors; 70 h is past both errors, so the command exits with 1. Common wrong answer: “40 h is an error for events because events land daily”: the SLA, not the delivery rhythm, decides. Interviewer follow-up: “the source is loaded every 15 minutes” → thresholds in minutes, freshness run on its own frequent schedule, and a filter so max() scans only recent partitions.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 2 · A volume test for the settlement files

# models/staging/_sources.yml (payments_raw.payments)
      - name: payments
        description: One row per settled payment (charges and refunds). Refund amounts are negative.
        data_tests:
          - volume_vs_trailing:
              arguments: {batch_column: _batch_date, lookback: 3}
              config:
                fail_calc: "coalesce(max(pct_of_trailing), 100)"
                warn_if: "not between 50 and 200"
                error_if: "not between 30 and 400"

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt test --select source:payments_raw   # the normal week
1 of 1 PASS source_volume_vs_trailing_payments_raw_payments__batch_date__3 ..... [PASS in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1

Terminal:

$ python scripts/load_raw.py --incident truncated
raw.events     41 rows from 7 files, newest delivery 2026-03-08
raw.payments   22 rows from 7 files, newest delivery 2026-03-08
newest files landed 1 h ago (incident: truncated)

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt test --select source:payments_raw   # after the truncated events file
1 of 1 PASS source_volume_vs_trailing_payments_raw_payments__batch_date__3 ..... [PASS in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1

import json
results = json.load(open("target/run_results.json", encoding="utf-8"))["results"]
status = lambda part: next(r["status"] for r in results if part in r["unique_id"])
print(status("volume_vs_trailing_payments"))
assert status("volume_vs_trailing_payments") == "pass"   # the settlement file for 8 March was complete

Output:

pass

Why. Newest batch 4 rows against an average of 2.7 is 150%, inside the warn band. The truncated incident only cut the events file; the provider’s settlement for 8 March is complete (3 rows, 90%), so this test rightly passes. Each producer can fail independently, so each source needs its own volume test. Common wrong answer: one volume test on fct_orders: by then a half day is already in the mart, and orders legitimately vary. Interviewer follow-up: “three payments a day is too small for percentages” → for tiny feeds use absolute bounds (at least one file and one row per day) and rely on reconciliation for completeness.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 3 · Why does this test never fail?

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt test --select test_name:null_rate   # as written
1 of 1 WARN 6 null_rate_stg_events_customer_id ................................. [WARN 6 in x.xxs]
[WARNING]: Got 6 results, configured to warn if > 2
Done. PASS=0 WARN=1 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt test --select test_name:null_rate   # severity line removed
1 of 1 FAIL 6 null_rate_stg_events_customer_id ................................. [FAIL 6 in x.xxs]
  Got 6 results, configured to fail if > 3
Done. PASS=0 WARN=0 ERROR=1 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1
[exit code 1]

import json
results = json.load(open("target/run_results.json", encoding="utf-8"))["results"]
status = lambda part: next(r["status"] for r in results if part in r["unique_id"])
print(status("null_rate"))
assert status("null_rate") == "fail"      # 6% > 3%: the build now stops

Output:

fail

Why. With severity: warn dbt never evaluates error_if; the default severity (error) checks error_if first and falls back to warn_if. Common wrong answer: lowering error_if further: it is ignored at any value. Interviewer follow-up: “now make it fail only in production, warn in dev” → make the thresholds depend on the target, for example error_if: "{{ '> 3' if target.name == 'prod' else '> 100' }}", and document why.

Solution 4 · Reconcile two marts: the funnel and the orders

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt test --select assert_funnel_matches_orders --store-failures   # first version
1 of 1 FAIL 1 assert_funnel_matches_orders ..................................... [FAIL 1 in x.xxs]
  Got 1 result, configured to fail if != 0
Done. PASS=0 WARN=0 ERROR=1 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1
[exit code 1]

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt show --limit 50 --inline "select * from main_dbt_test__audit.assert_funnel_matches_orders"
Previewing inline node:
| date_key | purchase_events | orders |
| -------- | --------------- | ------ |
| 20260302 |               5 |      4 |

# tests/assert_funnel_matches_orders.sql
-- Purchases counted by the funnel = orders in fct_orders + purchases rejected for an
-- unparseable amount, per UTC day. Two marts built from the same events must agree.
with orders as (
    select date_key, count(*) as orders from {{ ref('fct_orders') }} group by 1
),
rejected as (
    select cast(strftime(cast(event_at_utc as date), '%Y%m%d') as integer) as date_key,
           count(*) as rejected
    from {{ ref('stg_events') }}
    where event_type = 'purchase' and amount is null
    group by 1
)
select f.date_key, f.purchase_events, coalesce(o.orders, 0) as orders, coalesce(r.rejected, 0) as rejected
from {{ ref('fct_daily_funnel') }} as f
left join orders as o using (date_key)
left join rejected as r using (date_key)
where f.purchase_events <> coalesce(o.orders, 0) + coalesce(r.rejected, 0)

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt test --select assert_funnel_matches_orders   # with the rejects
1 of 1 PASS assert_funnel_matches_orders ....................................... [PASS in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1

import json
results = json.load(open("target/run_results.json", encoding="utf-8"))["results"]
status = lambda part: next(r["status"] for r in results if part in r["unique_id"])
assert status("assert_funnel_matches_orders") == "pass"
print("funnel and orders agree on every day")

Output:

funnel and orders agree on every day

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
status("assert_funnel_matches_orders") == "pass"
print("funnel and orders agree on every day")

Output:

funnel and orders agree on every day

Why. The funnel counts every purchase event; fct_orders drops purchases whose amount does not parse (e7 on 2 March). Comparable sides are “funnel purchases” and “orders + rejected”, the conservation rule of lesson 11, now per day. Common wrong answer: the first version, or adding a tolerance of 1 so it passes: that would also hide a real dropped order. Interviewer follow-up: “the funnel uses the user’s local date” → the two marts no longer share a grain; convert to one time zone before comparing, or the test fails around midnight.

    order by 1"
Previewing inline node:
| date_key | orders_usd | charges_usd | unexplained_usd |
| -------- | ---------- | ----------- | --------------- |
| 20260303 |        7.5 |         2.5 |              -5 |
| 20260306 |       89.0 |        64.0 |             -25 |

2 of 2 PASS assert_revenue_reconciles .......................................... [PASS in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=2 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=2

import json
results = json.load(open("target/run_results.json", encoding="utf-8"))["results"]
status = lambda part: next(r["status"] for r in results if part in r["unique_id"])
assert status("assert_revenue_reconciles") == "pass"

Why. The PR removed where payment_type = 'charge', so refunds (−5.00 for e11, −25.00 for e27) were netted into “charges”. Revenue and refunds are reconciled separately because orders and refunds are different facts. passages.text:
Solution 6 · Which edits break the contract?

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt run --select fct_orders.v2   # (a) swap the first two columns of the SELECT
1 of 1 OK created sql table model main_marts.fct_orders_v2 ..................... [OK in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt run --select fct_orders.v2   # (b) cast date_key to bigint
  | column_name | definition_type | contract_type | mismatch_reason    |
  | ----------- | --------------- | ------------- | ------------------ |
  | date_key    | BIGINT          | INTEGER       | data type mismatch |
Done. PASS=0 WARN=0 ERROR=1 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1
[exit code 1]

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt run --select fct_orders.v2   # (c) add a column is_large_order
  | column_name    | definition_type | contract_type | mismatch_reason     |
  | -------------- | --------------- | ------------- | ------------------- |
  | is_large_order | BOOLEAN         |               | missing in contract |
Done. PASS=0 WARN=0 ERROR=1 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1
[exit code 1]

# observed = {variant: status of fct_orders.v2 in that run}, read from run_results.json after each run
print(observed)
assert observed == {"a": "success", "b": "error", "c": "error"}

Output:

{'a': 'success', 'b': 'error', 'c': 'error'}

Why. (a) Column order is ignored; the table is created in the contract’s order. (b) BIGINT ≠ INTEGER: a data type mismatch, even though every value fits. (c) A new column is a non-breaking change for consumers, but it still has to be declared: “missing in contract”. Common wrong answer: “(c) passes because adding columns is non-breaking”: non-breaking means you may add it to the contract without a new version. Interviewer follow-up: “so is a contract just a test?” → no: it runs before the build, fixes the DDL types, and lets dbt classify changes as breaking against production.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 7 · A CI gate for a breaking change

# models/marts/_marts.yml (dim_customer, step 1)
  - name: dim_customer
    description: Conformed customer dimension. One row per customer plus an unknown member (customer_id = '-1').
    config:
      contract: {enforced: true}
      access: public
    columns:
      - name: customer_key
        data_type: varchar
        description: Surrogate key, md5(customer_id).
        data_tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: customer_id
        data_type: varchar
        description: Natural key from the CRM.
        data_tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: customer_name
        data_type: varchar
      - name: city
        data_type: varchar
      - name: signup_date
        data_type: date

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt build --select dim_customer   # with the new contract
1 of 7 OK created sql table model main_marts.dim_customer ...................... [OK in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=7 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=7

import subprocess
gate = ["dbt", "build", "--select", "state:modified+", "--state", "prod-artifacts",
        "--warn-error-options", '{"error": ["UnversionedBreakingChange"]}']
run = subprocess.run(gate, capture_output=True, text=True, encoding="utf-8")
log = run.stdout + run.stderr
print("exit code:", run.returncode)
print(next(line.strip() for line in log.splitlines() if "Breaking change" in line))
assert run.returncode == 2 and "Columns were removed" in log

Output:

exit code: 2
[WARNING]: Breaking change to contracted, unversioned model dim_customer (models\marts\dim_customer.sql)

Why. state:modified+ compares the contract with production’s manifest; removing a column of a contracted, unversioned model raises the UnversionedBreakingChange warning, and --warn-error-options makes it fatal, so the CI job fails before anything is built. Common wrong answer: --warn-error (all warnings become errors): the deprecation warnings for fct_orders v1 would then fail every pull request. Interviewer follow-up: “but the column really must go” → version dim_customer (exercise 8) or get the consumers’ sign-off and merge with an explicit override in the pipeline.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
['customer_key', 'customer_id', 'customer_name', 'city', 'signup_date']
v2: ['customer_key', 'customer_id', 'customer_name', 'customer_city', 'signup_date']

Why. Each version is its own table; the alias keeps v1 at the old name, so every existing query keeps working, while v2 is available as ref('dim_customer', v=2). Because fct_orders and the marketing model reference dim_customer (latest = v1), dbt warns that they depend on a version slated for deprecation: the migration list writes itself. Common wrong answer: setting latest_version: 2 straight away: every plain ref moves to v2 at once, which is the breaking change you wanted to avoid. Interviewer follow-up: “how do you know when v1 can go?” → no refs left in the project (dbt ls --select +dim_customer.v1), exposures checked, and warehouse query logs show no reads of the old table.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 9 · Take-home: reconcile refunds and document it

# tests/assert_refunds_reconcile.sql
-- Refund events (positive amounts) must match the provider's refunds (negative), per UTC day.
with events as (
    select cast(event_at_utc as date) as day, sum(amount) as refunds_usd
    from {{ ref('stg_events') }}
    where event_type = 'refund'
    group by 1
),
provider as (
    select captured_date_utc as day, -sum(amount_usd) as refunds_usd
    from {{ ref('stg_payments') }}
    where payment_type = 'refund'
    group by 1
)
select coalesce(e.day, p.day) as day, e.refunds_usd as events_usd, p.refunds_usd as provider_usd
from events as e
full outer join provider as p on e.day = p.day
where coalesce(e.refunds_usd, 0) <> coalesce(p.refunds_usd, 0)

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt test --select assert_refunds_reconcile
1 of 1 PASS assert_refunds_reconcile ........................................... [PASS in x.xxs]
Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=1

Terminal:

$ python scripts/test_inventory.py --catalogue TESTING.md
45 data tests
TESTING.md: catalogue rewritten (45 tests)

text = open("TESTING.md", encoding="utf-8").read()
catalogue = text.split("")[1]
rows = [line for line in catalogue.splitlines() if "singular" in line]
print("\n".join(rows))
assert any("assert_refunds_reconcile" in r for r in rows)

Output:

| staging | `stg_events` | singular: `assert_no_unparseable_amounts` | warn | any failure |
| staging | `stg_events` | singular: `assert_refunds_reconcile` | error | any failure |
| marts | `fct_orders.v2` | singular: `assert_purchases_conserved` | error | any failure |
| marts | `rec_daily_revenue` | singular: `assert_revenue_reconciles` | error | any failure |

Why. Both sides are reduced to “refunded USD per UTC day” with the same sign; the full outer join makes a refund that exists in only one system visible. Documenting the first action is what turns a test into an operational control. Common wrong answer: comparing sum(amount_usd) without flipping the sign: every refund day fails. Interviewer follow-up: “refund events arrive a day after the provider’s refund” → reconcile on a rolling window (for example two days) or match by order, and say which you chose and why in TESTING.md.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 10 · Design: a data contract for the payment provider

# contracts/payments.odcs.yaml
apiVersion: v3.2.0
kind: DataContract
id: leafy-payment-settlements
name: Payment provider settlement files
version: 1.0.0
status: active
team:
  name: finance-operations              # owns the relationship with the payment provider
description:
  purpose: Settled charges and refunds, one CSV per day, used to reconcile revenue.
schema:
  - name: payments
    physicalType: file
    properties:
      - name: payment_id
        logicalType: string
        required: true
        unique: true
      - name: order_id
        logicalType: string
        required: true
      - name: type
        logicalType: string
        required: true
        quality:
          - metric: invalidValues
            arguments:
              validValues: [charge, refund]
            mustBe: 0
      - name: amount_usd
        logicalType: number
        required: true
        description: USD with two decimals; refunds are negative.
      - name: currency
        logicalType: string
        required: true
      - name: captured_at_utc
        logicalType: timestamp
        required: true
    quality:
      - type: sql
        description: Charges are positive and refunds negative.
        query: select count(*) from payments where (type = 'charge' and amount_usd <= 0) or (type = 'refund' and amount_usd >= 0)
        mustBe: 0
slaProperties:
  - property: latency
    value: 36
    unit: h
servers:
  - server: landing
    type: local
    path: ./data/raw/payments/settlement_*.csv
    format: csv

import subprocess
run = lambda *args: subprocess.run(["datacontract", *args], capture_output=True, text=True, encoding="utf-8").returncode
codes = {"test v1": run("test", "contracts/payments.odcs.yaml"),
         "breaking v1 -> v2": run("breaking", "contracts/payments.odcs.yaml", "contracts/payments.v2.odcs.yaml")}
print(codes)
assert codes == {"test v1": 0, "breaking v1 -> v2": 1}

Output:

{'test v1': 0, 'breaking v1 -> v2': 1}

Why. The contract captures what the reconciliation silently relies on: one row per payment, two types, signed amounts, USD, a timestamp in UTC, a daily delivery. The cents proposal removes amount_usd, so it is breaking even though the information is the same; it needs a major version and an expand–contract plan. Common wrong answer: a contract with only names and types: the sign rule and the allowed values are what protect the reconciliation. Interviewer follow-up: “the provider is an external company that won’t run your tool” → you run the contract test at ingestion on each file, quarantine failures, and keep the contract as the documented basis for escalations.

passages.heading: Appendix B · Solutions
passages.text:
Solution 11 · Review: keep or drop these five tests?

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt build --select stg_events stg_payments dim_customer fct_orders rec_daily_revenue   # with the PR
Done. PASS=35 WARN=2 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=37

| Test | Verdict | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| (1) not_null currency_code | drop | the column is a literal 'USD': it cannot be NULL; accepted_values already guards a future change |
| (2) unique rec_daily_revenue.date_key | keep | finance queries this table by day; a join change could duplicate days and double the totals |
| (3) payments → events relationships | keep, warn | names the exact order missing from the web events; the reconciliation stays the error-level gate |
| (4) not_null event_type | keep | accepted_values ignores NULLs, so a NULL type would pass unnoticed |
| (5) accepted_values city | drop | a new city is business growth, not a data error: it would fail for good news |

Terminal (output trimmed):

$ dbt build --select stg_events stg_payments dim_customer fct_orders rec_daily_revenue   # after the review
Done. PASS=33 WARN=2 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=35

# baseline_tests: number of data tests in the manifest before the PR
import json
nodes = json.load(open("target/manifest.json", encoding="utf-8"))["nodes"].values()
tests = [n for n in nodes if n["resource_type"] == "test"]
present = {(n["attached_node"].split(".")[2], n["column_name"], n["test_metadata"]["name"])
           for n in tests if n.get("test_metadata") and n.get("attached_node")}
kept = {("stg_events", "event_type", "not_null"), ("stg_payments", "order_id", "relationships"),
        ("rec_daily_revenue", "date_key", "unique")}
dropped = {("fct_orders", "currency_code", "not_null"), ("dim_customer", "city", "accepted_values")}
print("tests before the PR:", baseline_tests, " after the review:", len(tests))
assert kept <= present and not (dropped & present) and len(tests) == baseline_tests + 3

Output:

tests before the PR: 44  after the review: 47

passages.text:
len(tests))
assert kept <= present and not (dropped & present) and len(tests) == baseline_tests + 3

Output:

tests before the PR: 44  after the review: 47

Why. “It passes” is not a reason to keep a test, and “it might be redundant” is not a reason to drop one: what matters is whether it can fail for a real problem and whether someone acts. Common wrong answer: dropping (4) as a duplicate of accepted_values: the NULL gap is exactly what makes it necessary. Interviewer follow-up: “marketing wants to know about new cities” → that is a report or a monitor (a weekly list of new values), not a failing test.

passages.heading: Dashboard storytelling: chart choice, decluttering and headline-first dashboards
passages.text:
Companion to dashboard-storytelling.html: same lessons, same numbering, same code, outputs and charts. Hints and solutions are in Appendices A and B.

Tested with: CPython 3.12.10 on Windows 11 (64-bit), matplotlib 3.11.2 (Agg backend, PNG output), NumPy 2.5.3, DuckDB 1.5.6 (Python package, only to read the CSV fixtures) and pytest 9.1.1. Every Python block and command with an output was executed while this document was built, and every chart image in images/ was drawn by the code shown next to it. The data is synthetic and deterministic (make_data.py, lesson 3). Power BI is the familiar baseline but was not executed: lesson 13 maps each idea to its Power BI feature, and the DAX and theme snippets there are labelled “not executed — requires Power BI Desktop”.

Gap deck: it teaches only what earlier decks leave out. Diagnosing metric changes: trees, mix shift, and the weekly business review already builds a headline-first WBR table and a five-line write-up (its lab steps 4–5); Metric design: define the number before writing SQL already defines the metrics. This deck adds the visual layer: chart choice, decluttering, headline-first dashboards, honest and accessible charts, a critique checklist and a redesign. New terms are defined on first use and collected in the glossary. Most lessons end with an On the job note.

Interview focus: the interview questions and exercises are based on common data-visualisation and dashboard interview patterns (research done in October 2026: “which chart and why”, “critique this dashboard”, misleading charts, two scales, accessibility for PL-300, “stakeholders say it is too complex”). All questions are original and use the Leafy data or the Fuel Smart portfolio.

Additions beyond the original brief are marked (added): an automated chart linter (dashlint.py) that turns the checkable half of the critique checklist into tests; a data-driven headline function so the title can never disagree with the numbers; incomplete (partial) periods as a misleading-chart pattern; WCAG contrast maths, the grayscale test and alt text within Power BI’s 250-character limit; a matplotlib → Power BI mapping, including a dynamic DAX headline (shown, not executed); a weekly critique routine with public practice sources.

passages.heading: 1. Dashboard storytelling
passages.text:
Diagnosing metric changes gave you the weekly business review (WBR) table and the five-line write-up. This deck adds the visual layer around them: choose the chart from the message, declutter it, put the finding in the title, lay out a page that reads top-left first, keep it honest and accessible, and critique any dashboard with one checklist. Every chart is drawn twice, before and after, from the same Leafy data.

- Part A, choose: message first; comparison, trend, composition, distribution and relationship charts.
- Part B, declutter: remove the noise, headline titles, colour and numbers with purpose.
- Part C, headline-first pages: the inverted-pyramid layout, KPI cards, and the same ideas in Power BI.
- Part D, honest and accessible: misleading charts, contrast and alt text, the critique checklist.
- Practice: the lab (critique and redesign Leafy's weekly dashboard, then your Fuel Smart page), a bug clinic, interview questions with model answers, and 10 exercises.

Every chart image was drawn by the code next to it while the deck was built. Power BI is mapped, not executed.

Additions beyond the brief (marked added): an automated chart linter (dashlint.py) that turns the checkable half of the critique checklist into tests; a data-driven headline function so the title can never disagree with the numbers; incomplete (partial) periods as a misleading-chart pattern; WCAG contrast maths, the grayscale test and alt text within Power BI’s 250-character limit; a matplotlib → Power BI mapping, including a dynamic DAX headline (shown, not executed); a weekly critique routine with public practice sources.

passages.heading: Why this matters · Why this matters on the job
passages.text:
Why this matters · the need behind the topic

A correct number on a confusing page is a wasted number. Leaders look at a dashboard for a few seconds before a meeting; if the page does not say what changed, why, and what to do, the decision is made on gut feel or on the wrong tile. Analytics engineers own the models and metrics behind those pages and are more and more often asked to build or review the pages too. This deck teaches the visual layer: choose the chart from the message, remove what carries no data, lead with the headline, and keep every chart honest and readable by everyone. It ends with a critique checklist you can partly automate.

Where you will use it

- The weekly business review page that leadership opens every Monday.
- A Power BI report you publish on top of your certified semantic model.
- The chart in an incident write-up or a pull request that proves a fix worked.
- The five-minute presentation at the end of a take-home assignment.
- Your portfolio dashboard: the first thing a hiring manager looks at.

What goes wrong without it

- The real problem (one platform, one release) hides in tile five of six.
- A partial week looks like a collapse and starts a fire drill.
- A truncated axis turns a 1.5 % gap into a crisis.
- Red/green status tiles are unreadable for about 1 in 12 men.
- Nobody opens the dashboard after the launch week.

Who expects you to know it

- Analytics engineers and BI developers: build and review the pages on top of their models.
- Data analysts: present findings every week.
- Data engineers: chart pipeline health, costs and incidents.
- Interviewers: “which chart and why” and “critique this dashboard” appear in most analytics loops; the PL-300 exam tests visual choice and accessibility.

> On the job: Your new manager forwards a six-tile Power BI page with the note: “Leadership says this tells them nothing. Can you fix it before Monday?” A strong answer is a 20-minute critique against a checklist, a headline computed from the model, a four-tier layout, and a page that passes automated checks for honesty and contrast before anyone sees it.

> The main idea: the page is part of the data product: choose, declutter and headline it as carefully as you model the numbers under it.

Read more: Power BI: tips for designing a great dashboard, Financial Times: Visual Vocabulary, Exam PL-300 study guide.

passages.heading: Why this matters · When to reach for it, and when not to
passages.text:
Why this matters · choosing the right tool

| Situation | Reach for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| One finding must reach busy readers (WBR, incident, executive update) | Headline title + KPI cards + one proving chart (lessons 9, 11–12) | The sentence is read first; the chart only has to prove it. |
| Comparing categories or ranking them | Sorted bars with direct labels (lesson 5) | Position and length are read most accurately. |
| Change over time | Line chart of complete periods (lesson 6) | Lines show direction and shape; partial periods lie. |
| Spread, waiting times, tails | Histogram or strip plot (lesson 7) | An average hides who waits a week. |
| Readers need exact values for many measures | A formatted table (the WBR table in Diagnosing metric changes) | Looking up values beats spotting patterns here; do not force a chart. |
| Open-ended exploration by analysts | Not a polished dashboard | Exploration needs many quick charts; polish only what others will reuse. |

How interviews test it

- “Which chart would you use to show X, and why not a pie?” (message first, encoding accuracy).
- “Here is a dashboard. What would you change?” (a structured walk: purpose, headline, honesty, chart fit, clutter, colour, accessibility, layout).
- “How can a chart mislead?” (truncated and dual axes, partial periods, cherry-picked windows).
- “How do you show two measures with different scales?” and “How do you make a report accessible?” (PL-300).

Where it sits in your learning path

- Builds on Metric design: define the number before writing SQL (what each number means) and Diagnosing metric changes: trees, mix shift, and the weekly business review (the WBR table and the five-line write-up, which this deck does not repeat).
- Next: put certified metrics in a semantic layer so the dashboard and its headline read the same definition.

> The main idea: reach for a headline-first page whenever someone must act on the numbers; keep exploration quick and unpolished.

Create the environment

# Windows PowerShell, from the folder that holds this deck
cd dashboard-storytelling-lab
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1          # macOS/Linux: source .venv/bin/activate

Check it

import sys, matplotlib, duckdb
print("Python", sys.version.split()[0], "· matplotlib", matplotlib.__version__,
      "· DuckDB", duckdb.__version__)
print("backend:", matplotlib.get_backend())

Output:

Python 3.12.10 · matplotlib 3.11.2 · DuckDB 1.5.6
backend: Agg

Agg is matplotlib’s non-interactive backend (the part that turns a figure into pixels): it draws straight into PNG files, needs no screen, and gives the same pixels on a laptop and a build server. Every block in this deck starts from the first part of chartkit.py, shown below. rcParams are matplotlib’s global defaults; STYLE switches off the noise once (lesson 8 explains each line), and the palette has only two kinds of colour: grays for context and one accent for the point (lesson 10 explains why).

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")                      # draw into files: no window, same pixels everywhere
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import duckdb
from pathlib import Path

passages.heading: 2. Set up, versions, and what was tested
passages.text:
# draw into files: no window, same pixels everywhere
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import duckdb
from pathlib import Path

INK, MUTED, GRAY, LIGHT = "#1f2a24", "#56605a", "#8b948f", "#e3e7e4"
ACCENT = "#c2410c"                          # the one colour that means "look here"

STYLE = {                                   # the quiet defaults every "after" chart starts from
    "figure.dpi": 100, "savefig.dpi": 100, "font.size": 10,
    "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "axes.edgecolor": GRAY,
    "axes.titlelocation": "left", "axes.titlesize": 12, "axes.titleweight": "bold",
    "axes.titlecolor": INK, "axes.labelcolor": MUTED, "axes.grid": False,
    "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "legend.frameon": False, "text.color": INK,
}

def use_style():
    plt.rcParams.update(STYLE)

def q(sql):
    """Run DuckDB SQL (it can read CSV files directly) and return a list of tuples."""
    return duckdb.sql(sql).fetchall()

def save(fig, path, dpi=None):
    """Save a PNG without machine-specific metadata, close the figure, report the file."""
    path = Path(path)
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    fig.savefig(path, dpi=dpi, bbox_inches="tight", metadata={"Software": None},
                pil_kwargs={"optimize": True})
    plt.close(fig)
    print("saved", path.as_posix())

> On the job: Headless rendering is how charts reach people without a BI tool: a nightly job that emails a PNG digest, a chart attached to a pull request or an incident ticket, a notebook in CI. Coming from C#: rcParams is like a shared theme resource dictionary in WPF; set it once instead of styling every control.

> The main idea: one folder, a dozen small helpers, real PNGs. The ideas are tool-independent; matplotlib just makes every step visible and testable.

Read more: Matplotlib: backends (Agg), Matplotlib: rcParams and style sheets, Matplotlib: savefig.

passages.heading: 3. The running example: Leafy’s weekly dashboard extract
passages.text:
Start here · one extract, planted traps, two earlier decks

Leafy is the series’ online plant shop. Its leadership team opens a weekly dashboard every Monday. make_data.py writes a small, deterministic extract: the same seed gives the same rows on every machine. The story is the one you diagnosed in Diagnosing metric changes: Android app 5.3 shipped on Monday 16 March and broke checkout. The numbers here are a separate synthetic extract built for charts, so they differ slightly from that deck.

for w, days, s, o, ns in weeks[-4:]:

passages.heading: 4. Start from the message, then choose the chart
passages.text:
Part A · what should the reader take away?

A message is the one sentence you want the reader to remember, written before you open a charting tool: “Organic search brings the most orders”, not “orders by channel”. A chart turns numbers into marks; the mapping from a number to a property of a mark (its position, length, angle, area or colour) is called a visual encoding. Decades of research on graphical perception rank how accurately people decode them: position on a common scale first, then length, then angle and slope, then area, then colour intensity. So the default answer is usually “put the number on a shared axis”.

| Message type | The reader asks | Default chart | Avoid |
|---|---|---|---|
| Comparison / ranking | Which is biggest? How do they rank? | Bars sorted by value (horizontal for long labels); a dot plot | Pies with many slices, unsorted bars, 3D |
| Trend (change over time) | Up, down, or unusual? | Line chart; columns for a handful of periods | Partial periods, uneven time steps, pies per month |
| Composition (part to whole) | What share is each part? Is the mix shifting? | One 100 % bar for a few parts; share-over-time lines | Pies with more than 3 parts, stacked areas with many layers |
| Distribution | How spread out? Who waits longest? | Histogram, strip plot, box plot | A single average bar |
| Relationship | Does X move with Y? | Scatter plot, outliers labelled | Two lines on twin axes |
| Deviation (added) | Above or below the target? | Bars diverging from the target or zero | Status shown by red/green alone |

The same numbers can carry different messages, and each message wants a different chart. Here are last week’s and this week’s orders per channel, drawn for two questions:

rows = q("""
    SELECT channel,
           SUM(orders) FILTER (WHERE week_start = '2026-03-16') AS this_week,
           SUM(orders) FILTER (WHERE week_start = '2026-03-09') AS last_week
    FROM 'data/channel_orders.csv'
    GROUP BY channel ORDER BY this_week, channel DESC""")
names = [r[0] for r in rows]
now, before = [r[1] for r in rows], [r[2] for r in rows]

fig, (a, b) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.4), sharey=True)
a.barh(names, now, color=GRAY, height=0.65)            # ranking: one sorted bar each
a.set_title("Which channel brings the most orders?")
b.hlines(names, now, before, color=LIGHT, lw=4)        # change: dot plot, last -> this week

passages.text:
bar each
a.set_title("Which channel brings the most orders?")
b.hlines(names, now, before, color=LIGHT, lw=4)        # change: dot plot, last -> this week
b.plot(before, names, "o", color=GRAY, label="last week")
b.plot(now, names, "o", color=ACCENT, label="this week")
b.legend(loc="lower right")
b.set_title("Which channel lost the most?")
save(fig, "images/a4-same-data.png")

Output:

saved images/a4-same-data.png

Left: sorted horizontal bars of orders by channel this week, Organic search longest. Right: a dot plot from last week to this week per channel; Organic search and Direct moved furthest.

The left panel answers “who is biggest” at a glance; the right panel answers “who changed most” (Organic search and Direct lost the most). Neither chart answers both questions well, which is why the message comes first.

> On the job: When a stakeholder asks for “a chart of orders by channel”, reply with the question: “Do you want to see which channel is biggest, or which one changed?” That one question decides the chart and often reveals the decision behind the request (the intake routine is in From vague ask to written spec).

> The main idea: write the one-sentence message first; then choose the chart whose encoding (preferably position on a shared axis) makes that sentence obvious.

passages.heading: 5. Comparison and ranking: sorted bars beat pies
passages.text:
Part A · which category is biggest, and by how much?

For a comparison the reader must judge sizes against each other. Bars put every value on the same baseline, so the eye compares lengths; a pie asks the eye to compare angles and areas, which it does badly, especially when slices are similar. Sort the bars by value so the ranking is free, use horizontal bars when labels are long, and write the values on the bars so the axis can go.

Before

A pie chart with seven rainbow-coloured slices of similar size and a legend on the right.

Seven similar slices and a legend: the reader looks back and forth between colours and names, and cannot tell that Email and Paid search tie.

After

Horizontal bars sorted by orders; Organic search highlighted at the top with 71 orders; Email and Paid search both 54.

Sorted, labelled bars: the ranking, the tie and the gap to the leader are visible in one look.

rows = q("""SELECT channel, orders FROM 'data/channel_orders.csv'
             WHERE week_start = '2026-03-16'
             ORDER BY orders, channel DESC""")     # barh draws bottom-up; ties broken by name
names, orders = [r[0] for r in rows], [r[1] for r in rows]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
colors = [ACCENT if o == max(orders) else GRAY for o in orders]
bars = ax.barh(names, orders, color=colors, height=0.65)
ax.bar_label(bars, padding=3, color=INK)              # values on the bars...
ax.set_xticks([])                                      # ...so the value axis can go
ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(length=0)
ax.set_title("Organic search brought the most orders this week")
save(fig, "images/a5-after.png")

total = sum(orders)
print({n: f"{360 * o / total:.1f}°" for n, o in zip(names, orders) if o in (54, 41)})

Output:

saved images/a5-after.png
{'Direct': '50.5°', 'Paid search': '66.6°', 'Email': '66.6°'}

The pie would draw Email and Paid search as two 66.6° slices pointing in different directions and Direct as a 50.5° slice: a 16° difference that readers routinely misjudge. The bars show the same facts as lengths on one baseline. Notice ORDER BY orders, channel DESC: with a tie, an order by value alone is not deterministic, so the two channels could swap places from one refresh to the next. Coming from C#: OrderByDescending(c => c.Orders).ThenBy(c => c.Name).

How the “before” pie was drawn

    ax.pie(orders, colors=plt.cm.rainbow([i / 6 for i in range(7)]), startangle=90)

> On the job: Pie charts are the most common thing reviewers ask you to change. Keep one only for two or three parts of a whole (“42 % of orders came from the app”). For everything else, a sorted bar chart is the safe default in Power BI, Tableau and matplotlib alike.

> The main idea: comparisons go on a shared baseline: sort the bars, break ties deterministically, label the values and drop the axis.

passages.heading: 6. Trend: lines for change over time
passages.text:
Part A · is it going up, down, or doing something unusual?

Time runs left to right on the x-axis, in even steps. A line connects the periods, which tells the reader “this is one continuous quantity; look at its direction and shape”. Columns work for a handful of periods; with ten or more, a line is easier to read. Mark the event that explains a change with an annotation: a short label attached to a point. A line chart may start its y-axis above zero when the reader needs to see small changes; this one starts at zero because the drop is large enough to see without zooming.

Before

Twelve columns in twelve colours with tiny rotated two-decimal labels; the last column is much shorter than the others.

Rainbow columns, unreadable labels, and a last column that looks like a collapse: it holds only 2 of 7 days.

After

A gray line of weekly net sales near 20 thousand dollars for ten weeks, then a highlighted drop to 17.4 thousand annotated with the Android app release.

One line, the event annotated where it happened, complete weeks only, and the title states the finding.

weeks = q("""SELECT week_start, MIN(days_in_data), SUM(net_sales)
              FROM 'data/weekly_platform.csv' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1""")
done = [(w, s) for w, days, s in weeks if days == 7]       # complete weeks only (lesson 14)

> On the job: The weekly trend is the most-viewed chart on most business dashboards. Two habits prevent most incidents: show complete periods only (or label the partial one clearly), and annotate releases, campaigns and outages on the chart so nobody has to ask “what happened that week?”.

> The main idea: trends are lines over even time steps; annotate the event that explains the change and never let a partial period pose as a full one.

passages.heading: 7. Composition, distribution and relationship
passages.text:
Part A · shares, spreads, and “does X move with Y?”

Three more message types, each with its usual trap. A composition chart shows parts of a whole; for a mix that shifts over time, plot each share as a line instead of stacking layers. A distribution chart shows how values spread; a histogram counts how many values fall into each bin, so the tail that an average hides becomes visible. A relationship chart puts one measure on each axis; a scatter plot shows whether they move together (correlation is not cause: say so when it matters).

Composition

Before

A stacked area chart of orders for web, iOS and Android; the top layer narrows at the end but it is hard to tell which platform changed.

Stacked areas: only the bottom layer sits on a flat baseline, so the Android change at the top is hard to read.

After

Two lines: Android share of sessions steady near 26 percent and Android share of orders falling from about 25 percent to 8 percent in the last week.

Two shares on one axis: Android still brings a quarter of the visits but no longer a quarter of the orders.

rows = q("""
    SELECT week_start,
           SUM(sessions) FILTER (WHERE platform = 'android') / SUM(sessions) AS sessions_share,
           SUM(orders)   FILTER (WHERE platform = 'android') / SUM(orders)   AS orders_share
    FROM 'data/weekly_platform.csv' WHERE days_in_data = 7
    GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1""")
xs = [r[0] for r in rows]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
ax.plot(xs, [r[1] for r in rows], color=GRAY, lw=2)
ax.plot(xs, [r[2] for r in rows], color=ACCENT, lw=2.4)
ax.text(xs[-1], rows[-1][1], "  share of sessions", color=MUTED, va="center")
ax.text(xs[-1], rows[-1][2], "  share of orders", color=ACCENT, va="center")
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.35)
ax.set_yticks([0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3], ["0%", "10%", "20%", "30%"])
ax.set_xticks(xs[::3], [f"{x.day} {x:%b}" for x in xs[::3]])
ax.tick_params(length=0)
ax.set_title("Android still brings a quarter of visits, but only 8% of orders")
save(fig, "images/a7-comp-after.png")
print(f"Android, last complete week: {rows[-1][1]:.1%} of sessions, {rows[-1][2]:.1%} of orders")

Output:

saved images/a7-comp-after.png
Android, last complete week: 26.0% of sessions, 8.2% of orders

Distribution

Before

Two bars of average delivery days, ParcelCo 3.0 and SwiftPost 3.0, nearly identical.

Two averages that look the same: the chart says “no difference”.

After

passages.text:
bars of average delivery days, ParcelCo 3.0 and SwiftPost 3.0, nearly identical.

After

passages.heading: 8. Declutter: remove everything that does not carry data
passages.text:
Part B · what can go, and in what order?

Clutter is every mark on a chart that costs the reader attention without telling them anything: frames, heavy grids, tick marks, legends they must look up, decimals nobody needs. Edward Tufte called the share of ink that shows data the data-ink ratio, and decoration that shows nothing chartjunk. The practical reason to remove them is cognitive load: the mental effort a reader spends decoding the chart instead of understanding the data. Decluttering is a sequence you can apply to any chart, in any tool. The first two steps are the reusable helpers below; STYLE (lesson 2) already applies some of them to every chart.

def declutter(ax, hide=()):
    """Remove what carries no data: box, tick marks, grid, legend frame.
    hide=("y",) also drops a value axis whose numbers are already written on the marks."""
    for side in ("top", "right"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)
    ax.grid(False)
    if "y" in hide:
        ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
        ax.set_yticks([])
    if "x" in hide:
        ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
        ax.set_xticks([])
    if ax.get_legend() is not None:
        ax.get_legend().remove()
    return ax

def label_end(ax, x, y, text, color, dy=0):
    """A direct label just right of the last point, in the line's colour: no legend lookup."""
    ax.annotate(text, (x, y), xytext=(6, dy), textcoords="offset points",
                va="center", color=color, fontsize=10, annotation_clip=False)

conv = q("""SELECT platform, week_start, orders / sessions FROM 'data/weekly_platform.csv'
            WHERE days_in_data = 7 ORDER BY platform, week_start""")
series = {p: [(w, c) for pp, w, c in conv if pp == p] for p in ("web", "ios", "android")}

fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 6.4))
for step, ax in enumerate(axs.flat, start=1):
    for p, pts in series.items():
        xs, ys = zip(*pts)
        color = (ACCENT if p == "android" else GRAY) if step == 4 else None
        ax.plot(xs, ys, label=p, color=color, marker="o" if step == 1 else None,
                lw=2.4 if step == 4 and p == "android" else 1.6)
    if step == 1:                                    # 1. what the defaults give you
        for spine in ax.spines.values():
            spine.set_visible(True)
        ax.grid(True)
        ax.legend(frameon=True)

        for p, dy in (("web", 6), ("ios", -6), ("android", 0)):
            label_end(ax, xs[-1], last[p], p, MUTED, dy)
        ax.set_title("3. Label the lines, format the axis", fontsize=10)
    else:                                            # 4. gray context, one accent, a message
        label_end(ax, xs[-1], last["android"], "Android", ACCENT)
        label_end(ax, xs[-1], (last["web"] + last["ios"]) / 2, "Web, iOS", MUTED)
        ax.set_title("4. Android conversion collapsed; web and iOS did not", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
save(fig, "images/b8-steps.png")

Output:

saved images/b8-steps.png

Four versions of the same three-line chart of conversion by platform: defaults with box, grid, markers and legend; then without box and grid; then with direct labels and percent axis; finally gray lines for web and iOS and an orange Android line that drops, under a title stating the finding.

| Remove | Keep (it carries data or context) |
|---|---|
| Box and background, heavy grid lines, tick marks | The zero baseline of bars; light grid lines only if readers must read exact values |
| Legends that force a lookup | Direct labels at the end of each line or on each bar |
| Markers on every point, data labels on every point | One highlighted point, or labels on the few values that matter |
| Decimals beyond what the decision needs; rotated text | Units (once, in the title or axis), scaled numbers such as $20K |
| 3D, shadows, gradients, decorative icons | Source, definition and freshness notes, in small muted text |

passages.heading: 8. Declutter: remove everything that does not carry data
passages.text:
the title or axis), scaled numbers such as $20K |
| 3D, shadows, gradients, decorative icons | Source, definition and freshness notes, in small muted text |

> On the job: In a review, “declutter” is the most common feedback and the cheapest to fix. Put the steps in a shared theme once (a matplotlib style, a Power BI report theme) so every new chart starts quiet, and spend review time on the message instead of the gridlines.

> The main idea: declutter in a fixed order (frame and grid, then legends and axes, then colour and title) until every remaining mark carries data or context.

Read more: Chartjunk, Matplotlib: spines, Storytelling with Data (blog and challenges).

passages.heading: 9. Headline titles: say the finding, computed from the data
passages.text:
Part B · what should the title say?

A topic title names what is plotted (“Net sales by week”). A headline title (also called an action title) states what the reader should conclude (“Net sales fell 15 % week over week to $17.4K”). The subtitle underneath carries the definition, unit, population and period, in smaller muted text. Readers read the title first and often only the title, so it should do the work. A headline typed by hand goes stale at the next refresh; compute it from the same numbers the chart uses.

def headline(metric, this, last, fmt=fmt_money, period="week over week"):
    """A title that states the finding, computed from the same numbers as the chart."""
    change = this / last - 1
    if abs(change) < 0.005:
        return f"{metric} was flat {period} at {fmt(this)}"
    verb = "rose" if change > 0 else "fell"
    return f"{metric} {verb} {abs(change):.0%} {period} to {fmt(this)}"

assert headline("Net sales", 17428.16, 20527.65) == "Net sales fell 15% week over week to $17.4K"
assert headline("Orders", 350, 347, fmt=str) == "Orders rose 1% week over week to 350"
assert headline("Orders", 348, 347, fmt=str) == "Orders was flat week over week at 348"
print(headline("Net sales", 17428.16, 20527.65))

Output:

Net sales fell 15% week over week to $17.4K

The third test exposes a grammar wrinkle (“Orders was flat”): a generated headline is a template, so give it metric names that read well (“Order count was flat”) and test the edge cases, as here. Then use it as the chart title, with a subtitle for the definition:

Before

A weekly net sales line under the topic title Weekly Net Sales (USD), with a y-axis label and no explanation.

A topic title: the reader must work out the finding, and the chart does not say which weeks or which definition.

After

The same line under the headline Net sales fell 15% week over week to $17.4K, a muted subtitle with the definition and period, and the last point highlighted.

A computed headline, a subtitle with definition and period, the evidence highlighted.

weeks = q("""SELECT week_start, SUM(net_sales) FROM 'data/weekly_platform.csv'
              WHERE days_in_data = 7 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1""")
xs, ys = [w for w, _ in weeks], [s for _, s in weeks]
for name, title in (("before", "Weekly Net Sales (USD)"), ("after", headline("Net sales", ys[-1], ys[-2]))):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))

| Use a… | When | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Headline title | The page exists to report a finding (WBR, incident, executive update) | “Net sales fell 15 % week over week to $17.4K” |
| Question title | A section that the reader explores with filters | “Which platform changed?” |
| Topic title + dynamic headline | Self-service pages whose finding changes with every filter | Topic title, plus a headline measure that recomputes (lesson 13) |

> On the job: The Diagnosing metric changes write-up starts with exactly this kind of sentence; on a dashboard, the same sentence becomes the page title. Generated headlines are also testable: the lab’s pytest checks that the headline agrees with the data, so a broken metric cannot hide behind an old title.

> The main idea: title = the finding, generated from the data and tested; subtitle = definition, unit and period; annotation = the evidence on the chart.

Read more: Storytelling with Data (blog and challenges), Nielsen Norman Group: inverted pyramid, Matplotlib: annotate.

passages.heading: 10. Colour and numbers with purpose
passages.text:
Part B · what does each colour mean, and how many digits?

A few visual properties, such as colour, size and position, are noticed before conscious attention: they are called preattentive attributes. That is why one orange line among gray ones is found instantly, and why seven bright colours make the eye search. Choose the palette type from the data: a categorical palette (distinct hues) for unordered groups, a sequential palette (light to dark) for ordered magnitudes, and a diverging palette (two hues from a neutral midpoint) for above/below a target. Two rules hold everywhere: gray is the default and an accent colour marks the point; and a colour means the same thing on every chart of the page.

import matplotlib as mpl
palettes = {
    "gray + one accent": [GRAY, GRAY, ACCENT, GRAY, GRAY],
    "categorical (Okabe-Ito)": ["#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7"],
    "sequential (Greens)": [mpl.colormaps["Greens"](v) for v in (0.25, 0.4, 0.55, 0.7, 0.85)],
    "diverging (PuOr)": [mpl.colormaps["PuOr"](v) for v in (0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9)],
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 2.6))
for row, (name, colors) in enumerate(palettes.items()):
    for k, c in enumerate(colors):
        ax.add_patch(mpl.patches.Rectangle((k, -row - 0.8), 0.92, 0.7, color=c))
    ax.text(-0.2, -row - 0.45, name, ha="right", va="center", color=INK)
ax.set_xlim(-0.1, 6)
ax.set_ylim(-len(palettes), 0)
ax.set_axis_off()
save(fig, "images/b10-palettes.png")

PLATFORM_COLOURS = {"web": GRAY, "ios": GRAY, "android": ACCENT}   # fixed, not by position
print(PLATFORM_COLOURS["android"])

Output:

saved images/b10-palettes.png
#c2410c

Four rows of colour swatches: gray with one orange accent; six Okabe-Ito categorical colours; five sequential greens from light to dark; five diverging purple-to-orange colours with a light middle.

Numbers need the same discipline. Scale them (“$17.4K”, not “17428.16”), keep three or four significant digits, put the unit once, and show the change of a rate in percentage points (“▼2.6 pts”), because “conversion fell 17 %” and “conversion fell 2.6 points” describe the same move and readers confuse them.

def fmt_money(x):
    """$17.4K, $1.2M, $640: scaled, three or four significant figures, sign in front."""
    sign, x = ("-" if x < 0 else ""), abs(x)
    for size, suffix in ((1e9, "B"), (1e6, "M"), (1e3, "K")):

passages.heading: 10. Colour and numbers with purpose
passages.text:
three or four significant figures, sign in front."""
    sign, x = ("-" if x < 0 else ""), abs(x)
    for size, suffix in ((1e9, "B"), (1e6, "M"), (1e3, "K")):
        if round(x / size, 1) >= 1:          # round first: 999,950 must become $1.0M, not $1000.0K
            return f"{sign}${x / size:.1f}{suffix}"
    return f"{sign}${x:,.0f}"

def fmt_pct(x, nd=1):
    return f"{100 * x:.{nd}f}%"

def fmt_change(this, last, kind="relative"):
    """'▼15%' for a relative change, '▼2.6 pts' for a change in a rate: arrow + number, never colour alone."""
    if kind == "points":
        d, text = 100 * (this - last), f"{abs(100 * (this - last)):.1f} pts"
    else:
        d, text = 100 * (this / last - 1), f"{abs(100 * (this / last - 1)):.0f}%"
    arrow = "▲" if d > 0.05 else "▼" if d < -0.05 else "■"
    return arrow + text

for x in (17428.16, 999_950, 1_234_567, -640.4, 59.69):
    print(f"{x:>14,.2f} -> {fmt_money(x)}")
print(fmt_pct(0.12357), fmt_change(0.12357, 0.14931, "points"), fmt_change(17428.16, 20527.65))
assert fmt_money(999_950) == "$1.0M" and fmt_change(1.0, 1.0) == "■0%"

Output:

     17,428.16 -> $17.4K
    999,950.00 -> $1.0M
  1,234,567.00 -> $1.2M
       -640.40 -> -$640
         59.69 -> $60
12.4% ▼2.6 pts ▼15%

> On the job: Colour by meaning, not by position: when a filter removes “web”, a colour assigned by order makes Android change from orange to blue between two screenshots in the same meeting. In Power BI, set data colours per category in the report theme or the format pane, and set number formats (display units, decimals) on the measure so every visual inherits them.

> The main idea: gray by default, one accent for the point, a fixed colour per category; numbers scaled, rounded once, and rate changes in points.

Read more: Okabe and Ito: colour universal design, Matplotlib: choosing colormaps, UK Analysis Function: colours in charts, Stephen Few: practical rules for using colour (PDF).

passages.heading: 11. Headline-first dashboards: the inverted pyramid
passages.text:
Part C · what goes where on the page?

A headline-first dashboard is a page whose top-left element states the finding, with everything below it ordered by importance. It borrows the journalists’ inverted pyramid: conclusion first, evidence next, background last, so a reader who stops early still leaves with the point. Eye-tracking studies of screens show an F-pattern: people read the top lines left to right, then scan down the left edge. Put the headline where that scan starts and keep the most important tiles in the top rows.

layout = [["headline"] * 4,
          ["k1", "k2", "k3", "k4"],
          ["driver", "driver", "split", "split"],
          ["detail", "detail", "notes", "notes"]]
text = {"headline": "1 · Headline sentence + why (subtitle: period, freshness, partial data)",
        "k1": "2 · KPI card", "k2": "KPI card", "k3": "KPI card", "k4": "KPI card",
        "driver": "3 · The chart that proves the headline\n(trend with the event annotated)",
        "split": "3 · Where it happened\n(the segment that moved)",
        "detail": "4 · Detail: breakdown or table", "notes": "4 · Definitions, links, owner"}
fig, axd = plt.subplot_mosaic(layout, figsize=(9, 5.4), height_ratios=[0.55, 0.9, 2.1, 1.3])
for name, ax in axd.items():
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    for spine in ax.spines.values():
        spine.set_visible(True)
        spine.set_color(GRAY)
    ax.set_facecolor("#f4f6f4")
    ax.text(0.03, 0.5, text[name], transform=ax.transAxes, va="center", fontsize=9,
            color=ACCENT if name == "headline" else INK,
            fontweight="bold" if name == "headline" else "normal")
save(fig, "images/c11-wireframe.png")

Output:

saved images/c11-wireframe.png

A wireframe with four rows: a full-width headline bar; four equal KPI cards; a wide chart proving the headline next to a chart of the segment that moved; and a row with a detail breakdown and a notes panel.

| Tier | What goes there | Example: Leafy’s operations page |
|---|---|---|
| 1 · Headline | One sentence with a number and a direction, then one sentence of cause; a subtitle with period, time zone and data freshness | “1 in 5 SwiftPost parcels took a week or more” · “ParcelCo had none; both average about 3 days” |

passages.heading: 11. Headline-first dashboards: the inverted pyramid
passages.text:
cause; a subtitle with period, time zone and data freshness | “1 in 5 SwiftPost parcels took a week or more” · “ParcelCo had none; both average about 3 days” |
| 2 · KPI cards | 3–5 numbers the audience owns, each with a comparison | Parcels delivered within 4 days, share taking 7+ days, median days, delivery tickets |
| 3 · Drivers | One or two charts that prove the headline and locate it | Delivery-days histogram per carrier (lesson 7); weekly share of 7+ day parcels |
| 4 · Detail | Breakdowns, the formatted table, definitions, links, owner | Late parcels by region; the SLA definition; carrier contacts and the page owner |

Rules that keep the pyramid intact: one page, one audience, one question (leadership’s Monday question is not the operations team’s SLA question); tiers 1–3 fit on one screen without scrolling; no more than about six visuals; equal-sized tiles only when the items are equally important. The WBR table from Diagnosing metric changes belongs in tier 4 or on its own “numbers” page: it is for looking values up, the charts above it are for seeing the story.

> On the job: Sketch the four tiers on paper or in a slide before opening the BI tool, and show the sketch to the person who will read the page. Five minutes of “is this the question you ask on Monday?” saves the rebuild that usually follows a dashboard built from a list of requested metrics.

> The main idea: top-left states the finding; then KPI cards with comparisons, then the charts that prove and locate it, then detail. One page, one audience, one question.

Read more: Nielsen Norman Group: F-shaped reading pattern, Nielsen Norman Group: inverted pyramid, Power BI: tips for designing a great dashboard, Matplotlib: subplot_mosaic.

passages.heading: 12. KPI cards and when a table wins
passages.text:
Part C · what makes a number meaningful at a glance?

A KPI card is a tile showing one key number. A number alone means nothing (“Net sales $17.4K”: good or bad?); a card needs four parts: a label, the value, the change with an arrow and words (never colour alone), and a comparison that gives it meaning: last period, the same period last year, a target, or the normal range (here the median of the previous eight weeks). A sparkline is a tiny line chart without axes that can sit next to the number to show its recent shape.

def kpi_card(ax, label, value, change, note, bad=False):
    """Label, big number, change (arrow + words), and the comparison that gives it meaning."""
    ax.set_axis_off()
    put = lambda y, s, **kw: ax.text(0, y, s, transform=ax.transAxes, va="center", **kw)
    put(0.88, label.upper(), fontsize=9, color=MUTED)
    put(0.58, value, fontsize=22, fontweight="bold", color=INK)
    put(0.28, change, fontsize=11, color=ACCENT if bad else INK)
    put(0.06, note, fontsize=9, color=MUTED)

import statistics
weeks = q("""SELECT week_start, SUM(sessions), SUM(orders), SUM(net_sales)
              FROM 'data/weekly_platform.csv' WHERE days_in_data = 7 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1""")
(_, s0, o0, n0), (_, s1, o1, n1) = weeks[-2], weeks[-1]
normal = statistics.median(r[3] for r in weeks[-9:-1])      # the 8 weeks before this one

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11, 1.7))
kpi_card(axs[0], "Net sales", fmt_money(n1), fmt_change(n1, n0) + " vs last week",
         f"8-week median {fmt_money(normal)}", bad=n1 < n0)
kpi_card(axs[1], "Orders", f"{o1:,}", fmt_change(o1, o0) + " vs last week", f"last week {o0:,}", bad=o1 < o0)
kpi_card(axs[2], "Session conversion", fmt_pct(o1 / s1), fmt_change(o1 / s1, o0 / s0, "points")
         + " vs last week", f"last week {fmt_pct(o0 / s0)}", bad=o1 / s1 < o0 / s0)
kpi_card(axs[3], "Average order value", f"${n1 / o1:,.2f}", fmt_change(n1 / o1, n0 / o0)
         + " vs last week", f"last week ${n0 / o0:,.2f}")
save(fig, "images/c12-after.png")

with plt.style.context("default"):
    cur = q("""SELECT SUM(net_sales), SUM(orders), SUM(orders) / SUM(sessions),
                      SUM(net_sales) / SUM(orders)
               FROM 'data/weekly_platform.csv'
