Solution 10 · Stretch: sync one day from a complete snapshot

con.execute("""CREATE TABLE fct AS SELECT order_id, order_date::DATE AS order_date, status,
    false AS is_deleted FROM (VALUES (101, '2026-03-01', 'placed'), (102, '2026-03-01', 'shipped'),
    (103, '2026-03-01', 'placed'), (104, '2026-03-02', 'placed')) AS v(order_id, order_date, status)""")
con.execute("""CREATE TABLE snap AS FROM (VALUES (101, 'shipped'), (102, 'shipped'), (108, 'placed'))
               AS v(order_id, status)""")

def sync_day(day):
    if q("SELECT count(*) FROM snap")[0][0] == 0:
        raise ValueError("empty snapshot: refusing to delete a whole day")
    return q(f"""MERGE INTO fct AS t
USING snap AS s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND t.status IS DISTINCT FROM s.status THEN UPDATE SET status = s.status
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT VALUES (s.order_id, DATE '{day}', s.status, false)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND t.order_date = DATE '{day}' AND NOT t.is_deleted
    THEN UPDATE SET is_deleted = true""")[0][0]

print("changed:", sync_day("2026-03-01"), "| again:", sync_day("2026-03-01"))
rows = q("SELECT order_id, status, is_deleted FROM fct ORDER BY order_id")
print(rows)
assert rows == [(101, "shipped", False), (102, "shipped", False), (103, "placed", True),
                (104, "placed", False), (108, "placed", False)]
con.execute("DELETE FROM snap")
try:
    sync_day("2026-03-01")
except ValueError as e:
    print("empty file:", e)

Output:

changed: 3 | again: 0
[(101, 'shipped', False), (102, 'shipped', False), (103, 'placed', True), (104, 'placed', False), (108, 'placed', False)]
empty file: empty snapshot: refusing to delete a whole day

Without the t.order_date = … condition, order 104 (2 March) is also “not matched by source” and gets deleted: the snapshot is complete only for its own day. The second run changes nothing, and an empty file is rejected before any row is touched (in production, compare with yesterday’s count rather than only with zero). Common wrong answer: putting the date filter in USING or ON: the target rows of other days still reach the BY SOURCE branch. Interviewer follow-up: “What if an order moves from 1 to 2 March?” The 1 March snapshot deletes it and the 2 March snapshot must re-insert it, so process the day snapshots in one transaction, or move rows with a matched update when the key is found in another day’s snapshot.

passages.heading: What it is
passages.text:
uv is a Python development tool that manages Python versions, project dependencies, virtual environments, scripts, and command-line tools. Feature overview

A project holds code and configuration; an environment holds the interpreter and installed packages it uses. Separate environments let projects use different package versions without affecting one another. Usually each project has one .venv/, shared by its Python files.

Think of projects as kitchens and environments as their cupboards: each kitchen keeps the ingredients it needs. In C#, .csproj declares NuGet dependencies; in a uv project, pyproject.toml declares Python dependencies and .venv/ holds installed packages.

passages.heading: Main features
passages.text:
| Feature | Main commands |
| --- | --- |
| Install and select Python | uv python install, uv python pin |
| Create projects and manage dependencies | uv init, uv add, uv remove |
| Restore reproducible environments | uv lock, uv sync |
| Run project code and scripts | uv run |
| Run tools in separate environments | uvx, uv tool install |
| Manage environments with a pip-style interface | uv venv, uv pip install |

passages.heading: Common workflows
passages.text:
Run commands in a terminal. Versions, package names, folders, and filenames below are examples; substitute your own. Installation options

Install and select Python

uv python install 3.12         # Install a Python version
uv python list --only-installed
uv python find 3.12            # Show the interpreter path
uv python pin 3.12             # Select this version for the current project

Pinning writes .python-version; installing through uv does not automatically replace the system's python command. Python guide

Create a project and run code

uv init --app --no-package --python 3.12 my-project
cd my-project
uv add requests               # Add a runtime dependency
uv add --dev pytest ruff       # Add development tools
uv run main.py                # Run the generated starter script
uv run python --version       # Check the project's Python

For an existing folder, use uv init --app --no-package --python 3.12 inside it. Run project commands from the folder containing pyproject.toml. uv run prepares the environment automatically; activation is unnecessary.

Restore, inspect, and update dependencies

uv sync                       # Install the project's locked dependencies
uv sync --locked              # Fail if the lockfile needs updating (useful in CI)
uv tree                       # Inspect the dependency tree
uv lock --upgrade-package requests  # Update an existing dependency's lock entry
uv sync                       # Install the newly locked versions
uv remove requests            # Remove a dependency when no longer needed

| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| pyproject.toml | Project metadata and dependency requirements |
| .python-version | Selected Python version |
| uv.lock | Exact resolved package versions; managed by uv |
| .venv/ | Local environment; can be recreated with uv sync |

Commit configuration and the lockfile to version control; exclude .venv/. Project guide

Run an existing standalone script

Outside a project:

uv run --python 3.12 script.py
uv run --python 3.12 --with requests script.py  # Supply a dependency for this run
uv add --script script.py requests            # Store dependencies in the script
uv run script.py

Script guide

Run or install tools

uvx ruff check .              # Check code without adding Ruff to the project
uvx ruff format .             # Format code; modifies files

passages.heading: Common workflows
passages.text:
or install tools

uvx ruff check .              # Check code without adding Ruff to the project
uvx ruff format .             # Format code; modifies files
uv tool install ruff          # Install the tool for use across projects
uv tool list
uv tool upgrade ruff

uvx means uv tool run; . means the current folder. For a tool declared in a project, use uv run ruff check . to use its project version. Tool guide

Use an existing requirements.txt

uv venv --python 3.12
uv pip install --python .venv -r requirements.txt

Activate the environment before running python script.py directly:

# macOS/Linux (bash or zsh)
source .venv/bin/activate
python script.py
deactivate

# Windows PowerShell
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python script.py
deactivate

uv pip install installs packages into an environment; uv add also records project dependencies. Environment guide

passages.heading: Help and updates
passages.text:
uv --version
uv --help
uv add --help
uv self update                # For installations using the standalone installer

For package-manager installations, update uv through that package manager. Update guide

passages.heading: What it is
passages.text: DuckDB is an embedded SQL database built for analytics: filtering, joining, grouping, and summarizing data. It runs inside a local process without a separate database server and can query files directly. Use it through the command-line tool or a programming-language client. DuckDB overview

passages.heading: Main features
passages.text:
| Feature                               | Example                               |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Query CSV, Parquet, and JSON directly | SELECT * FROM 'data.csv';           |
| Analyze data with SQL                 | Joins, aggregations, window functions |
| Use temporary or saved databases      | duckdb or duckdb analytics.duckdb |
| Import data into tables               | CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT ...      |
| Export query results                  | COPY (...) TO ...                   |
| Run saved SQL scripts                 | .read query.sql                     |

passages.heading: Start or open a database
passages.text:
Run in a terminal; assume the DuckDB CLI is installed and available on PATH. Installation options

duckdb --version
duckdb                         # Temporary in-memory database

To open or create a saved database, use this instead:

duckdb analytics.duckdb

At the D prompt, enter SQL ending in ;. Dot commands such as .exit need no semicolon. In-memory tables disappear on exit; tables in a database file persist. CLI guide

passages.heading: Query files directly
Inspect and summarize data
passages.text:
DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM 'data.csv'; -- Column names and types
SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM 'data.csv';

For a file containing country and amount columns:

SELECT country, SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM 'data.csv'
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY total_amount DESC;

SQL introduction

passages.heading: Import a file into a .duckdb database
passages.text:
A .duckdb file is a database that can hold multiple tables. To turn data.csv into a saved database, create data.duckdb and import the CSV rows into a table named records. The CSV remains available; the database stores its own copy.

Step by step

1. In your terminal, from the folder containing data.csv, open or create the database:

duckdb data.duckdb

2. At DuckDB's D prompt, run:

CREATE TABLE records AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('data.csv');
SHOW TABLES;
SELECT * FROM records LIMIT 10;

Then type this to close DuckDB and return to your terminal:

.exit

3. Later, reopen the saved database from your terminal:

duckdb data.duckdb

At the D prompt, query the stored table:

SELECT * FROM records LIMIT 10;

The table is now stored in data.duckdb; reading it no longer requires the original CSV. Run CREATE TABLE only for the initial import. Later changes to the CSV do not automatically update the stored table. CSV import, Persistent databases

Import in one terminal command

As an alternative to the initial interactive import:

duckdb data.duckdb -c "CREATE TABLE records AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('data.csv');"

The same pattern works for other formats. These examples add separate tables to the database:

duckdb data.duckdb -c "CREATE TABLE parquet_records AS SELECT * FROM read_parquet('data.parquet');"
duckdb data.duckdb -c "CREATE TABLE json_records AS SELECT * FROM read_json('data.json');"

Parquet import, JSON import

passages.heading: Create a table or view
Export results
Run one query or a saved SQL file
passages.text:
From a terminal:

duckdb -c "SELECT * FROM 'data.csv' LIMIT 10;"
duckdb data.duckdb -c "SELECT * FROM records LIMIT 10;"

For an interactive session, first run duckdb data.duckdb in your terminal. Then, at its D prompt, load a saved SQL file with:

.read query.sql

In bash or zsh, input redirection also works:

duckdb < query.sql
duckdb data.duckdb < query.sql

CLI scripting

passages.heading: Daily analytics engineering (AE) and data engineering (DE) work
passages.text:
DuckDB can act as a local SQL workbench between receiving data and building or checking a production pipeline. These are practical applications of its file readers, SQL engine, and exporters.

| Daily task                          | How DuckDB helps                                                                        | Typical result                                     |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Inspect a new source                | Profile a vendor CSV or API JSON export; check types, missing values, and ranges        | Understand the schema before building ingestion    |
| Check data quality                  | Find duplicate keys, null required fields, and unexpected values                        | Identify bad records before loading them           |
| Develop transformations and metrics | Join extracts, test deduplication, and calculate aggregates on a representative dataset | Validate model logic and expected output           |
| Investigate a broken report         | Query source and warehouse exports side by side                                         | Isolate missing rows or changed values             |
| Prepare a batch                     | Combine files, normalize fields, and write Parquet                                      | Produce an output ready for the next pipeline step |
| Automate recurring checks           | Save SQL in a file and run it from a script or scheduled job                            | Repeat the same analysis for each delivery         |

Inspect and validate a delivery

For an orders.csv containing order_id and amount:

SUMMARIZE SELECT * FROM 'orders.csv'; -- Types, ranges, null percentages, etc.

SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS occurrences
FROM 'orders.csv'
WHERE order_id IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

SELECT * FROM 'orders.csv'
WHERE order_id IS NULL OR amount IS NULL;

For these example rules, the last two queries should return no rows. A query returning bad records still succeeds as SQL; an automated check must inspect its result and fail the job when violations exist. Profiling reference

Combine and transform a batch

For Parquet files containing country and numeric amount columns:

COPY (

passages.heading: Daily analytics engineering (AE) and data engineering (DE) work
passages.text:
the job when violations exist. Profiling reference

Combine and transform a batch

For Parquet files containing country and numeric amount columns:

COPY (
    SELECT UPPER(TRIM(country)) AS country, SUM(amount) AS total_amount
    FROM read_parquet('incoming/*.parquet')
    GROUP BY UPPER(TRIM(country))
) TO 'country_totals.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET);

The wildcard reads the matching files as one dataset. For files with different column layouts, read_parquet('incoming/*.parquet', union_by_name = true) aligns columns by name and fills missing columns with nulls; check that this matches the data contract. Multiple files, Parquet export

Reconcile source and target extracts

Suppose source.csv and target.parquet contain the same expected order_id and amount fields:

-- Rows in the source that are missing or different in the target.
SELECT order_id, amount FROM 'source.csv'
EXCEPT ALL
SELECT order_id, amount FROM 'target.parquet';

Run the comparison in reverse to find extra target rows. EXCEPT ALL also detects differences in duplicate counts. Align types, rounding, and the reporting period before comparing. Set operations

For a repeatable workflow: inspect → check → transform → compare → export. Save the queries in version control. Run a saved script from the terminal with:

duckdb -bail -c ".read pipeline.sql"

-bail stops on SQL errors; data-quality rules still need explicit pass/fail handling. CLI options

Use DuckDB for local analysis and batch work that fits the machine's CPU, memory, and disk. It can spill some workloads to disk when data exceeds memory. Validate SQL compatibility when moving logic to another database. Workload tuning

passages.heading: Useful commands inside DuckDB
passages.text:
.help
.timer on
.mode markdown
.mode duckbox
.exit

These list commands, enable timings, select Markdown output, restore default output, and exit. Use duckdb --help in the terminal for startup options. CLI reference
